types.description:
RecordAnnotation marks a message as a stored record: an event held in full by
 the record_store service and projectable to timeseries stores. A record
 IS an event (it flows through eventbus); every record declares a key field
 (unique identifier) and an owner field (ownership/identity).
types.schema_json:
{
  "name": "RecordAnnotation",
  "package": "spec",
  "description": "RecordAnnotation marks a message as a stored record: an event held in full by
 the record_store service and projectable to timeseries stores. A record
 IS an event (it flows through eventbus); every record declares a key field
 (unique identifier) and an owner field (ownership/identity).",
  "fields": [
    {
      "name": "key",
      "type": "string",
      "description": "key is the proto field name used as the unique record identifier.",
      "constraints": [
        "maximum size: 32768 bytes (default)"
      ],
      "constraint_infos": [
        {
          "rule": "default_max_size",
          "target": "field",
          "value_kind": "int",
          "int_value": 32768,
          "defaulted": true,
          "unit": "bytes",
          "source": "default_bound"
        }
      ]
    },
    {
      "name": "owner",
      "type": "string",
      "description": "owner is the proto field name that identifies the record's owner (e.g. spiffe_id).",
      "constraints": [
        "maximum size: 32768 bytes (default)"
      ],
      "constraint_infos": [
        {
          "rule": "default_max_size",
          "target": "field",
          "value_kind": "int",
          "int_value": 32768,
          "defaulted": true,
          "unit": "bytes",
          "source": "default_bound"
        }
      ]
    },
    {
      "name": "c2s",
      "type": "message",
      "description": "c2s, when present, exposes the record's publish RPC to external clients (via
 gateway). A record IS an event; this declares its producer surface the same
 way spec.event does. See EventAnnotation.",
      "message": {
        "name": "MethodC2SAnnotation",
        "package": "spec",
        "description": "MethodC2SAnnotation overrides service-level defaults for a single C2S RPC.
 Only valid on methods within a service_c2s service.",
        "fields": [
          {
            "name": "auth_disabled",
            "type": "bool",
            "description": "auth_disabled: no token required for this RPC.
 Used for public endpoints like OIDC discovery and JWKS."
          },
          {
            "name": "auth_any_user",
            "type": "bool",
            "description": "auth_any_user: any authenticated user can call this RPC
 (no entitlement check). Used for user-facing endpoints where
 any valid token is sufficient (e.g., token exchange, event streams)."
          },
          {
            "name": "target_namespace_field",
            "type": "string",
            "description": "target_namespace_field names the request field whose string value carries
 the target namespace path (e.g. "/io/example/tenant"). When set, the C2S
 authorizer enforces the level-or-below rule: the caller's namespace (from
 the bearer token's `namespace` claim) must equal the target namespace or
 be a strict path-segment ancestor of it. The field must exist on the
 request message and be of type string.

 Use the proto field name (snake_case as declared), e.g. "tenant_namespace".
 Leave unset for RPCs whose target is implicit (e.g. List* methods that
 scope the response to the caller's subtree at the handler).",
            "constraints": [
              "maximum size: 32768 bytes (default)"
            ],
            "constraint_infos": [
              {
                "rule": "default_max_size",
                "target": "field",
                "value_kind": "int",
                "int_value": 32768,
                "defaulted": true,
                "unit": "bytes",
                "source": "default_bound"
              }
            ]
          }
        ]
      }
    },
    {
      "name": "s2s",
      "type": "message",
      "description": "s2s, when present, exposes the record's publish RPC to internal services.
 It is the PRODUCER surface only; the consumer surface is s2s_subscribe.",
      "message": {
        "name": "MethodS2SAnnotation",
        "package": "spec",
        "description": "MethodS2SAnnotation overrides service-level defaults for a single S2S RPC.
 Only valid on methods within a service_s2s service.",
        "fields": [
          {
            "name": "auth_services",
            "type": "string",
            "description": "auth_services overrides the service-level default for this method.",
            "repeated": true,
            "constraints": [
              "maximum size: 1024 elements (default)",
              "maximum element size: 32768 bytes (default)"
            ],
            "constraint_infos": [
              {
                "rule": "default_max_size",
                "target": "field",
                "value_kind": "int",
                "int_value": 1024,
                "defaulted": true,
                "unit": "elements",
                "source": "default_bound"
              },
              {
                "rule": "default_max_element_size",
                "target": "element",
                "value_kind": "int",
                "int_value": 32768,
                "defaulted": true,
                "unit": "bytes",
                "source": "default_bound"
              }
            ]
          },
          {
            "name": "auth_disabled",
            "type": "bool",
            "description": "auth_disabled: this RPC handles its own authentication internally.
 The caller interceptor skips this RPC entirely. Used for bootstrap
 bootstrap token-minting RPCs where callers authenticate via
 credentials in the request body (cred pair JWT), not via bearer token."
          },
          {
            "name": "routing_only_services",
            "type": "string",
            "description": "routing_only_services narrows the TYPE a named subscriber's generated
 handler receives. Only meaningful on s2s_subscribe (the consumer half of a
 record/event surface); ignored everywhere else.

 Listing a service here GRANTS it nothing. Authorization stays auth_services'
 job alone; this field only narrows what an already-authorized subscriber's
 generated code is typed to see. auth_services keeps its existing meaning
 unchanged, and a subscriber not listed here keeps receiving the full
 message exactly as before (this is additive).

 For a listed subscriber, tacplus synthesizes

   message <T>RoutingEnvelope {
     string delivery_id = 1;  // <T>'s (spec.record).key field
     string recipient   = 2;  // <T>'s (spec.store_principal) field
     string namespace   = 3;  // <T>'s (spec.store_namespace) field
   }

 and that subscriber's generated Handler takes <T>RoutingEnvelope instead of
 <T>. Generation FAILS for a type flagged here that declares no
 (spec.store_principal) field (and likewise no (spec.record).key or
 (spec.store_namespace) field, or one of the three that is not a string):
 an envelope with an empty recipient is a routing table nobody can route
 with, so it is refused rather than emitted.

 WHAT THIS IS NOT. This is a TYPED boundary, not a memory guarantee. The
 FULL message body still arrives on the wire and is still fully decoded
 inside the subscriber's process; the generated dispatch projects the three
 fields out and drops the decoded message immediately afterwards. The body
 is therefore still reachable from a heap dump, a debugger, or anything that
 logs the decode buffer. What this field delivers is that the subscriber's
 own handler CANNOT be written against the body, because its argument type
 does not have one. Narrowing the wire itself is a separate, broker-side
 change and is not what this field does.",
            "repeated": true,
            "constraints": [
              "maximum size: 1024 elements (default)",
              "maximum element size: 32768 bytes (default)"
            ],
            "constraint_infos": [
              {
                "rule": "default_max_size",
                "target": "field",
                "value_kind": "int",
                "int_value": 1024,
                "defaulted": true,
                "unit": "elements",
                "source": "default_bound"
              },
              {
                "rule": "default_max_element_size",
                "target": "element",
                "value_kind": "int",
                "int_value": 32768,
                "defaulted": true,
                "unit": "bytes",
                "source": "default_bound"
              }
            ]
          }
        ]
      }
    },
    {
      "name": "min_group_size",
      "type": "int32",
      "description": "min_group_size is the smallest result size this record's size-only query
 surfaces will disclose. 0 / unset = no guard (additive, like owner_default).

 "Size-only" is the line: it covers the surfaces that return a size and no
 rows (Get<T>Count, Subscribe<T>Count, and the QueryStats.size that
 Update<T>Query returns for its newly-installed predicate). It deliberately
 does NOT cover List<T>'s total_count, which accompanies rows the caller has
 just been handed and so discloses nothing the rows themselves do not. A
 future change that makes a paged read return counts without rows has
 crossed that line."
    },
    {
      "name": "residency",
      "type": "message",
      "description": "residency is this record type's lifecycle, as two numbers.

   idle_seconds            no read and no write for this long -> the row
                           leaves MEMORY and lives on disk only. The next
                           touch reloads it; nothing is lost.
   deleted_max_age_seconds flagged deleted (see (spec.deleted_flag)) AND
                           older than this -> the row is purged at the next
                           sweep. Gone, not tiered.

 It is a data-lifecycle property of the type inside ONE store, not a choice
 of backing store: field 50024 (cold_store) was retired above because
 "tiering is internal to the store service", and that ruling stands. Tiering
 is a CONSEQUENCE of these two clocks, never a declared class — which is why
 the HOT/WARM/COLD preset enum is gone. There is no "never leaves memory";
 long-lived, config-shaped data just carries a long idle_seconds.

 Both numbers are per type and both always have a value: 0/unset means "apply
 the platform default" (see parser.DefaultResidencyIdleSeconds and
 parser.DefaultResidencyDeletedMaxAgeSeconds), never "never". Unset is
 therefore additive in the same way min_group_size and owner_default are.

 The idle clock lives ONLY in memory: a read never restamps
 (spec.store_epoch), never writes the event log, never touches disk.
 store_epoch keeps its own meaning — last WRITE, durable — and is what
 deleted_max_age_seconds measures the delete from.

 Example:
   option (spec.record) = {
     key: "accounting_id" owner: "spiffe_id"
     residency: {idle_seconds: 3600 deleted_max_age_seconds: 2592000}
   };",
      "message": {
        "name": "ResidencyPolicy",
        "package": "spec",
        "description": "ResidencyPolicy states a record type's lifecycle as two clocks. It replaced
 the HOT/WARM/COLD preset enum on 2026-09-20: tiering is a consequence of the
 clocks, not a declared class, and there is no "never leaves memory".

 Both fields: 0/unset means APPLY THE PLATFORM DEFAULT, never "never". The
 defaults are parser.DefaultResidencyIdleSeconds and
 parser.DefaultResidencyDeletedMaxAgeSeconds.",
        "fields": [
          {
            "name": "idle_seconds",
            "type": "int64",
            "description": "idle_seconds is how long a row may go with NO read and NO write before it is
 evicted from memory. It lives on disk beneath, complete and queryable, and
 the next touch reloads it — eviction is cache maintenance, never data loss.

 A read that counts is a Get by key and every row actually RETURNED by List
 or Watch. A Count, a Subscribe…Count, and a row that merely matches a
 predicate do not, or a dashboard counting a dataset would keep it resident."
          },
          {
            "name": "deleted_max_age_seconds",
            "type": "int64",
            "description": "deleted_max_age_seconds is how long a row flagged deleted (see
 (spec.deleted_flag)) survives after the delete write. Measured from that
 write's (spec.store_epoch). Past it the row is DEAD: never loaded into
 memory again, removed by the next sweep, not tiered and not readable.

 A record type that declares no (spec.deleted_flag) field has nothing for
 this clock to measure; it is carried anyway rather than refused, because a
 type that later gains the marker should not also have to gain a number."
          }
        ]
      }
    },
    {
      "name": "mutability",
      "type": "enum",
      "description": "mutability is whether this record type's rows may be changed after they are
 written. It is an ATTRIBUTE, orthogonal to residency: an immutable type
 (accounting) and a mutable one are both legitimate under any pair of
 residency clocks.

 Unset = MUTABILITY_CRUD, which is what every record does today.

 MUTABILITY_APPEND_ONLY is enforced at BOTH ends or it is decoration: the
 generator emits no row-mutating RPC for the type (ValidateMutabilityAnnotations
 refuses one at generation), and the generated service wrapper refuses to host
 one. This is the same two-ended shape (spec.record).min_group_size already has.",
      "enum_values": [
        {
          "name": "MUTABILITY_CRUD",
          "number": 1,
          "description": "CRUD: rows may be updated and deleted by key."
        },
        {
          "name": "MUTABILITY_APPEND_ONLY",
          "number": 2,
          "description": "APPEND_ONLY: rows are written once. No row-mutating RPC is generated for
 the type and the generated wrapper refuses to host one. Its disk slices are
 pure appends — sealed, checksummable units."
        }
      ]
    },
    {
      "name": "s2s_subscribe",
      "type": "message (recursive reference: spec.MethodS2SAnnotation)",
      "description": "s2s_subscribe, when present, exposes the record's SUBSCRIBE RPC to the named
 internal services. It is the consumer half of the pair whose producer half
 is s2s (field 4), and it exists because a topic has two boundaries and only
 one of them was declarable.

 A record's synthesized <Record>Bus topic wrapper hosts both PublishTo<T> and
 SubscribeTo<T>. s2s names who may PUBLISH. Nothing named who may CONSUME, so
 the subscribe RPC could only ever fall back to the state service's
 service-level list, which for a synthesized wrapper is resolved from the
 owning PACKAGE — and the record store that consumes every record topic is
 never in the owning package. Under per-topic authorization that is
 fail-closed: the store is denied on every topic it exists to read.

 Declared rather than inferred on purpose. Treating "the record store" as an
 implicitly authorized consumer would put an undeclared trust relationship in
 the generator with no proto anyone could read to audit it, and would silently
 grant or silently withhold access to any FUTURE consumer of a record topic.
 Who may read a record's stream is exactly as much a policy statement as who
 may write it, so it is written down in the same place, in the same shape.

 Same semantics as s2s: ["*"] is any authenticated service, an explicit list
 is exactly that list, and an absent annotation leaves the service-level
 default in place (i.e. this is additive — a record that declares none keeps
 today's behaviour).

 Example — a stored record consumed by the record store:
   option (spec.record) = {
     key: "accounting_id" owner: "spiffe_id"
     s2s: {auth_services: ["*"]}              // anyone may publish
     s2s_subscribe: {auth_services: ["recordstore"]}  // only the store may read
   };"
    },
    {
      "name": "s2s_read",
      "type": "message (recursive reference: spec.MethodS2SAnnotation)",
      "description": "s2s_read, when present, exposes this record's STORED-ROW READ surface to the
 named internal services — the record query plane's S2S half, hosted by the
 record store.

 It is the third member of a set whose other two already exist, and it is
 declared for exactly the reason s2s_subscribe is. A record type has three
 boundaries, not two:

   s2s            who may PUBLISH onto the record's topic  (write the stream)
   s2s_subscribe  who may CONSUME the record's topic       (tail the stream)
   s2s_read       who may READ the record's STORED ROWS    (query the store)

 Until this field existed the third boundary had no per-record declaration at
 all: every record's read RPCs carried the TRAIT-WIDE (spec.trait).auth_services
 list, so authorizing one service to read one record type authorized it to read
 EVERY record type in the fleet. That is precisely what
 decisions/mcp-generation-and-service-owned-data-2026-08-31.md §2 rules out —
 "The record store grants entitlements per service, per record type, INDEPENDENTLY" —
 and it is why that document's §1 calls the shared `query` trait superseded.
 The trait-wide list stays as the fallback for records that declare nothing,
 so this is additive exactly the way s2s_subscribe, min_group_size and
 owner_default are.

 Declared rather than inferred, on the same reasoning s2s_subscribe records:
 treating "the service that produces a record type" as an implicitly
 authorized reader would put an undeclared trust relationship in the
 generator with no proto anyone could read to audit it. A producer is not
 automatically a reader — §2's whole point is that read and write rights are
 granted independently — so the read right is written down where the other two
 are, in the same shape.

 PAIRED CONTROL. This is the grant half. The USE half is
 (spec.record_read) on the reading service's own proto, and the generator
 refuses a build where one is declared without the other: a service that
 declares (spec.record_read) on a record whose s2s_read does not name it
 fails generation rather than emitting a client that would be denied at
 runtime. Neither end can drift from the other, because neither end works
 alone.

 Same semantics as s2s and s2s_subscribe: ["*"] is any authenticated service,
 an explicit list is exactly that list, and an absent annotation leaves the
 trait-wide default in place.

 Declaring it also makes the record's KEY field an EQ criterion on the
 generated <T>Filter, whether or not the key carries its own
 (spec.query_field). Point-read-by-key is the read surface's most basic
 question and the plane could not express it otherwise; see
 record_map.go's keyFilterCriterion.

 Example — a record its own producer reads back:
   option (spec.record) = {
     key: "delivery_id" owner: "spiffe_id"
     s2s: {auth_services: ["messaging"]}
     s2s_subscribe: {auth_services: ["recordstore"]}
     s2s_read: {auth_services: ["messaging"]}
   };

 CROSS-TENANT DOCTRINE. auth_services is an identity grant, not a namespace
 scope: an authorized peer service reads FLEET-WIDE, across every tenant's
 rows, same as today. The C2S half of this same plane (spec.c2s_read below)
 pins the caller to their own token namespace; the S2S half deliberately does
 not, because narrowing a peer's reads to its own service namespace would not
 be a tenant boundary — it would break every cross-tenant peer aggregation
 this plane exists to serve (see the identical reasoning already written
 where it is enforced in code:
 pkg/internal/java/types/recordnamespace_gen.go's "C2S ONLY" comment).
 Which rows a peer may see is the auth_services decision, made before the
 handler runs — there is no second, namespace-shaped decision underneath it.

 This changes for ONE case: a tenant-owned service's own S2S RecordMap reads
 (a caller whose token namespace is /tenants/<t>, calling a service declared
 (spec.service).tenant_owned) gain the same pin+filters the C2S half already
 has — /system/* callers are unaffected and stay fleet-wide. That is separate,
 not-yet-generated runtime behavior (tenant-owned-service-identity goal item
 3); until it lands, every S2S reader — tenant-owned service or not — reads
 fleet-wide exactly as described above."
    },
    {
      "name": "c2s_read",
      "type": "message (recursive reference: spec.MethodS2SAnnotation)",
      "description": "c2s_read, when present, names the services allowed to RE-EXPOSE this
 record's stored rows TO THEIR OWN END USERS — the client-facing read plane,
 hosted by the reading service itself and never by the record store.

 It is the FOURTH boundary, and it is not a narrowing of the third:

   s2s            who may PUBLISH onto the record's topic  (write the stream)
   s2s_subscribe  who may CONSUME the record's topic       (tail the stream)
   s2s_read       who may READ the record's STORED ROWS    (query the store)
   c2s_read       who may DISCLOSE those rows TO A PERSON  (re-expose them)

 A service can hold s2s_read without c2s_read and that combination is the
 common one: read a record type to make an internal decision, and never show
 it to anyone. Making disclosure a separate grant is what keeps that
 distinction sayable, and it keeps the RECORD OWNER in the loop on every
 re-exposure of its data rather than only on the first read of it.

 TWO SEMANTIC DIFFERENCES FROM s2s_read, both deliberate:

   ["*"] FAILS GENERATION. On s2s_read the wildcard means "any authenticated
       peer inside the fleet", which is broad but is a statement someone
       might mean. "Any service may show my rows to any of its users" is not
       a statement anyone means to make, so it is refused rather than
       supported.
   c2s_read IMPLIES s2s_read for the same service, and the pair with the
       second half missing fails generation. The generated c2s handler's
       entire data path IS the s2s reader; a disclosure grant without a read
       grant is a surface that cannot execute.

 PAIRED CONTROL, exactly as s2s_read is. This is the grant half; the use half
 is (spec.record_read).c2s on the reading service's own proto, and
 ValidateRecordReadAnnotations refuses a build in which one is declared
 without the other, in both directions.

 Example — a record its producer also shows to its users:
   option (spec.record) = {
     key: "activity_id" owner: "spiffe_id"
     s2s:           {auth_services: ["assistant"]}
     s2s_subscribe: {auth_services: ["recordstore"]}
     s2s_read:      {auth_services: ["assistant"]}
     c2s_read:      {auth_services: ["assistant"]}
   };"
    },
    {
      "name": "private",
      "type": "bool",
      "description": "private marks this record type as belonging to exactly one principal —
 "a user's data and nobody else's, ever." Unset = MUTABILITY_CRUD's kind of
 default: today's behaviour, where a record's boundary is its tenant
 (namespace) and every service auth_services names may see every row in it.

 The FIELD NAME here is deliberately NOT reused for the parsed annotation
 key an author-facing check would grep for: it is carried internally as
 "record_private" (see descriptor.go), never bare "private" — that string
 already names the UNRELATED per-FIELD statedb marker
 (spec.private = 50013, "field can never be accessed by other services").
 The two guard completely different things at completely different scopes
 (a whole record type here, one state field there) and must never be
 confused by a validator or a human skimming annotation keys.

 What true means, once the generated pins land (tracked, not yet emitted by
 this field alone):
   - The row's owner is stamped from the caller's `sub` at write time,
     never caller-supplied — (spec.store_principal) already does the stamp.
   - Every generated read path (Get, List, Watch, Count, Sample, the
     record-plane readers, the S2S readers) pins owner == caller BEFORE any
     other criterion — a pin the query cannot see, not a filter it can
     widen.
   - No admin or tenant override: a tenant admin's token reads nothing from
     a private record, by generation, not by policy.
   - A service reading on a user's behalf must carry that user's delegated
     token (the `act` claim); its own service identity alone gets
     PERMISSION_DENIED.

 What this field alone already means, checked at generation time
 (ValidateRecordPrivateAnnotations):
   - the record MUST also declare (spec.store_principal) on the field
     holding its owner — that is what the generated pin will bind to, and
     a private record naming no such field has nothing to pin, the same
     "record nobody remembered to annotate" failure (spec.store_namespace)
     already refuses for the weaker tenant boundary.
   - the record refuses s2s_subscribe. A subscriber to a record's raw
     topic is a SERVICE, not a per-request caller — there is no principal
     in scope for a stream handler to pin against, so declaring both is a
     fleet-wide broadcast of every row ever written, the exact thing
     `private` exists to prevent.
   - the record refuses s2s_read, for the same reason one surface over. The
     record query plane's S2S half is peer-facing: the caller is a SERVICE
     identity, so there is no principal for the owner pin to bind to and the
     only gate the generated wrapper can apply is the (spec.store_namespace)
     tenant backstop. The plane therefore emits NO peer-facing read RPC for
     a private type (record_map.go), and the grant is refused here rather
     than accepted and authorizing nothing. c2s_read falls with it — the c2s
     reader's data path IS the s2s reader — and so does the matching
     (spec.record_read) on any would-be reader.
 s2s stays declarable: that is the WRITE topic, not a read. The read surface
 a private record keeps is the plane's C2S half, which carries a user token
 — the one identity the owner pin can bind to. That pin is the remaining,
 not-yet-emitted half of this annotation (decisions/
 identity-people-tenant-devices-private-2026-09-21.md §4).

 Example — a record only its own owner may ever read:
   option (spec.record) = {
     key: "rule_id" owner: "spiffe_id"
     s2s: {auth_services: ["profile"]}
     private: true
   };"
    }
  ]
}

 generated code is typed to see. auth_services keeps its existing meaning
 unchanged, and a subscriber not listed here keeps receiving the full
 message exactly as before (this is additive).

 For a listed subscriber, tacplus synthesizes

   message <T>RoutingEnvelope {
     string delivery_id = 1;  // <T>'s (spec.record).key field
     string recipient   = 2;  // <T>'s (spec.store_principal) field
     string namespace   = 3;  // <T>'s (spec.store_namespace) field
   }

 and that subscriber's generated Handler takes <T>RoutingEnvelope instead of
 <T>. Generation FAILS for a type flagged here that declares no
 (spec.store_principal) field (and likewise no (spec.record).key or
 (spec.store_namespace) field, or one of the three that is not a string):
 an envelope with an empty recipient is a routing table nobody can route
 with, so it is refused rather than emitted.

 WHAT THIS IS NOT. This is a TYPED boundary, not a memory guarantee. The
 FULL message body still arrives on the wire and is still fully decoded
 inside the subscriber's process; the generated dispatch projects the three
 fields out and drops the decoded message immediately afterwards. The body
 is therefore still reachable from a heap dump, a debugger, or anything that
 logs the decode buffer. What this field delivers is that the subscriber's
 own handler CANNOT be written against the body, because its argument type
 does not have one. Narrowing the wire itself is a separate, broker-side
 change and is not what this field does.

fields.name: min_group_size
fields.description:
min_group_size is the smallest result size this record's size-only query
 surfaces will disclose. 0 / unset = no guard (additive, like owner_default).

 "Size-only" is the line: it covers the surfaces that return a size and no
 rows (Get<T>Count, Subscribe<T>Count, and the QueryStats.size that
 Update<T>Query returns for its newly-installed predicate). It deliberately
 does NOT cover List<T>'s total_count, which accompanies rows the caller has
 just been handed and so discloses nothing the rows themselves do not. A
 future change that makes a paged read return counts without rows has
 crossed that line.

fields.name: residency
fields.description:
residency is this record type's lifecycle, as two numbers.

   idle_seconds            no read and no write for this long -> the row
                           leaves MEMORY and lives on disk only. The next
                           touch reloads it; nothing is lost.
   deleted_max_age_seconds flagged deleted (see (spec.deleted_flag)) AND
                           older than this -> the row is purged at the next
                           sweep. Gone, not tiered.

 It is a data-lifecycle property of the type inside ONE store, not a choice
 of backing store: field 50024 (cold_store) was retired above because
 "tiering is internal to the store service", and that ruling stands. Tiering
 is a CONSEQUENCE of these two clocks, never a declared class — which is why
 the HOT/WARM/COLD preset enum is gone. There is no "never leaves memory";
 long-lived, config-shaped data just carries a long idle_seconds.

 Both numbers are per type and both always have a value: 0/unset means "apply
 the platform default" (see parser.DefaultResidencyIdleSeconds and
 parser.DefaultResidencyDeletedMaxAgeSeconds), never "never". Unset is
 therefore additive in the same way min_group_size and owner_default are.

 The idle clock lives ONLY in memory: a read never restamps
 (spec.store_epoch), never writes the event log, never touches disk.
 store_epoch keeps its own meaning — last WRITE, durable — and is what
 deleted_max_age_seconds measures the delete from.

 Example:
   option (spec.record) = {
     key: "accounting_id" owner: "spiffe_id"
     residency: {idle_seconds: 3600 deleted_max_age_seconds: 2592000}
   };

message.name: ResidencyPolicy
message.description:
ResidencyPolicy states a record type's lifecycle as two clocks. It replaced
 the HOT/WARM/COLD preset enum on 2026-09-20: tiering is a consequence of the
 clocks, not a declared class, and there is no "never leaves memory".

 Both fields: 0/unset means APPLY THE PLATFORM DEFAULT, never "never". The
 defaults are parser.DefaultResidencyIdleSeconds and
 parser.DefaultResidencyDeletedMaxAgeSeconds.

fields.name: idle_seconds
fields.description:
idle_seconds is how long a row may go with NO read and NO write before it is
 evicted from memory. It lives on disk beneath, complete and queryable, and
 the next touch reloads it — eviction is cache maintenance, never data loss.

 A read that counts is a Get by key and every row actually RETURNED by List
 or Watch. A Count, a Subscribe…Count, and a row that merely matches a
 predicate do not, or a dashboard counting a dataset would keep it resident.

fields.name: deleted_max_age_seconds
fields.description:
deleted_max_age_seconds is how long a row flagged deleted (see
 (spec.deleted_flag)) survives after the delete write. Measured from that
 write's (spec.store_epoch). Past it the row is DEAD: never loaded into
 memory again, removed by the next sweep, not tiered and not readable.

 A record type that declares no (spec.deleted_flag) field has nothing for
 this clock to measure; it is carried anyway rather than refused, because a
 type that later gains the marker should not also have to gain a number.

fields.name: mutability
fields.description:
mutability is whether this record type's rows may be changed after they are
 written. It is an ATTRIBUTE, orthogonal to residency: an immutable type
 (accounting) and a mutable one are both legitimate under any pair of
 residency clocks.

 Unset = MUTABILITY_CRUD, which is what every record does today.

 MUTABILITY_APPEND_ONLY is enforced at BOTH ends or it is decoration: the
 generator emits no row-mutating RPC for the type (ValidateMutabilityAnnotations
 refuses one at generation), and the generated service wrapper refuses to host
 one. This is the same two-ended shape (spec.record).min_group_size already has.

enum_values.name: MUTABILITY_CRUD
enum_values.description: CRUD: rows may be updated and deleted by key.

enum_values.name: MUTABILITY_APPEND_ONLY
enum_values.description:
APPEND_ONLY: rows are written once. No row-mutating RPC is generated for
 the type and the generated wrapper refuses to host one. Its disk slices are
 pure appends — sealed, checksummable units.

fields.name: s2s_subscribe
fields.description:
s2s_subscribe, when present, exposes the record's SUBSCRIBE RPC to the named
 internal services. It is the consumer half of the pair whose producer half
 is s2s (field 4), and it exists because a topic has two boundaries and only
 one of them was declarable.

 A record's synthesized <Record>Bus topic wrapper hosts both PublishTo<T> and
 SubscribeTo<T>. s2s names who may PUBLISH. Nothing named who may CONSUME, so
 the subscribe RPC could only ever fall back to the state service's
 service-level list, which for a synthesized wrapper is resolved from the
 owning PACKAGE — and the record store that consumes every record topic is
 never in the owning package. Under per-topic authorization that is
 fail-closed: the store is denied on every topic it exists to read.

 Declared rather than inferred on purpose. Treating "the record store" as an
 implicitly authorized consumer would put an undeclared trust relationship in
 the generator with no proto anyone could read to audit it, and would silently
 grant or silently withhold access to any FUTURE consumer of a record topic.
 Who may read a record's stream is exactly as much a policy statement as who
 may write it, so it is written down in the same place, in the same shape.

 Same semantics as s2s: ["*"] is any authenticated service, an explicit list
 is exactly that list, and an absent annotation leaves the service-level
 default in place (i.e. this is additive — a record that declares none keeps
 today's behaviour).

 Example — a stored record consumed by the record store:
   option (spec.record) = {
     key: "accounting_id" owner: "spiffe_id"
     s2s: {auth_services: ["*"]}              // anyone may publish
     s2s_subscribe: {auth_services: ["recordstore"]}  // only the store may read
   };

fields.name: s2s_read
fields.description:
s2s_read, when present, exposes this record's STORED-ROW READ surface to the
 named internal services — the record query plane's S2S half, hosted by the
 record store.

 It is the third member of a set whose other two already exist, and it is
 declared for exactly the reason s2s_subscribe is. A record type has three
 boundaries, not two:

   s2s            who may PUBLISH onto the record's topic  (write the stream)
   s2s_subscribe  who may CONSUME the record's topic       (tail the stream)
   s2s_read       who may READ the record's STORED ROWS    (query the store)

 Until this field existed the third boundary had no per-record declaration at
 all: every record's read RPCs carried the TRAIT-WIDE (spec.trait).auth_services
 list, so authorizing one service to read one record type authorized it to read
 EVERY record type in the fleet. That is precisely what
 decisions/mcp-generation-and-service-owned-data-2026-08-31.md §2 rules out —
 "The record store grants entitlements per service, per record type, INDEPENDENTLY" —
 and it is why that document's §1 calls the shared `query` trait superseded.
 The trait-wide list stays as the fallback for records that declare nothing,
 so this is additive exactly the way s2s_subscribe, min_group_size and
 owner_default are.

 Declared rather than inferred, on the same reasoning s2s_subscribe records:
 treating "the service that produces a record type" as an implicitly
 authorized reader would put an undeclared trust relationship in the
 generator with no proto anyone could read to audit it. A producer is not
 automatically a reader — §2's whole point is that read and write rights are
 granted independently — so the read right is written down where the other two
 are, in the same shape.

 PAIRED CONTROL. This is the grant half. The USE half is
 (spec.record_read) on the reading service's own proto, and the generator
 refuses a build where one is declared without the other: a service that
 declares (spec.record_read) on a record whose s2s_read does not name it
 fails generation rather than emitting a client that would be denied at
 runtime. Neither end can drift from the other, because neither end works
 alone.

 Same semantics as s2s and s2s_subscribe: ["*"] is any authenticated service,
 an explicit list is exactly that list, and an absent annotation leaves the
 trait-wide default in place.

 Declaring it also makes the record's KEY field an EQ criterion on the
 generated <T>Filter, whether or not the key carries its own
 (spec.query_field). Point-read-by-key is the read surface's most basic
 question and the plane could not express it otherwise; see
 record_map.go's keyFilterCriterion.

 Example — a record its own producer reads back:
   option (spec.record) = {
     key: "delivery_id" owner: "spiffe_id"
     s2s: {auth_services: ["messaging"]}
     s2s_subscribe: {auth_services: ["recordstore"]}
     s2s_read: {auth_services: ["messaging"]}
   };

 CROSS-TENANT DOCTRINE. auth_services is an identity grant, not a namespace
 scope: an authorized peer service reads FLEET-WIDE, across every tenant's
 rows, same as today. The C2S half of this same plane (spec.c2s_read below)
 pins the caller to their own token namespace; the S2S half deliberately does
 not, because narrowing a peer's reads to its own service namespace would not
 be a tenant boundary — it would break every cross-tenant peer aggregation
 this plane exists to serve (see the identical reasoning already written
 where it is enforced in code:
 pkg/internal/java/types/recordnamespace_gen.go's "C2S ONLY" comment).
 Which rows a peer may see is the auth_services decision, made before the
 handler runs — there is no second, namespace-shaped decision underneath it.

 This changes for ONE case: a tenant-owned service's own S2S RecordMap reads
 (a caller whose token namespace is /tenants/<t>, calling a service declared
 (spec.service).tenant_owned) gain the same pin+filters the C2S half already
 has — /system/* callers are unaffected and stay fleet-wide. That is separate,
 not-yet-generated runtime behavior (tenant-owned-service-identity goal item
 3); until it lands, every S2S reader — tenant-owned service or not — reads
 fleet-wide exactly as described above.

fields.name: c2s_read
fields.description:
c2s_read, when present, names the services allowed to RE-EXPOSE this
 record's stored rows TO THEIR OWN END USERS — the client-facing read plane,
 hosted by the reading service itself and never by the record store.

 It is the FOURTH boundary, and it is not a narrowing of the third:

   s2s            who may PUBLISH onto the record's topic  (write the stream)
   s2s_subscribe  who may CONSUME the record's topic       (tail the stream)
   s2s_read       who may READ the record's STORED ROWS    (query the store)
   c2s_read       who may DISCLOSE those rows TO A PERSON  (re-expose them)

 A service can hold s2s_read without c2s_read and that combination is the
 common one: read a record type to make an internal decision, and never show
 it to anyone. Making disclosure a separate grant is what keeps that
 distinction sayable, and it keeps the RECORD OWNER in the loop on every
 re-exposure of its data rather than only on the first read of it.

 TWO SEMANTIC DIFFERENCES FROM s2s_read, both deliberate:

   ["*"] FAILS GENERATION. On s2s_read the wildcard means "any authenticated
       peer inside the fleet", which is broad but is a statement someone
       might mean. "Any service may show my rows to any of its users" is not
       a statement anyone means to make, so it is refused rather than
       supported.
   c2s_read IMPLIES s2s_read for the same service, and the pair with the
       second half missing fails generation. The generated c2s handler's
       entire data path IS the s2s reader; a disclosure grant without a read
       grant is a surface that cannot execute.

 PAIRED CONTROL, exactly as s2s_read is. This is the grant half; the use half
 is (spec.record_read).c2s on the reading service's own proto, and
 ValidateRecordReadAnnotations refuses a build in which one is declared
 without the other, in both directions.

 Example — a record its producer also shows to its users:
   option (spec.record) = {
     key: "activity_id" owner: "spiffe_id"
     s2s:           {auth_services: ["assistant"]}
     s2s_subscribe: {auth_services: ["recordstore"]}
     s2s_read:      {auth_services: ["assistant"]}
     c2s_read:      {auth_services: ["assistant"]}
   };

fields.name: private
fields.description:
private marks this record type as belonging to exactly one principal —
 "a user's data and nobody else's, ever." Unset = MUTABILITY_CRUD's kind of
 default: today's behaviour, where a record's boundary is its tenant
 (namespace) and every service auth_services names may see every row in it.

 The FIELD NAME here is deliberately NOT reused for the parsed annotation
 key an author-facing check would grep for: it is carried internally as
 "record_private" (see descriptor.go), never bare "private" — that string
 already names the UNRELATED per-FIELD statedb marker
 (spec.private = 50013, "field can never be accessed by other services").
 The two guard completely different things at completely different scopes
 (a whole record type here, one state field there) and must never be
 confused by a validator or a human skimming annotation keys.

 What true means, once the generated pins land (tracked, not yet emitted by
 this field alone):
   - The row's owner is stamped from the caller's `sub` at write time,
     never caller-supplied — (spec.store_principal) already does the stamp.
   - Every generated read path (Get, List, Watch, Count, Sample, the
     record-plane readers, the S2S readers) pins owner == caller BEFORE any
     other criterion — a pin the query cannot see, not a filter it can
     widen.
   - No admin or tenant override: a tenant admin's token reads nothing from
     a private record, by generation, not by policy.
   - A service reading on a user's behalf must carry that user's delegated
     token (the `act` claim); its own service identity alone gets
     PERMISSION_DENIED.

 What this field alone already means, checked at generation time
 (ValidateRecordPrivateAnnotations):
   - the record MUST also declare (spec.store_principal) on the field
     holding its owner — that is what the generated pin will bind to, and
     a private record naming no such field has nothing to pin, the same
     "record nobody remembered to annotate" failure (spec.store_namespace)
     already refuses for the weaker tenant boundary.
   - the record refuses s2s_subscribe. A subscriber to a record's raw
     topic is a SERVICE, not a per-request caller — there is no principal
     in scope for a stream handler to pin against, so declaring both is a
     fleet-wide broadcast of every row ever written, the exact thing
     `private` exists to prevent.
   - the record refuses s2s_read, for the same reason one surface over. The
     record query plane's S2S half is peer-facing: the caller is a SERVICE
     identity, so there is no principal for the owner pin to bind to and the
     only gate the generated wrapper can apply is the (spec.store_namespace)
     tenant backstop. The plane therefore emits NO peer-facing read RPC for
     a private type (record_map.go), and the grant is refused here rather
     than accepted and authorizing nothing. c2s_read falls with it — the c2s
     reader's data path IS the s2s reader — and so does the matching
     (spec.record_read) on any would-be reader.
 s2s stays declarable: that is the WRITE topic, not a read. The read surface
 a private record keeps is the plane's C2S half, which carries a user token
 — the one identity the owner pin can bind to. That pin is the remaining,
 not-yet-emitted half of this annotation (decisions/
 identity-people-tenant-devices-private-2026-09-21.md §4).

 Example — a record only its own owner may ever read:
   option (spec.record) = {
     key: "rule_id" owner: "spiffe_id"
     s2s: {auth_services: ["profile"]}
     private: true
   };

types.name: RecordRead
types.description:
RecordRead declares that this service reads a (spec.record) type's STORED
 ROWS through the record query plane's S2S half.

 The USE half of the paired control whose grant half is
 (spec.record).s2s_read. See spec.record_read in the FileOptions block above
 for what it generates and why the transport dependency is implied rather than
 restated.

fields.name: record
fields.description:
record is the fully-qualified record message name, "package.Message"
 (e.g. "messaging.Message"). Proto package names are globally unique, so no
 file path is needed; tacplus resolves the name to its declaring file.

 A name that resolves to no message, or to a message carrying no
 (spec.record), is a hard generation failure — the same fail-loud posture
 (spec.record).key already takes for a key naming a field that does not
 exist.

fields.name: c2s
fields.description:
c2s, when present, asks for a CLIENT-FACING read surface over this record's
 rows, emitted into THIS service's own proto as a synthesized sibling
 service (`<Service>Records`) carrying Get<T> and List<T>.

 Absent — which is every declaration that predates this field — the reader
 gets the s2s typed reader and nothing else, byte for byte as before.

 The grant half is (spec.record).c2s_read on the record, and it must name
 this service. See the C2SScope comments for what the emitted surface is
 allowed to return.

message.name: RecordReadC2S
message.description:
RecordReadC2S is the USE half of the client-facing read plane: what
 (spec.record_read).c2s asks tacplus to emit.

fields.name: scope
fields.description: scope names which rows the surface may return. See C2SScope.

enum_values.name: C2S_SCOPE_PRINCIPAL
enum_values.description:
PRINCIPAL: rows whose owning-principal field equals the caller's subject,
 AND whose namespace equals the caller's tenant. "My own rows."

 The principal field is resolved exactly as the egress row filter resolves
 it — (spec.store_principal) on a record field, else (spec.record).owner —
 and ONLY when that field is also an EQ criterion on the generated <T>Filter.
 When it resolves to nothing, generation FAILS rather than degrading to a
 tenant-wide read: on ScottyActivity and AccountingRecord the declared
 `owner` is the PUBLISHING SERVICE, so a filter on it would show a human
 every row in its tenant while looking like it showed them their own.

enum_values.name: C2S_SCOPE_NAMESPACE
enum_values.description:
NAMESPACE: every row in the caller's tenant, with no principal narrowing.
 A legitimate shape — an org-wide audit feed — but a disclosure decision, so
 it must be written down and can never be what absence means.

 DECLARED BUT NOT IMPLEMENTED in v1: generation fails with an explicit
 "declared but not implemented" error. The value exists so it cannot be
 invented twice with two meanings.

fields.name: exposure
fields.description:
exposure is stamped onto the emitted RPCs' (spec.rpc). INTERNAL (the
 default) keeps the surface inside the cluster boundary; EXTERNAL publishes
 it through the gateway, which is what a mobile or browser client needs.

enum_values.name: RPC_EXPOSURE_INTERNAL
enum_values.description: RPC_EXPOSURE_INTERNAL: reachable only from inside the cluster boundary.

enum_values.name: RPC_EXPOSURE_EXTERNAL
enum_values.description: RPC_EXPOSURE_EXTERNAL: reachable from outside the cluster boundary.

types.description:

 (spec.record_read).c2s asks tacplus to emit.

types.name: RecordStoreAnnotation
types.description:
RecordStoreAnnotation marks a service proto as the full-record store.
 Services with this annotation auto-subscribe to EventBus topics that publish
 the record types they store (currently spec.record). Hot/cold tiering is
 internal to the service.

types.name: RedactOption
types.description:
RedactOption configures a field (or, at message level via (spec.data_entitlement),
 a whole message default) with a data-entitlement mode.

types.name: RequiresDeviceWhen
types.description:
RequiresDeviceWhen is the condition (spec.rpc).requires_device_when gates on.
 Both halves are resolved at generation time against the rpc's request
 descriptor: an unknown field, a field that is not a plain string or enum, or
 an enum value name the enum does not have all fail generation rather than
 becoming a comparison that is silently never true.

fields.name: field
fields.description:
field is a top-level field name on the RPC's request message. It must be a
 plain (non-repeated, non-map, no explicit presence) string or enum field.

fields.name: equals
fields.description:
equals is the value that field must hold for the gate to apply — the enum
 value's short name (e.g. "RULE_EFFECT_DELEGATION") for an enum field, or
 the literal string for a string field.
