types.name: MintDelegateOfflineTokenRequest
types.description:
MintDelegateOfflineTokenRequest is the input for runtime delegation (C2S).
 The user's own identity is the caller's bearer token; only the delegate to
 bind the Offline Token to, and an optional narrowing scope, are carried here.

fields.name: delegate_name
fields.description:
delegate_name is the Delegate.name of the agent this OT is minted for. It
 becomes the token's act claim. Paired with delegate_namespace: the name
 alone does not identify a delegate.

fields.name: delegate_namespace
fields.description:
delegate_namespace is the Delegate.tenant_namespace completing the
 (name, namespace) key. Empty means the /system delegate of that name.

fields.name: scope
fields.description:
scope narrows the delegation below the platform default. Unset means the
 platform default; every later mint intersects fresh OPA output with this,
 so it can only ever narrow, never widen.

message.name: TokenEntitlements
message.description:
TokenEntitlements holds compressed C2S entitlements embedded in user tokens.
 OPA returns this structure directly; the token authority embeds it in the JWT service_entitlements claim.
 grants may contain exact or wildcard grant tokens; generated helpers normalize them before authorization.

fields.name: grants
fields.description: grants is a flat list of generated grant tokens, e.g. PACKAGE_SERVICE_RPC.

fields.name: data_grants
fields.description:
data_grants is a flat list of generated data-entitlement grant tokens, e.g.
 PACKAGE_RECORD_FIELD. A data grant names what the caller may SEE RAW: a MAY_*
 redact field with a matching grant egresses raw; absent a grant the field gets
 its most-protective default (MAY_REDACT -> REDACT, MAY_ANONYMIZE -> ANONYMIZE).
 Stamped by OPA at token-exchange time alongside grants — an identity property,
 never a request parameter.

fields.name: principal_scope
fields.description:
principal_scope is how wide the caller's authority over PRINCIPALS is, as a
 spec.PrincipalScope enum VALUE NAME (e.g. "PRINCIPAL_SCOPE_ANY"). It is the
 claim the generated (spec.owner_default) guard reads to tell an owner acting
 on its own row from a principal whose authority is wider than itself.
 Absent, empty, PRINCIPAL_SCOPE_UNSPECIFIED and PRINCIPAL_SCOPE_SELF_ONLY all
 mean self-scoped: the guard fails closed, so a policy that stamps nothing
 leaves every caller exactly as narrow as it is today.
 Stamped by OPA at token-exchange time alongside grants — an identity
 property, never a request parameter.

fields.name: azp
fields.description:
azp restricts these entitlements to tokens with a matching authorized party.
 Empty = entitlements apply regardless of azp.

types.name: MintDelegateOfflineTokenResponse
types.description:
MintDelegateOfflineTokenResponse returns ONLY the one-time code. The Offline
 Token itself is withheld and never transits the user's client; the delegate
 obtains it via RedeemDelegateOfflineToken.

fields.name: code
fields.description:
code is the short-lived, single-use redemption code the user hands to the
 delegate. Opaque; kernel holds the minted OT against it.

fields.name: expires_at_ms
fields.description: expires_at_ms is when the code stops being redeemable, epoch milliseconds.

types.name: MintDelegatedTokenRequest
types.description:

 minting. The delegate's own identity is verified from its S2S bearer token
 (Authorization header), not carried in the request — only the Grant id it
 holds and asserts is.

fields.name: grant_id
fields.description: grant_id is the opaque Grant.id the caller (a delegate) holds and asserts.

 The token can be in either parsed form (header/payload maps) or encoded form
 (JWT compact serialization).

fields.name: header
fields.description: Header contains the JWT header claims (e.g., alg, typ, kid)

fields.name: payload
fields.description:
JWT payload claims stored as string values. Numeric claims (exp, iat, nbf)
 are stored as decimal string representations (e.g., "1742403600").

fields.name: signature
fields.description: Signature is the base64url-encoded signature

fields.name: base64
fields.description:
Base64 contains the complete JWT compact serialization
 (header.payload.signature). Each segment is base64url-encoded, but the
 dotted compact string is not itself a single base64 value.

types.name: MintExternalServiceTokenRequest
types.description:
MintExternalServiceTokenRequest is the input for minting a service's OWN
 identity token for an off-cluster audience (e.g. a workload identity
 federation jwt-bearer assertion). The token minter answers with
 TokenMintResponse.access_token: sub = the caller's SPIFFE ID, aud = aud,
 iss = the fleet issuer, signed ES256, a fresh jti on every call, and an exp
 no more than 600 seconds out. Callers must not cache or reuse the result.

fields.name: input_token
fields.description:
input_token is the caller's kernel-signed service token (the
 self-authenticating credential, as on MintServiceToken's exchange path).

fields.name: aud
fields.description: aud is the external audience, e.g. "https://api.anthropic.com".

fields.name: exp
fields.description:
exp is the requested expiry (Unix seconds); the minter rejects a value
 more than 600 seconds out.

types.name: MintServiceTokenRequest
types.description:
MintServiceTokenRequest is the input for service-token minting.

 Credential proof: exactly one of input_token, cloud_proof, kubernetes_token,
 or external_oidc_token authenticates the caller. The kernel groups these into a
 oneof (credential_proof) and routes on the discriminator; clients may set a
 single flat field — proto3 oneof membership is a property of the parsing
 descriptor, so a flat field at the same tag/wire type is decoded into the
 matching oneof case and remains wire-compatible.

message.name: CloudIdentityProof
message.description:
CloudIdentityProof carries a cloud-native identity assertion.
 Exactly one of presigned_request or identity_token must be set,
 determined by the cloud vendor.

fields.name: vendor
fields.description: vendor identifies the cloud provider that issued this proof.

fields.name: presigned_request
fields.description:
presigned_request is used for AWS: a signed STS GetCallerIdentity
 request that the server executes to verify the caller's IAM identity.
 The request has a short TTL to prevent replay.

message.name: PresignedHttpRequest
message.description:
PresignedHttpRequest carries a pre-signed HTTP request that the server
 executes on behalf of the caller. For AWS, this is a SigV4-signed
 STS GetCallerIdentity request.

fields.name: method
fields.description: method is the HTTP method (e.g. "POST").

fields.name: url
fields.description: url is the full request URL including query parameters.

fields.name: headers
fields.description:
headers are the signed HTTP headers that must be forwarded verbatim.
 Keys are header names, values are header values.

fields.name: body
fields.description: body is the request body (e.g. "Action=GetCallerIdentity&Version=2011-06-15").

fields.name: identity_token
fields.description:
identity_token is used for GCP and Azure: a signed JWT or OAuth2
 token obtained from the cloud metadata service. The server validates
 it against the provider's public JWKS/OIDC endpoint.

enum_values.name: TOKEN_PURPOSE_REFRESH
enum_values.description: Refresh token — long-lived, used to obtain new access tokens.

enum_values.name: TOKEN_PURPOSE_ACCESS
enum_values.description: Access token — short-lived, carries entitlements for a specific service.

enum_values.name: TOKEN_PURPOSE_SERVICE
enum_values.description: Service token — access token scoped to a specific target service (aud).

enum_values.name: TOKEN_PURPOSE_BOOTSTRAP
enum_values.description:
Bootstrap token — very short-lived, used to bootstrap a child workload.
 Parent mints this via WorkloadMint and passes it to the child process.
 Child exchanges it with the token authority for a real access + refresh pair.

enum_values.name: TOKEN_PURPOSE_LOCALITY
enum_values.description:
Locality token — rotated by parent, shared with all children.
 Children present this on refresh to prove they can still reach their parent.

fields.name: kubernetes_token
fields.description:
kubernetes_token is a projected Kubernetes service-account JWT carrying the
 configured kernel workload audience ("kernel"; it must NOT
 be the "kmaker" audience). The kernel maps the verified
 (namespace, service account) to a Delegate. Tag 8 matches the kernel's
 credential_proof oneof so a flat field here is wire-compatible.

fields.name: external_oidc_token
fields.description:
external_oidc_token is an OIDC ID token minted natively by tenant-owned CI
 (e.g. a GitHub Actions OIDC token or a GitLab CI ID token), presented so
 that CI may act as a tenant-scoped service. The kernel verifies the token
 against the tenant's enrolled-issuer list (KernelTenantConfig) and maps the
 verified issuer plus claims to an enrolled config via a Delegate matcher.
 Tag 9 matches the kernel's credential_proof oneof so a flat field here is
 wire-compatible.

types.name: MintUserTokenRequest
types.description: MintUserTokenRequest is the input for user-token minting.

fields.name: broker_kind
fields.description:
broker_kind is the class of proof this call presents. Kernel refuses if
 the resolved Delegate's auth_broker_kinds does not contain it.

enum_values.name: AUTH_BROKER_KIND_IDP
enum_values.description:
An IdP assertion the broker has already validated (oauth). Kernel
 trusts the broker's attestation — today's behaviour, unchanged.

enum_values.name: AUTH_BROKER_KIND_DEVICE
enum_values.description:
Possession of a personal principal's device key. Kernel verifies the
 proof itself; may mint only a /users/<xid> personal token.

enum_values.name: AUTH_BROKER_KIND_EMAIL_LINK
enum_values.description: Control of an email address a tenant authorized.

enum_values.name: AUTH_BROKER_KIND_PERSONAL_LINK
enum_values.description: An admin-issued link accepted on the member's own device.

fields.name: proof_token
fields.description:
proof_token is the principal-held proof (a device- or link-signed JWT)
 that kernel verifies ITSELF. Required for every kind except IDP.

types.name: RedeemDelegateOfflineTokenRequest
types.description:
RedeemDelegateOfflineTokenRequest is the input for a delegate redeeming a
 one-time code (S2S). The delegate's own identity is verified from its S2S
 bearer token, not carried here — kernel requires it to equal the withheld
 token's act claim.

types.name: WorkloadMintRequest
types.description:
WorkloadMintRequest mints a child workload identity. The child's SPIFFE ID is
 the parent's spiffe_id + "/workloads/" + workload_name; the parent is the
 caller, unless the caller is a workload broker naming another service.

fields.name: terminal
fields.description: terminal marks the child as unable to mint further children.

fields.name: exp
fields.description: exp is the desired expiry for the bootstrap token (0 = kernel default).

fields.name: parent_spiffe_id
fields.description:
parent_spiffe_id roots the child under another service's identity: the
 coop minting a pigeon for the dog that asked for it, so the pigeon is
 that tenant's by construction. Only a caller the authority configures as
 a workload broker may set it (kernel Delegate.workload_broker); for
 anyone else it is refused. Empty: the parent is the caller.

message.name: X509CertRequest
message.description:
X509CertRequest represents a certificate signing request (CSR) for generating X.509 certificates.
 It contains the public key to be certified, validity period, key usage constraints,
 and issuer information needed to create a signed certificate.

fields.name: key
fields.description: Key is the public key to be certified

message.name: PublicKey
message.description:
PublicKey represents a public cryptographic key.
 The key is stored as a base64-encoded PEM block in PKIX format.
 Use NewProtoPublicKey() in Go or similar constructors in other languages to create.

fields.name: id
fields.description: Id is a unique identifier for the key (corresponds to kid in JWK)

fields.name: base64
fields.description: Base64 contains the base64url-encoded PEM public key block

fields.name: created
fields.description:
Created is the Unix epoch timestamp (seconds) when the key was created
 Valid range: 1735689600 (2025-01-01) to 8045740800 (2225-01-01)

fields.name: exp
fields.description: Exp is the expiration timestamp (Unix time) for the certificate

fields.name: metadata
fields.description: Metadata contains additional information about the certificate request

fields.name: key_usage
fields.description: KeyUsage specifies the intended cryptographic operations (e.g., "digitalSignature", "keyEncipherment")

enum_values.description: X509KeyUsageDigitalSignature indicates digital signature usage

fields.name: round
fields.description:
round is unset on the first event of a SubscribeTrace stream, which
 carries only the server-generated trace_id (see eventbus's
 WatchTraceHandler); it is set on every subsequent per-hop event.

message.name: TraceRound
message.description: TraceRound identifies a single service hop in a traced request.

fields.name: rpc
fields.description:
rpc identifies the specific service and method being traced using the
 generated AccountingMethod enum type. Exactly one field is set to the
 corresponding RPC enum value; all others default to 0.

message.name: AccountingMethod
message.description: AccountingMethod identifies which RPC an event relates to.

fields.name: kind
fields.description: kind classifies where in the request lifecycle this event was emitted.

fields.name: error
fields.description:
error is set on response events when the request failed (auth rejection,
 backend unavailable, handler error, etc.). Empty on success.

types.name: TraceRequest
types.description:
TraceRequest replaces google.protobuf.Empty on the gRPC wire for RPCs with
 empty input types. This ensures every RPC can be traced, even read-only
 endpoints that take no parameters. The handler interface stays arg-free —
 TraceRequest has no user-meaningful fields.

types.name: TraceRound
types.description: TraceRound identifies a single service hop in a traced request.

enums.name: TraceEventKind
enums.description:
TraceEvent is published per-hop to the trace topic when a traced message
 passes through a service. EventBus matches these to active WatchTrace streams
 by trace_id. Ordering is determined by timestamp_ms in TraceRound.
 TraceEventKind classifies the trace event within the request lifecycle.
 External events are emitted by the gateway (edge); internal events are
 emitted by backend services.

# tacplus Registry

This file is embedded in `registry.json` and describes how to navigate it.

## Overview

This registry describes a tacplus-generated service mesh with:
- **219** message types across **42** packages
- **26** RPCs across **9** gRPC services
- **3** state boundaries

## Structure

The registry is a recursive `PackageNode` tree. Each node has:
- `name` — short package name
- `full_path` — slash-separated path from root
- `children` — sub-packages
- `proto_packages` — declared protobuf package names represented by a leaf node
- `vservices` — virtual service identities declared by proto files in a leaf node
- `client_dependencies` — declared `grpc_*_client` edges with `surface_kind`
- `types` — message type descriptors (`TypeInfo`)
- `rpcs` — RPC descriptors (`RpcInfo`)
- `boundaries` — state boundary descriptors (`BoundaryInfo`)

Navigate by traversing `children` to reach any package. Directory paths are navigation
labels; use `proto_packages`, `TypeInfo.package`, and `ServiceInfo.package` for
declared protobuf identity.

## Self-Description

The `$schema` field points to `registry.schema.json` (JSON Schema format).
The type definitions under `sys/tacplus` describe this document's own structure:
`PackageNode`, `TypeInfo`, `FieldInfo`, `RpcInfo`, `BoundaryInfo`, `EnumValueInfo`.

# tacplus Generated API

This document defines the public API surfaces tacplus generates and the
behavioral guarantees those surfaces provide. `USER.md` explains how to declare
these surfaces in proto and `tacplus.yaml`; `DEVELOPMENT.md` explains how the
compiler preserves them.

The rule of thumb is simple: hand-written service code implements business
logic at the generated handler seam. Everything else that is common across
services or languages is generated and owned by tacplus.

## Generated Surface

For a proto package that declares services, state, stores, or client
dependencies, tacplus emits the full service surface in the full-service
targets (`go`, `rust`, `java`):

| Surface | Contract |
|---|---|
| ServiceManager | Owns startup, identity, config, state-store connection, TLS, generated clients, server wrappers, health, tracing, and shutdown. |
| Handler | The only business-logic seam. Implementers provide handler methods; generated wrappers call them after auth and validation. |
| Service wrappers | Enforce authentication, authorization, inbound validation, namespace policy, tracing/accounting, handler dispatch, outbound validation, and stable status-code mapping. Auth precedes validation — see the pipeline below. |
| Client managers | Expose typed C2S/W2S/S2S/C2D clients selected by proto annotations and `tacplus.yaml` transport settings, subject to the target language support matrix. |
| State clients | Expose typed read/write/watch access to proto-declared state roots, with imports restricted to generated read-only accessors. |
| Typed disk persistence | Exposes typed snapshot and redo-log persistence for generated store/state types when enabled by the generated service/store config. |
| registry.json | Exposes the normalized semantic IR: types, services, auth metadata, RPC verb/pattern metadata, state roots, projections, annotations, and generated surface metadata. |

No full-service language is the reference implementation. The contract is the
annotated proto model plus the generated API behavior described here. Go, Java
and Rust are the three server backends and are at parity on the record plane —
the `(spec.store_namespace)` / `(spec.store_principal)` / `(spec.record).private`
egress row filters (see [Egress row filters](#watch-contract) below) are
generated by all three. Python, TypeScript, Swift and C# remain client-only and
generate no service wrapper, so a record read surface cannot be hosted in any of
them.

Client-only targets do not implement the service runtime contract, and split
into two tiers. `swift` and `csharp` are "lite" client targets: they emit C2D,
C2S, and W2S client surfaces. Swift's W2S covers unary (HTTP/JSON) and
server-streaming (SSE) methods; C#'s W2S is unary-only. A method neither tier
can carry — client-streaming and bidi, which the gateway serves over WebSocket,
plus every streaming method for C# — is emitted as a compile-time-unavailable
stub rather than omitted, so a mixed service still compiles and no declared
method silently disappears. Unlike the full-client tier, both currently emit no
client-side request validation and no default request deadline. `python` and
`typescript` are full-client targets: they emit every client surface (C2D, C2S,
W2S, and REST) with client-side validation. Both tiers reject S2S clients,
server wrappers, ServiceManager runtime, EventBus runtime, health runtime, SMB
runtime, service state, and service stores loudly, instead of silently producing
partial service code.

## ServiceManager

The ServiceManager (`sm`) is the top-level reachable surface for generated
runtime infrastructure. Generated helpers and wrappers may exist internally, but
application code should reach generated capabilities through `sm`.

The ServiceManager is responsible for:

- loading generated config and runtime environment;
- creating and refreshing identity tokens;
- obtaining and renewing TLS material;
- connecting to the state store and declared service dependencies;
- exposing typed state, store, and service clients;
- installing generated server wrappers around the handler;
- publishing health/readiness and trace/accounting events;
- shutting down owned tasks, streams, and clients.

If a service implementation manually wires raw gRPC servers, auth interceptors,
state-watch loops, bearer headers, or generated transport clients that should be
available through `sm`, that is either a caller bug or a missing generated
surface.

### Certificate Delivery Streams

Generated ServiceManagers own long-lived certificate delivery streams in
full-service targets (`go`, `rust`, `java`). The contract applies to both
auto-TLS (`X509Mint`/`ManageCert`) and SMB member certificate
(`SmbCertService`/`ManageSmbCert`) streams.

Certificate streams are startup-critical until the first usable credential is
installed. After that first credential, they are renewal-critical: failures must
be retried without leaving the service permanently stale or pairing an old
certificate with a new private key. Handlers only install delivered credentials
through the generated handler seam.

Startup follows this state machine:

1. Resolve the authority endpoint for the current attempt.
2. Generate a pending private key and CSR.
3. Open the certificate stream with a cancellable attempt context.
4. Wait for the first delivery.
5. Promote the pending key only after the matching certificate delivery is
   accepted by the generated handler seam.
6. Report startup success only after the first credential has been installed.

Startup attempts use bounded exponential backoff with a shutdown escape. If the
attempt budget is exhausted before first delivery, startup fails loudly.
Shutdown or cancellation exits without reporting a false startup success.

**Readiness and reconnects (Go, Java, Rust).** The gRPC health endpoint that
Kubernetes readiness probes read starts NOT_SERVING and flips to SERVING only
when bootstrap has completed, the last effective health status is not
UNHEALTHY, and every required s2s channel is up: each event-bus subscription
the service declares, and each s2s target listed explicitly through
`grpc_s2s_client` (targets discovered through `s2s_client_all` do not gate).
It flips back to NOT_SERVING while any of them is down. Only readiness is
gated; the status published to ServiceHealthState is not, since peers resolve
each other through it. Every s2s reconnect loop (service resolution,
subscriptions, publishers) backs off from 500ms doubling to a 30s cap, from
one shared chassis constant per language.

Required failure behavior:

| Case | Generated behavior |
|---|---|
| Authority unreachable before first delivery | Retry with bounded backoff; exhaust budget as startup error. |
| Stream open error before first delivery | Retry with bounded backoff; exhaust budget as startup error. |
| Clean stream end before first delivery | Startup error for that attempt; retry until the startup budget is exhausted. |
| Server error before first delivery | Startup error for that attempt; retry until the startup budget is exhausted. |
| First-delivery handler failure | Fatal startup error; do not retry because local installation failed. |
| Shutdown before first delivery | Exit promptly and do not mark startup successful. |
| Clean stream end after first delivery | Reconnect while running, with backoff and endpoint re-resolution inside the loop. |
| Server error after first delivery | Reconnect while running, with backoff and endpoint re-resolution inside the loop. |
| Renewal handler failure | Log and retry; keep the last active credential. |
| Renewal CSR/key generation failure | Log and retry; keep the last active credential. |

Every renewal attempt uses a pending key distinct from the active key. The
active key must not be replaced at CSR generation time. Promotion is atomic:
generate pending key, send the CSR built from it, receive the matching
certificate chain, invoke the generated handler seam with the pending key and
delivered certificate, and promote pending to active only if the handler returns
success. On stream error, clean stream end, handler failure, cancellation, or
shutdown, the pending key is discarded and the service keeps using the last
active credential until a future renewal succeeds.

Every stream attempt must have a cancellable context or equivalent cancellation
handle. On every exit path, including clean stream end, server error, startup
failure, handler failure, timeout, and shutdown, generated code cancels or
half-closes the stream or call before retrying or returning. Reconnect loops
re-resolve the authority endpoint on every attempt; a certificate stream must
not pin a dead channel, stub, observer, or connection forever after the
authority endpoint changes.

SMB member certificate delivery follows the same state machine and staging
rules. The delivered per-SMB CA certificate is the trust anchor for the
black-box member mesh. The true root CA and any CA private key must not enter
generated black-box runtime configuration. The generated SMB handler seam
receives the delivered member certificate chain, the pending member private key,
and the delivered per-SMB CA certificate; the pending member key is promoted
only after that handler seam succeeds.

The behavioral fixture for this contract drives both auto-TLS and SMB loops
through first delivery success, renewal success, clean end before and after
first delivery, server error before and after first delivery, authority
unreachable, first-delivery handler failure, renewal handler failure, and
shutdown during startup and renewal attempts. Template-level regression tests
pin the state-machine markers where a full runtime fixture is not practical.

The fixture does NOT currently exercise endpoint re-resolution after reconnect
or CSR/key generation failure injection. Reconnect behavior is tested (the loop
does reconnect after post-delivery errors), but re-resolution to a changed
endpoint is not pinned. The contract requires it (see the required failure
table above), and template code implements it, but no behavioral test verifies
it.

## Handler And Wrappers

Handlers are the only generated seam intended for handwritten business logic.
The generated wrapper owns the request pipeline:

1. Decode the proto message.
2. Authenticate and authorize when auth is enabled. This precedes validation so
   an unauthenticated caller cannot drive the validation path or distinguish
   outcomes by the validation errors it returns.
3. Validate inbound request constraints before handler dispatch.
4. Enforce subject/object namespace rules when the proto declares namespace
   fields: a subject may act only at or below its namespace level.
5. Call the handler.
6. Validate each outbound response or stream item before sending it.
7. Map failures to stable generated error/status codes.
8. Emit trace/accounting/health hooks where the generated service surface
   requires them.

Outbound validation applies to user-defined response messages on every
generated full-service send path, including gRPC unary/streaming and W2S
REST/SSE translation. `google.protobuf.*` well-known responses such as
`Empty` carry no tacplus `assert_*` constraints, so generated wrappers pass
them through without a validation call.

**W2S REST/SSE egress validation scope**: the generated W2S server dispatch
(Rust `rest_dispatch.rs.tmpl`, Go `rest_dispatch.go.tmpl`, Java
`RestDispatch.java.tmpl`) validates both unary responses and SSE stream items
before sending. Python and TypeScript are client-only targets and do not host
a W2S server.

**W2S REST/SSE ingress validation scope**: the generated W2S server dispatch
(Rust `rest_dispatch.rs.tmpl`, Go `rest_dispatch.go.tmpl`, Java
`RestDispatch.java.tmpl`) validates the decoded request on both the unary and
the SSE leg before forwarding it to the backend gRPC service, rejecting a
failure as `400` with `request validation failed`. As with egress, requests
whose input type is `google.protobuf.*` (including `Empty`) carry no tacplus
`assert_*` constraints and are forwarded without a validation call. Python and
TypeScript are client-only targets and do not host a W2S server.

All three languages plan the same route table and dispatch arms from one
shared planner (`pkg/internal/common/restdispatch`): which routes exist, what
each dials, whom it entitles callers against, and which methods can be
dispatched at all are decided once, and each language renders only its own
client, JSON and validator names. A `(spec.rest_browser)` `redirect_field` is
carried in every language's route table as its proto3 JSON name
(`redirectUrl`); because the Go and Java JSON helpers emit the proto field
name (`redirect_url`), their route entries also carry that spelling and the
redirect lookup accepts either. A redirect URL that is not a valid HTTP header
value (control or non-ASCII bytes) is answered `502` in all three languages,
never written into `Location`.

The planner refuses, at generation time, a dispatchable route whose request
or response is a `google.protobuf.*` well-known type other than `Empty`, and a
server-streaming route whose response is `Empty`: the dispatchers encode and
decode with the generated per-message helpers, which do not exist for the
protobuf runtime's types, and there is nothing to stream for `Empty`. Wrap
such a payload in a message of your own.

Auth-disabled methods skip token lookup and authorization but still validate
messages. Auth-enabled methods must not reach the handler without a valid token
and a satisfied authorization decision.

## Transport Surfaces

Service shape is declared in proto. `tacplus.yaml` only chooses which transport
surfaces to emit for the current package and language.

| Surface | Meaning | Transport |
|---|---|---|
| C2S | client to service | native gRPC |
| W2S | web to service | gRPC-over-HTTP/REST surface suitable for browser callers |
| S2S | service to service | native gRPC with service identity tokens |
| C2D | client to daemon | local IPC gRPC, such as Unix domain sockets or named pipes |

C2S and W2S are not mutually exclusive for full-service targets. A native/server
package may enable either or both. Browser web apps should enable W2S and should
not enable C2S.

C2D is a local daemon IPC surface; it does not introduce SMN/SMB mesh work.
The lite client targets (`swift`, `csharp`) emit C2D, C2S, and W2S clients
(Swift's W2S is unary + server-streaming over SSE, C#'s is unary-only; the
streaming methods neither can carry are emitted as unavailable stubs);
the full-client targets (`python`, `typescript`) additionally emit REST clients.

**C2D server auth-skip scope**: Rust, Go and Java host a generated C2D server
for the package's own `service_c2d` services, mounted by the generated
ServiceManager on the declared `socket_path` (Unix domain socket; required, no
default): `C2dServer` in `service_manager.rs.tmpl`, `grpcserver.C2DServer`
(`newC2DServer` in the Go ServiceManager) and `grpcserver.C2DServer`
(`ServiceManager.newC2DServer` in Java). The services are hosted on that socket
only, never on the TLS gRPC listener; a service with no other gRPC surface
starts no TLS server at all. Every hosted `service_c2d` service must declare the
same `socket_path`, since one ServiceManager runs one c2d server. The server
removes a stale socket file, binds, and sets the socket file to owner-only
(0600); if it cannot, it refuses to serve. The wrapper skips token
authentication by design: the auth boundary is the socket permission
(filesystem ACL), not a bearer token. It still validates request/response
constraints and runs the full handler pipeline; only the token-lookup and
authorization steps are bypassed, via the `IsC2D` flag on the service
descriptor, and the ServiceManager wires no authorizer into a c2d wrapper. A
Go or Java c2d server that fails to start ends `Run`/`run` with the error; the
Rust ServiceManager logs it. Python and TypeScript are client-only targets.

**C2D standalone host**: a local daemon has no cluster, so it cannot call
`New`/`create`/`new()` (config load, identity manager, state store) or `Run`.
For a build whose every hosted service is `service_c2d` and that declares
nothing cluster-bound (no state, S2S client, subscription, record reader, disk
store or `requires_device` gate), the generated ServiceManager package also
emits a standalone host entry: Go `sm.ServeC2DStandalone(ctx, socketPath, h)`,
Java `ServiceManager.serveC2DStandalone(socketPath, handler, stop)`, Rust
`ServiceManager::serve_c2d_standalone(socket_path, handler, shutdown)`. It
builds the generated wrappers from the generated `Handler` and serves them
through the same c2d mount `Run` uses, so the validation, the auth skip and the
0600 fail-closed socket are identical; it loads no config, mints no identity,
opens no state store and starts no TLS server. It serves until the context is
cancelled (Go), the `stop` future completes (Java) or the `shutdown` future
resolves (Rust), drains in-flight RPCs, removes the socket and then calls the
handler's shutdown (bounded at 30 s in Go and Rust); a socket that cannot be
bound or locked down is returned (thrown in Java) without calling it. A daemon
passes the generated constant for the declared path (Go `sm.C2DSocketPath`,
Java `ServiceManager.C2D_SOCKET_PATH`, Rust `s2sm::C2D_SOCKET_PATH`, which
`Run` also serves on and clients dial); a test passes its own path so it never
takes over the socket of a daemon running on the same host. The decision is
one shared rule (`service.HostsC2DStandalone`); every other shape keeps
`New` + `Run` only, including a c2d-only daemon that also reads state or calls
a peer, because that daemon needs the cluster `Run` brings up.

### Client Send Contract

Generated clients validate before sending. Auth scope depends on the call
shape:

- **Unary / server-streaming**: a fresh token is obtained per CALL; if the
  identity manager cannot provide one, the call fails before leaving the
  process.
- **Client-streaming / bidi**: auth is STREAM-OPEN scoped — exactly one token
  is attached to the stream headers when the stream opens (gRPC metadata
  cannot change mid-stream). There is deliberately no per-send token
  preflight: it would mint a token the server never sees while still being
  able to fail a legitimate send. A server that rejects an expired stream
  credential terminates the stream; the generated reconnect paths (e.g.
  EventBus subscribers) obtain a fresh token per reconnect attempt.

Auth-disabled calls bypass token lookup.

Generated mutation helpers do not retry by default unless the generated API
explicitly marks the operation as safe. Read-like helpers may use generated
retry/backoff policy.

## State And Store Access

A message annotated as service state becomes a typed state root. The generated
surface includes:

- a state service with typed Get/Set/Watch/Delete-style RPCs for the declared
  boundaries;
- typed state clients surfaced from the ServiceManager;
- generated import accessors for read-only cross-service state imports;
- server-side enforcement that imports cannot write through raw RPCs;
- view services for declared read-only unions across compatible roots;
- topic, queue, command, persistence, and eviction behavior declared by proto
  annotations.

Services own their state. Other services access exported state through declared
imports and generated read-only accessors, not by manually dialing backing state
services.

No state store implements `(spec.persistence)` today. Kernel does not: kernel is
in-memory coordination plus its own identity snapshot, and holds no durable user
data. Setting the annotation on a state root whose `(spec.service_state).label`
includes `kernel` is a generation error — *durable data belongs in the record store
records*. On any other state root the annotation is accepted and carried
descriptively into `registry.json` (`BoundaryInfo.persistence`) for a future store
that implements it; it produces no durability behavior on its own. Generated state
clients carry no local durability either — no state client in any language writes a
boundary to local disk.

## Typed Disk Persistence

This section is about `(spec.service_store)` typed disk persistence and
`grpcconfig.disk_persistence`; it is unrelated to `(spec.persistence)`, which is a
descriptive request for state-boundary durability that no store implements today.

Typed disk persistence is the generated disk analogue of typed HTTP clients:
code reads and writes proto types with generated serialization and validation,
not raw JSON or ad hoc file I/O.

The generated contract is:

- JSON plus newline framing only; no alternate on-disk format;
- write paths use generated `ToJSON` helpers;
- read paths use generated `FromJSON` helpers and then `Validate`;
- invalid data on read fails closed;
- single-writer, single-process, local-filesystem only;
- same-directory atomic rename and file/parent-directory fsync for replacement
  writes;
- archive rotation for replaced or compacted files;
- redo logs append newline-delimited records and compact by snapshotting the
  latest keyed state;
- restore handles active, temporary, and in-progress promoted files without
  silently dropping a committed baseline.

The ServiceManager owns scheduled redo-log lifecycle when the init-time
`grpcconfig.Config.disk_persistence` setting is present. Generated
ServiceManagers open one redo-log handle per hosted keyed `service_store`,
expose those handles to service code, and run deterministic per-store roll
schedulers. This setting is not hot-reloaded; service code should append through
the ServiceManager-owned handles and should not run its own backup loop for
generated stores.

### Archive to an object store (Java; Go and Rust library layer)

Set `grpcconfig.disk_persistence.archive` to ship each writer's redo log to an
object store and restore from it after losing the local volume. The generated
ServiceManager wires it in Java only; Python and TypeScript ignore the field.
Go and Rust ship the same archive layer as a library (`ArchiveShipper`,
`ArchiveSink`, `DirArchiveSink`, `RestoreArchive` / `restore_archive`, and
`RedoLog.Rotate` / `rotate`) for a service that opens its own log; they have no
GCS sink and their ServiceManager does not read `archive` (see
`roadmap/LANGUAGE_PARITY.md`). Names below are the Java ones.

- **Segments.** Each roll queues the rolled redo log as a segment. The local
  file is removed only after the archive holds it, so a failing upload never
  loses a segment. Uploads run FIFO on a daemon thread, retry with backoff (at
  most five minutes), and never block an append.
- **Rotation.** `RedoLog.rotate()` closes the active log, queues it as the next
  segment and opens a fresh active log. It takes no snapshot and folds no
  baseline, so it costs the writes since the last rotation, not the size of the
  store. The segment stays on the local volume after it ships, and
  `RedoLog.restore` replays it (baseline, then the kept segments in order, then
  the active log), until a later `roll` folds it into a baseline and deletes it.
  The first rotation after a roll carries that roll's baseline. A rotation with
  nothing appended since the last one ships nothing. Set
  `archive.segment_interval_seconds` to rotate on an interval
  (`RollSchedule.runRotateScheduler` for a hand-opened log); 0, the default,
  turns it off and `roll` behaves as before.
- **Checkpoints.** Every `archive.checkpoint_interval_seconds` (default 86400)
  the full store state is shipped as a checkpoint, recorded under the redo
  position it covers: the newest segment rolled at that moment. The position and
  the snapshot are read under the same lock as a roll, so no roll can split them.
- **Layout.** Objects live under `<prefix>/<member>/<store>/segments/<seq>` and
  `<prefix>/<member>/<store>/checkpoints/<seq>`, with `seq` zero-padded to twenty
  digits so names sort in roll order. `member` is the writer's instance id, so
  several writers ship independently.
- **Restore.** `ArchiveRestore.restore(sink, prefix, member, store, inserter)`
  loads the newest checkpoint, then replays every segment shipped after its
  position, in order, into an empty store. Records are deduplicated across the
  chain, last write wins, so a delete after the checkpoint arrives as a tombstone
  for the consumer's `Inserter` to honour. A missing segment is an error, never a
  partial restore. Restore must name the writer's original `member`.
- **Recovery point.** A write is in the archive only once a rotation or a roll
  has shipped it. Writes made since then are lost with the volume, so the worst
  case is one `archive.segment_interval_seconds` when it is set, and one
  `roll_interval_seconds` (default 86400) when it is not. Set the segment
  interval short and leave the roll interval long: a roll is a compaction that
  snapshots and rewrites the whole store, a rotation is not.
- **Credentials.** The archive sink is Google Cloud Storage, authenticated as the
  workload's ambient identity (Application Default Credentials). No key is read
  from config. The sink is compiled in only when the project pins
  `com.google.cloud:google-cloud-storage` in `dependencies.yaml`; a service that
  sets `archive` in a build without that pin fails at startup.
- **Observability.** A failed upload logs a `WARNING` with the object name and
  retry delay. `RedoLog.shipPending()` (objects not yet shipped, the lag) and
  `RedoLog.shipFailures()` (failed attempts) report the same numbers to code.

### Append-only history and plain file reads (Java)

A redo log is keyed and deduplicated on read, so it is the wrong primitive for a
full history such as a daily tombstone file. Java also exposes the primitives
for files that are neither snapshots nor redo logs. Go and Rust have
`AppendLog` (issue #70) but not `PlainFile`; Python and TypeScript have neither
(see `roadmap/LANGUAGE_PARITY.md`).

- **`AppendLog.append(base, relPath, line, mode)`** writes `line` verbatim
  followed by one `\n`, creating `relPath`'s parent directories and the file
  itself. It fsyncs before returning. `relPath` is the caller's path: there is no
  store namespace segment and no forced `.log` suffix. `mode` is the Unix
  permission applied on create (`0` leaves the default). A `line` containing
  `\n` is rejected as `INVALID_ARGUMENT`.
- **`AppendLog.readLines(base, relPath)`** returns every complete line in order,
  each without its terminator, with no dedup. An absent file reads as no lines.
  A trailing fragment with no terminator (a crash mid-append) is not a line and
  is dropped; the next `append` removes it before writing.
- **`PlainFile.readAll`, `PlainFile.exists`, `PlainFile.list`** read a whole
  file, test for its presence, and list a directory's entries, sorted. A missing
  file in `readAll` is `NOT_FOUND`; a missing directory in `list` is empty.
- All paths are relative to `base`. An absolute path, or one that resolves
  outside `base`, is rejected as `INVALID_ARGUMENT`.
- Errors are `DiskStoreException`: `io` for I/O failures.

## Collection RPCs

Collection-returning RPCs are explicit. A multi-result read declares a
`method_collection` mode and bound; tacplus derives transport tier, flow
control, and public handler/client shapes from that declaration.

A unary response whose only meaningful field is one repeated result field is
the Tier-1 collection convention and must be annotated. Tacplus rejects that
shape when `method_collection` is absent because there is no safe way to infer
bounds, transport tier, or public handler/client shape from proto alone.
Composite responses that happen to contain repeated nested fields are not
treated as collection reads unless annotated.

### Modes

| Mode | Contract |
|---|---|
| SNAPSHOT | Finite point-in-time result. Requires a positive `max_items`; terminates. |
| WATCH | Open-ended change stream. Requires an explicit `from_revision`; does not self-terminate. |
| PAGE | Unary, client-driven window over an ordered set. Requires `order_by` and a positive `default_page_size`; the client resumes with an opaque `page_token`. |

An unbounded non-async read is invalid. If a read is unbounded, it is a WATCH.

### Snapshot Tiers

Tacplus computes `max_items * item_bytes` and selects a delivery tier:

| Tier | Wire shape | Handler surface | Client surface |
|---|---|---|---|
| Tier 1 | unary response with exactly one repeated field | materialized collection | materialized collection |
| Tier 2 | server-streaming items | materialized collection | materialized collection |
| Tier 3 | server-streaming items | lazy producer/iterator | lazy iterator/stream |

Tier-2 and Tier-3 proto methods are ordinary gRPC server-streaming methods. The
streamed message is the item. Tier-1 proto methods are ordinary unary methods
whose response contains exactly one repeated field.

### WATCH Contract

A WATCH proto method is an ordinary server-streaming RPC whose response is an
author-declared envelope:

- `snapshot_item` entries establish the initial state;
- `snapshot_done` carries the revision at which that snapshot is complete;
- `delta` entries carry later changes;
- stale `from_revision` returns `OUT_OF_RANGE`, prompting the client to relist.

The handler returns a language-appropriate `WatchSource` shape containing scope,
snapshot producer, revision, and change producer. The generated wrapper owns
envelope framing, replay-ring lookup, relist behavior, teardown, and flow
control. The replay ring lives in a shared per-language collection runtime lib,
keyed by scope and bounded by `replay_depth`.

The ring is ordered by one int64 field on the `delta`, named by
`(spec.method_collection).revision_field` and defaulting to `revision`. The
default suits a purpose-built change envelope (`<T>WatchChange { item;
revision }`); a delta that IS the row — an append-only record has no update or
delete frame to distinguish — names the sequence the row already carries
instead, rather than growing a second ordering field that must agree with the
first forever. The named field must exist and be a singular int64: generation
fails otherwise, including for the default, rather than emitting a wrapper that
only fails later in `cargo`/`javac`/`go build`.

The wrapper also owns the egress row filters on this seam, exactly as on the
unary and PAGE seams (Go, Rust and Java): every `snapshot_item` and every `delta`
is checked before it is sent — a row whose `(spec.store_principal)` field is
not the caller's is skipped, and a row whose `(spec.store_namespace)` field is
not the caller's tenant trips the abort backstop. `snapshot_done` carries no
row and is always sent. The `delta` may be the row itself or an envelope with
one level of singular message fields around it; a pinned row inside a
repeated, map or oneof field of the delta fails generation, as does a pinned
row on any non-WATCH streaming shape (Tier-2/Tier-3 SNAPSHOT, plain server
streams), which have no per-item hook.

**Go, Java and Rust are at parity on the record plane.** All three render the
egress filter above on every record-bearing seam — the unary response, the PAGE
window, WATCH's per-item hook, and the query predicate — so any of the three may
generate a service wrapper for a `store_namespace` / `store_principal` /
`(spec.record).private`-annotated response, and all three spell the same abort,
the same `linked`-claim widening and the same operator-facing diagnostics. The
three generators are held to one behaviour by
`pkg/internal/common/record_egress_parity_test.go`, which fails the build if one
of them drops a rule the other two keep, and the filters are generated and
compiled side by side in all three by the `proto-recordegress` fixture leg of
`cross-test/current-generation`.

Two refusals remain, and both are deliberate rather than gaps:

- **A pinned row on a streaming shape with no per-item hook** — a Tier-2/Tier-3
  SNAPSHOT or a plain server stream, and a WATCH `delta` carrying pinned rows in
  a repeated, map or oneof field. There is nowhere to put the check, so
  generation refuses instead of emitting a wrapper that under-enforces. Go and
  Rust refuse exactly this set; it is not a language difference.
- **A private-record read with no caller principal to pin against** — a
  `(spec.record).private` read on a surface no user token reaches, or over a
  private row whose owner no annotation names. The owner pin has nothing to
  compare rows against, so the read cannot be hosted in Go, Java or Rust. This
  one is language-independent by construction, not a property of any generator.

### PAGE Contract

A PAGE proto method is an ordinary **unary** RPC. The request carries the filter
fields plus `int32 page_size` and `string page_token`; the response carries
exactly one `repeated` items field, `string next_page_token`, and an optional
`int64 total_count`. Generation rejects a request that declares `page_token` /
`page_size` (or a response with `next_page_token`) but lacks
`COLLECTION_MODE_PAGE` — otherwise it would silently degrade to an unbounded
unary with no page ceiling.

The generated wrapper owns the page mechanics; the handler is a keyset producer:

- `page_token` decodes to a keyset cursor (the `order_by` key of the last row).
  A malformed token is `INVALID_ARGUMENT` — never a silent reset to the first
  page (which would skip rows and read as success).
- The effective page size is `page_size` when positive, else `default_page_size`,
  clamped to the trust tier's `MaxPageSize` (`Ceilings.MaxItems`: 100 anon /
  10k C2S-auth / 1M S2S). This is the per-call row ceiling that SNAPSHOT's
  `max_items` provides statically and that streaming reads lack.
- The handler receives `PageParams{limit, after}` plus the request and returns a
  `Page{items, nextAfter, total}` (`total = -1` means "unknown", not "empty").
  The wrapper encodes `nextAfter` into `next_page_token` (empty on the last
  page) and sets `total_count` only when the handler computed it.

The `page_token` is opaque, versioned, and **byte-identical across all
full-service backends** — base64url(no pad) of `{"v":1,"k":[...]}` over the
`order_by` key — so a token minted against one backend decodes on any other.
Pages are best-effort keyset over `order_by` (stable when the sort key is
monotonic/immutable); they are not a point-in-time snapshot unless the handler
bakes a revision into the key.

Each language exposes two client seams: an explicit single-page call
(`{Method}Page` → items + `next_page_token` + total) and an auto-pager (the
natural method name) that follows `next_page_token` until exhausted —
`iter.Seq2` (Go), an async generator (TypeScript), an async generator (Python),
a `futures::Stream` (Rust), and a lazy `Iterator` (Java). The auto-pager
advances the token on a request clone, so the caller's request is not mutated.

### Flow Control And Teardown

Generated stream wrappers must respect transport backpressure and deterministic
cleanup. Java uses `ServerCallStreamObserver` readiness hooks. TypeScript uses
`write()` backpressure and `drain`. Go, Rust, and Python rely on their native
stream/cancellation semantics.

Idle-timeout backstop — scope. The generated idle-timeout backstop applies to
**long-lived WATCH streams**: the replay Ring waits for the next delta and, if
none arrives within the caller's trust-tier `STREAM_IDLE_TIMEOUT`, ends the
stream with `DEADLINE_EXCEEDED` — a living query must not pin a connection
forever while idle. It does **not** apply to finite **Tier-3 SNAPSHOT cursors**:
a cursor is a bounded pull over a materialized result set, so its teardown is
driven by exhaustion, client cancellation, or the request context deadline, not
a server-side idle timer. (The cursor producer is a synchronous pull — an
`iter.Seq2` / equivalent — that cannot be preempted mid-`Next` without leaking
the producer goroutine, so a per-item idle timer is deliberately not generated;
a handler whose producer can wedge must honor the context itself.)

## EventBus Topics

EventBus participation in generated service runtimes is declared, never
inferred. A topic is a message
carrying `(spec.service_event)` (with `label` naming the broker service) plus a
field carrying `(spec.topic) = true`. Producers and consumers declare
`(spec.event_publish)` / `(spec.event_watch)` with a `topic_ref` in the
canonical format, parsed from the right so dotted packages work:

```text
<proto-package>.<topic-message>.<topic-field>
e.g. telemetry.AgenticCodeEventBus.event_stream
```

Full-service generation validates every `topic_ref` before emitting code: it must match the
grammar, resolve to exactly one package/message/field, point at a
`(spec.service_event)` message and a `(spec.topic)` field, and preserve the
field's protobuf type as the event type. Ambiguity or absence fails generation.

Typed EventBus Subscribe responses use a metadata-bearing envelope, not a bare
event payload. Field 1 is the record metadata and field 2 is the typed event
payload. The metadata wire fields are stable across languages:
`key = 1`, `topic = 2`, `partition = 3`, `offset = 4`, and
`timestamp = 5`.

EventBus publish/watch RPCs are derived RPCs, and **auth uses the standard
method auth model, not an EventBus-specific vocabulary**: the
`event_publish`/`event_watch` annotations carry the normal `method_s2s` /
`method_c2s` shapes, and generation copies that policy onto the derived RPC's
metadata exactly as if hand-authored. Topic declarations are collected from all
loaded descriptors, but publish/watch bindings attach only to the **current
actor's own protos** — importing a proto never makes a service (or the broker
itself) a producer or subscriber.

**Consumer-scoped routing envelope.** `s2s_subscribe` carries, alongside
`auth_services`, an additive `routing_only_services` list. It is declared by the
topic **owner** on its own `(spec.record)`/`(spec.event)` — never by the
subscriber, which cannot be trusted to choose its own blast radius — and names
the subset of the already-authorized `auth_services` whose generated subscriber
`Handler` is typed for a synthesized `<T>RoutingEnvelope`
(`{delivery_id, recipient, namespace}`) instead of the full `<T>`. The three
slots are projected from the source type's own annotations —
`(spec.record).key`, `(spec.store_principal)`, `(spec.store_namespace)` — and a
flagged type that cannot fill all three, or whose slots are not singular
strings, **fails generation** rather than emitting a half-empty envelope.
Listing a service grants it nothing; it must still appear in `auth_services`.
Omitting the field changes nothing: every subscriber not named keeps the full
type, unchanged.

This is a **type** boundary, not a memory one. The full message still arrives on
the wire and is still decoded in the subscriber's process; the generated
dispatch projects the three fields out of it and drops the decoded message.
Narrowing the wire itself is a broker-side change and is not what this
annotation does.

The registry carries the same boundary by annotation rather than by field
spelling: `FieldInfo.store_principal`, `FieldInfo.store_namespace` and
`FieldInfo.record_key` mark which field plays which role, so a registry consumer
never has to match on a field being literally named `recipient` or `namespace`.

## RPC Patterns And Verbs

Every RPC resolves to exactly one pattern from a closed set, with one static
access kind: `GET` (READ) · `LIST` (READ; SNAPSHOT or PAGE) · `WATCH` (READ) ·
`CREATE`/`UPDATE`/`DELETE` (WRITE) · `ACTION` · `CLIENT_STREAM` · `BIDI`
(declared access, default WRITE). One method = one verb = one access kind;
branching a method's meaning on input is an architectural-norm violation (see
`DEVELOPMENT.md`).

RPC names are `Verb<Noun>` (PascalCase, verb first) against a **closed verb
registry**. A verb exists only if the operation cannot be expressed as
Get/List/Watch/Create/Update/Delete without losing meaning (the fold test);
synonyms fold to canonicals and are rejected:

- **Core (6)**: Get, List (replaces Search/Query/Find), Watch, Create, Update,
  Delete.
- **Action (16)**: Mint, Revoke, Authorize, Send, Publish, Subscribe, Broker,
  Execute, Cancel, Acquire, Release, Retry, Reset, Ping, Proxy, Merge. `Subscribe` and `Broker`
  are canonical action verbs (not folded to `Watch`); the messaging verbs are
  `Send`/`Publish`/`Subscribe`/`Broker`. Stateful vs stateless rule:
  `Create`/`Delete` for stored resources; `Mint`/`Revoke` for self-contained
  credentials (a JWT is `MintToken`, never `CreateSession`). Protocol-mandated
  URL paths (OAuth/OIDC) live on `rest_path`; the *name*
  conforms to the registry.
- **AI/Agent (7)**: Generate, Embed, Classify, Rank, Assist, Guard, Evaluate —
  all under the `AGENT` entitlement scope. Fold rules: Summarize/Translate/
  Rewrite/Redact→Generate; Moderate/Detect→Classify; Rerank→Rank;
  Plan/Critique→Assist; semantic Search→List.

The registry is governed: core/action verbs admit rarely under strict review;
agent verbs have a lighter bar but the registry stays closed. The authored
compiler dictionary is `pkg/internal/common/verbs/registry.json`; generated
service semantic output lands in the build artifact `registry.json` `RpcInfo`
(see Tracing And Registry).
`EnforceVerbs` is part of descriptor parsing for generated-auth surfaces:
non-canonical verbs, folded synonyms, noun-first names, and
verb/pattern/cardinality mismatches fail generation before registry,
entitlement, or REST metadata can be emitted. Full design genealogy:
the archived RPC_PATTERNS_AND_VERBS_PLAN (not in this repository).

## Auth And Namespace Policy

Auth policy is declared in proto service and method annotations. Generated code
performs token verification, service/user authorization, entitlement checks, and
namespace enforcement before handler dispatch.

Subject namespace and object namespace are distinct. When both are declared, the
subject namespace must be at or above the object namespace. Generated code must
deny namespace-mismatched calls before the handler. Channels with auth disabled
do not perform token lookup but still validate message constraints.

## SPIFFE Identity

All SPIFFE identity construction, parsing, and comparison goes through the
generated `sys/spiffe` — no generated code or downstream service formats or
splits `spiffe://...` strings by hand.

**Trust domain.** The URI authority: a single globally unique instance name
containing no `/` (e.g. `example.com`). Configured per deployment
(`spiffe_trust_domain`); a missing or malformed value fails loudly — there is
no default.

**URI layout** (typed, self-describing — the kind is recoverable from fixed
tags, no side channel needed):

```text
spiffe://<trust_domain>/
  system/<location...>/services/<service>[/workloads/<child>...]
  tenants/<tenant>/users/<user>
  tenants/<tenant>/workspaces/<workspace>...
  tenants/<tenant>/...[/clients/<client>]
  tenants/<tenant>/...[/credentials/<kind>/<id>]
  tenants/<tenant>/...[/data/<kind>/<id>]
  users/<xid>
```

`/system` holds infrastructure/service identities; `/tenants` holds
tenant-scoped principals and resources; `/users/<xid>` is a user principal
that exists outside every tenant (one minted opaque id), and its namespace is
`/users/<xid>`. It is exactly two segments and is its own subtree: it is not
at or below any `/tenants/...` namespace, and no `/tenants/...` namespace is
at or below it. The `<location...>` tiers between
`/system/` and `services` are opaque and variable-arity (the parser keys off
the `services` tag). Reserved tags (`system`, `tenants`, `services`,
`workloads`, `users`, `workspaces`, `clients`, `credentials`, `data`) are
rejected as namespace segments at every depth.

**Segment grammar**: `[A-Za-z0-9][A-Za-z0-9._-]*`. Empty segments, separators,
traversal, query/fragment, control characters, and encoded separators are
rejected. **Reject by default; never sanitize-and-accept.** Richer external
identifiers go through `opaque_segment(kind, value)` (SHA-256 over
`kind‖0x1F‖NFC(value)`, truncated to 160 bits, lowercase base32 no-pad) —
byte-identical across supported target surfaces.

**Service identity and matching.** The canonical service SPIFFE ID —
`spiffe://<td>/system[/<loc>...]/services/<svc>` — is what the cert minter
emits as the X509 URI SAN and what the generated go/rust/java peer verifiers
require (parsed via sys/spiffe; `SubjectKind == Service`, trust domain equal,
service label equal). S2S `auth_services` checks match on the
location-agnostic `service_path()` (the bare service label, location tiers
stripped), so the same service matches in any cloud/account/az/cluster. A `"*"`
pattern admits service subjects only; a workload subject matches only a pattern
that names `/workloads/` (see `PIGEON_SERVICE_PATH` in docs/USER.md).

**Token claims.** The SPIFFE ID is *derived* from claims, never carried as a
claim: `namespace` is the authorization-tree path; `sub` is the stable
principal id (not a URI); `sub_type` ∈ {service, workload, user, client,
external}; `azp` is the attestation context (kernel/oauth/cloud-auth) —
attestation is never encoded in the subject path, so the same human in the
same tenant role has the same subject regardless of login method.
`/tenants/<t>/users/<u>` is a tenant-scoped role, not the global human; the
person is correlated only via the stable IDP `sub`. External tokens are
rejected by generated internal auth.

Full design rationale and decision record:
the archived SPIFFE_IDENTITY_NORMALIZATION_PLAN (not in this repository).

## Validation And Errors

Every generated language enforces the same field constraints, default collection
bounds, oneof scalar string/bytes bounds, maximum message nesting depth, enum
vocabulary, and message validation semantics. Generated validators reject
nested message graphs deeper than 24 levels and reject enum numeric values not
declared in the proto. A declared zero/sentinel enum value is allowed unless
`assert_enum_defined` is present. Generated code should fail closed for invalid
proto shapes, invalid runtime config, invalid tokens, unsafe transport setup,
and failed validation.

Generated types and wrappers should expose tacplus structured errors/status
codes rather than language-specific exception behavior at public seams.

## Tracing And Registry

Generated service wrappers emit typed trace/accounting data where the surface
requires it. Request handlers are responsible for propagating non-empty
`trace_id` fields into downstream requests they create.

Durable accounting (an `accountingrecord.AccountingRecord` event-bus topic)
never holds an RPC in Go, Java, Rust, Python or TypeScript. The sink hands each
record to a bounded in-process spool of 4096 records and returns; the publisher
replays the spool, in order, as the event bus drains it. A record is dropped only
when the spool is full or (Go, Java, Rust) the service is shutting down, and each
drop is logged at ERROR with a running total (issue #34).

With `grpcconfig.disk_persistence` set, Go, Java and Rust make the spool durable
(issue #70). The spool is an append-only log under `disk_persistence.dir`
(`accounting-spool/records.log`, one base64 record per line), and a cursor
(`accounting-spool/cursor`) counts the records the event bus has acknowledged. A
record is appended to the log before it is queued for the publisher, and a restart
replays every record not yet acknowledged, in order. Delivery is at-least-once: a
crash can republish up to 64 records the bus already acknowledged, so consumers
must deduplicate on `accounting_id`. A record emitted but not yet appended when the
process dies is lost; that window is the time between emit and the spool's append.
The on-disk spool is bounded at 64 MiB; records past it are dropped and counted.
The durable spool is not on the RPC path: the append and its fsync run on the
spool task, never inside an RPC. Without `disk_persistence` the spool stays in
memory, as before, and is lost on restart. Python and TypeScript have only the
in-memory spool (see `roadmap/LANGUAGE_PARITY.md`).

`registry.json` is the machine-readable semantic IR. Service-local generators
must read `registry.json`, not parse proto files directly, when they need
tacplus semantics such as projections, store metadata, auth metadata, or
generated surface information.

For generated-auth RPCs, `RpcInfo` includes both transport/auth metadata and
governed classification metadata. A **C2S** generated-auth method that cannot
classify fails generation (the external surface is strict). An **S2S** or
**C2D** generated-auth method that cannot classify does NOT fail generation:
its `RpcInfo` is emitted with `verb_status = "unclassified"` (or `"exempt"`
when the method carries no auth model at all), the folded verb recorded in
`folded_to_verb`, and the governed classification fields (`rpc_verb`,
`rpc_noun`, `method_pattern`, `access_kind`, …) left empty. Internal surfaces
are looser because store/infra RPCs legitimately fall outside the C2S verb
dictionary; the recorded `verb_status` is the signal, not a hard failure. When
classification succeeds:

- `rpc_verb` and `rpc_noun` from the canonical `Verb<Noun>` split.
- `method_pattern`: `GET`, `LIST`, `WATCH`, `CREATE`, `UPDATE`, `DELETE`,
  `ACTION`, `CLIENT_STREAM`, or `BIDI`.
- `access_kind`: `READ` or `WRITE`.
- `verb_class`: `core`, `action`, or `agent`.
- `entitlement_scopes`: grant scopes that admit the method, ordered broad to
  narrow.
- `retry_policy`: `READ_ONLY`, `WATCH_RECONNECT`, `IDEMPOTENCY_REQUIRED`, or
  `NO_GENERATED_AUTO_RETRY`.
- `capability_scope`: primary package capability bucket for capability-any
  expansion (`READ`, `WRITE`, `WATCH`, `PAGE`, or `AGENT`).
- `verb_definition`, `verb_boundary`, and `audit_meaning`: governed dictionary
  metadata for documentation, review, and operator/security surfaces.
- `rejected_verbs`: known non-canonical verbs that fold to `rpc_verb` and are
  rejected by generation.
- `allowed_patterns`: method patterns the canonical verb may resolve to.
- `handler_shape`: `UNARY`, `SERVER_STREAM`, `CLIENT_STREAM`, or `BIDI`.

The root `entitlement_grants` array is the generated grant catalog for C2S
authorization tooling. It includes entitlement-checked C2S methods, not
`auth_disabled` or `auth_any_user` methods. Exact grants identify one
package/service/RPC token. Wildcard grants such as `PACKAGE_ANY`,
`PACKAGE_READ_ANY`, `PACKAGE_WATCH_ANY`, and `PACKAGE_PAGE_ANY` are convenience
values whose `expands_to` list contains the exact grants they imply. Runtime
authorizers should authorize against exact grants after expansion; wildcard
values are not runtime magic. Each grant, and each service, carries `source`:
the `tacplus.yaml` layer name of the proto source its package came from (omitted
when none was declared). Treat it as a classification input to your own policy,
not as proof of authority.

Empty classification fields are invalid for **C2S** generated-auth surfaces
(they hard-fail generation). On S2S/C2D surfaces empty fields are permitted and
accompanied by a non-`classified` `verb_status`, as described above. Consumers
should read the generated fields (and `verb_status`) rather than inventing a
second classifier.

### Record Dispatch To Timeseries Projections

A subscription to a source that has `(spec.timeseries_type)` projections (a
`(spec.transformation)` of a record, or a message naming it in
`timeseries_type.source`) runs a generated record dispatch on every delivered
event, after the subscription's own handler: each projection the event yields is
extracted and handed, **typed**, to that projection's insert callback, which the
service author registers on the ServiceManager before `run`. A source with the
injected trace-round `noop` set writes no row; a projection whose callback is
unset is skipped; a callback's failure fails that delivery. One callback per
projection, shared by every subscription to its source.

| Language | Registration | Callback | Dispatch |
|----------|--------------|----------|----------|
| Go | `sm.Set<P>InsertFunc(fn)` | `func(ctx context.Context, row *<P>) error`, synchronous | `Handle<Source>(ctx, event, insert<P>...)` |
| Java | `sm.set<P>Insert(fn)` | `<Source>Projections.<P>Insert`: `void insert(<P> row) throws Exception`, synchronous | `<Source>Projections.handle<Source>(event, insert<P>...)` |
| Rust | `sm.set_<p>_insert(\|row\| async move { .. })` on the owned manager | `<P>Insert`: `Fn(<P>Row) -> Pin<Box<dyn Future<Output = Result<(), Box<dyn Error + Send + Sync>>> + Send>>`, asynchronous | `handle_<source>(&event, insert_<p>...).await` |

`<P>` is the projection message. Go and Java pass the extracted projection
message itself; their column list and ordered row stay available as
`<P>TimeseriesColumns` / `<P>ToTimeseriesRow` (Go) and `Timeseries<P>.columns` /
`toRow` (Java). Rust passes the generated flattened `<P>Row`, the struct its
timeseries helpers already define for batch insertion.

The shapes differ on purpose; parity is in capability, not in shape. Go and Java
run the callback synchronously on the subscription's delivery goroutine or
thread: the next event waits for it, with nothing else to schedule. The Rust
service runs on tokio, where a blocking callback would stall the executor, so its
callback returns a future that the subscription awaits; delivery order is the same
as in Go and Java. No language is made to adopt another's shape.

The dispatch is generated beside the projections and called through the source's
own package, so a subscribed source with a projection declared in another package
fails generation instead of being silently left out of the dispatch.

## Parity

A generated API is complete only when behavior is equivalent across the
supported languages for the same proto model. Parity is measured against proto
annotations, semantic registry metadata, generated-contract tests, and
soundness checks, not against any single language implementation.
