## PC-L-9 — ServiceManager teardown leak evidence is synthetic

**Status:** closed for goroutines; the open-FD leg runs on Linux only.

`cross-test/chaos/leaksoak` generates a real Go model, runs the generated
`chassis/servicemanager` ServiceManager through eight create/teardown cycles in
that model's own process, and feeds the real `runtime.NumGoroutine()` trend into
the unchanged `oracle.LeakOracle`. A live ServiceManager holds ten goroutines and
settles back to the baseline after `Close()`; the harness fails if the live count
never exceeds the baseline, so it cannot pass green by measuring nothing. Proven
by reverting: a single parked goroutine per cycle turns the oracle red with a
rising per-cycle `no_resource_leak` violation.

**Remaining:** open FDs are scraped from `/proc/self/fd`, which does not exist on
macOS, so the oracle's `OpenFDs` leg is inert on a developer Mac and live in
Linux CI. Closing that would need an FD-count mechanism that is neither cgo nor
`lsof`-shelling.

---

## SEC-2 — SPIFFE soundness checks formatting, not parsing

**Status:** the gate is real and does fire, but its scope is narrower than the
name implies.

`assert_spiffe_soundness` in `cross-test/current-generation/run.sh` rejects raw
`spiffe://` **construction** in generated code outside `sys/spiffe` — printf
verbs, `format!`/`{}`, `${}`, f-strings, and concatenation onto a spiffe literal.
That is genuine coverage of the construction side.

It asserts nothing about **parsing**. Generated code that splits a SPIFFE ID on
`/`, strips a prefix by index, or otherwise decomposes an ID by hand passes
cleanly. Since the whole point is that SPIFFE handling goes through the generated
helpers, half the surface is unguarded.

**To close:** extend the assertion with prefix/split parsing patterns, then prove
it fires on a deliberately hand-rolled parse. A pattern added without that proof
would be indistinguishable from one that can never match — see the parity gate
whose `find` patterns matched nothing and printed SKIP on every run.

---

## NEW-21 — empty-trust-domain classifier is pinned by existence only — CLOSED (Go, Java, Rust)

**Status (2026-10-15):** closed in all three. Go emits
`s2sm_identity_error_test.go` and Java `ServiceManagerIdentityErrorTest` beside
every ServiceManager; Rust's ServiceManager now carries
`#[cfg(test)] mod identity_error_tests` over the real
`is_permanent_identity_init_error` (the boxed `TokenMinterNotConfigured` the
retry loop sees is permanent; an error with the same text is not; transient
failures stay retryable), and `current-generation` runs `cargo test --lib` on
the generated model crate in every Rust service fixture and fails unless
`identity_error_tests::missing_token_minter_is_permanent ... ok` is in the log,
so the gate cannot pass by running zero tests. Rust has no trust-domain case:
an empty trust domain is refused by `SpiffeServerCertVerifier::new` before the
retry loop. Proven red: with the downcast replaced by a message match,
`the_same_text_is_not_the_typed_error` fails. The history below is the
original finding.

`isPermanentIdentityInitError` exists in the go and java ServiceManager templates
and is referenced from the retry path. The only tests are template regression
pins — `lib_templates_regression_test.go` and
`runtime_templates_regression_test.go` assert the *strings*
`"func isPermanentIdentityInitError(err error) bool"` and
`"if isPermanentIdentityInitError(idErr) {"` appear in the template text.

Nothing calls the function. A classifier that returned the wrong answer for every
input — turning a permanent failure into an infinite retry, or aborting on a
transient one — would keep both pins green. Three tolerance branches downstream
are likewise unexercised.

**To close:** table-driven tests over the real classifier in each language,
covering the permanent case, the transient case, and the wrapped-error case (go's
`errors.Is` branch and Java's cause-chain walk).

---

## NEW-46 — nothing asserts a sys-fold is complete

**Status:** no gate exists.

When a fold subsumes messages or fields, nothing checks that the folded result
preserves the set it replaced. A fold that silently dropped a message or a field
would generate cleanly and pass every gate; the loss would surface later as a
missing type at a call site, far from the cause.

**To close:** a soundness rule that compares the pre-fold and post-fold
message/field sets and fails on anything absent from the result. `cmd/soundness`
is the natural home — it already walks the model and already has a matrix-report
format for per-rule coverage.

---

## PC-W-5 — `proxy_dispatch::validate_request()` still has no in-repo caller

**Status:** the REST leg is now closed; the gRPC-proxy leg is not.

W2S request (ingress) validation in the generated REST dispatch is wired and
pinned in Rust, Go and Java: `cross-test/w2s-validate` hosts the real
generated `rest_dispatch::dispatch` / `dispatch_stream` (Rust),
`restdispatch.Dispatch` / `DispatchStream` (Go) and `RestDispatch.dispatch` /
`dispatchStream` (Java) against a real gRPC backend and proves an
`assert_email` violation is rejected `400` without reaching the backend, with
a valid request as the negative control.

`proxy_dispatch::validate_request(grpc_path, proto_bytes)` is a different seam:
it decodes raw proto frames, so its caller is the gateway's `proxy_grpc` layer,
which lives in the consuming repo and not here. Nothing in this repo calls it,
and no fixture can call it meaningfully without hosting a gRPC proxy — the
generated code contains the capability but never the call site, so a test that
invoked it directly would prove only that the function compiles.

**To close:** a fixture that generates a gateway (`spec.service.gateway`) and
hosts a real gRPC proxy hop in front of a backend service, so frames reach
`validate_request` the way production frames do. That is a materially larger
harness than the REST fixture, which needs no proxy at all.

---

## C2D-1 — the C2D server runs through its standalone host, not through `Run`

**Status:** Go, Java and Rust covered up to the c2d mount `Run` shares with the
standalone host; `Run`'s own call of that mount is not executed.

`cross-test/c2d-server` (`just c2d-server`) generates a c2d-only, cluster-free
daemon, compiles the whole generated model, and starts it through the
generated standalone host entry (Go `sm.ServeC2DStandalone`, Java
`ServiceManager.serveC2DStandalone`, Rust `ServiceManager::serve_c2d_standalone`)
from code outside the generated packages, exactly as a cluster-less daemon's
main does, on the declared socket (the generated `C2DSocketPath` /
`C2D_SOCKET_PATH`). It calls it over the socket through the generated c2dm
client: a tokenless valid call, request and response validation, server
streaming, the 0600 mode, stale-socket removal, and on stop the drain, socket
cleanup and exactly one handler shutdown. Proven by reverting, 2026-10-15:
dropping unary request validation from the Go, Java or Rust wrapper generator,
or dropping the handler shutdown call from any of the three entries, turns
the matching leg red. Earlier (2026-10-14): dropping the c2d auth skip from
the Go wrapper, or widening the chmod in either Go or Java chassis, turned it
red.

What it does not run is the `Run()` / `run()` line that mounts the same
server on `C2DSocketPath`: `Run` needs a live cluster (config, identity, state
store) that no in-repo fixture provides, so that line is pinned by the gate's
grep and by the mixed TLS + c2d render tests (`c2d_server_render_test.go`
under go/types and java/types), not executed.

**To close:** a ServiceManager harness that can boot `Run` against a fake
cluster.

---

## DS-1 — the GCS archive sink is compiled, never run against a bucket

**Status:** open.

`GcsArchiveSink` (Java, emitted only for a project that pins
`com.google.cloud:google-cloud-storage`) is compiled by the `current-generation`
`proto-quorumwrite` leg and its emission is asserted there. Nothing runs it. The
`DiskStoreTest` self-test exercises the shipping, retry and restore chain against
an in-memory `ArchiveSink`, so the chain is covered; the GCS calls (object create,
get, prefix list, ambient credentials) are not, and no gate has a bucket or
emulator to talk to.

To close it: a gate leg that points `archive.gcs_bucket` at a GCS emulator (or a
disposable test bucket behind a CI secret), ships one store through a real roll
and checkpoint, and restores it into an empty store. The ServiceManager's archive
wiring (`openDiskStoreLogs`, `attachArchive`) is in the same position: compiled
and grep-asserted, not run with `archive` set.

---

## How to close one of these

Two things make a fix real here, and only the second is usually skipped:

1. Something must CALL the capability, not merely contain it.
2. A test must FAIL when that call is removed. Verify this by actually removing
   it and watching the test go red.

If a check can only ever skip on current fixtures, label it NOT COVERAGE
explicitly, the way the TLS-degrade parity leg in `current-generation` does —
a silent SKIP reads as a pass to everyone who did not write it.
docs.MODEL_STRESS_TEST_PLAN.md:
> **ARCHIVED 2026-06-11.** Phase 1 implemented at `cross-test/chaos/` (code comments cite this file's section numbers — kept intact). Testing principles moved to `../DEVELOPMENT.md` (Runtime Chaos Testing Principles). Phases 2–4 are `../MVP_PLAN.md` → Later work.

# Model Stress, Resilience & Interop Test Plan

> **Status: proposed, not yet implemented.** A follow-on testing program. Independent of
> the in-flight findings-fix pass; can be built in parallel but is not a per-commit gate.
> Authored 2026-06-07.

A live, multi-language, multi-pod chaos/soak harness that exercises the tacplus-generated
**`model`** runtime under failure. Every existing gate is static or single-process
(`cross-test/current-generation` = does it compile; `cross-test/consumer-contract` = does the
rivet works; `cmd/soundness` = static parity). **Nothing exercises the model as a running mesh
under churn** — which is exactly where the runtime risks live (WATCH dropped/duplicate deltas,
per-scope task/feed leaks, unbounded shutdown, 30s stream teardown, fail-closed-vs-open auth,
stale caches). ROADMAP Track B blocks promoting the control-plane soundness rows to
build-failing "until the runtime suite corroborates the generated behavior" — **this harness is
that runtime suite.**

## 1. What it tests (four goals)

1. **Cross-language interop** — a Go client ↔ Rust server, TS ↔ Java, etc. The NxN matrix.
   The property unique to tacplus (5 languages from one model); the highest-value goal.
2. **Resilience** — instances recover from faults (SM lifecycle: identity/token, TLS,
   state-store connect, health, graceful + crash recovery, watch reconnect).
3. **Soak / leak** — sustained churn over hours surfaces leaks and gray failures (goroutines/
   threads/FDs/memory trends), e.g. the per-scope ring/drain leaks.
4. **Correctness under churn** — clients get *correct* data; watches resume gapless & ordered;
   auth stays fail-closed.

## 1a. Two profiles, one reusable harness

There are **two distinct tests** with different scopes, and they should **share one harness**
(orchestrator, chaos engine, invariant-oracle framework, report format) parameterized by *what
pods to deploy* and *which invariants apply*:

- **Profile A — Compiler/Model (this document, lives in `tacplus`).** Tests the
  **tacplus-generated `model` itself**, consumer-agnostic: synthetic multi-language nodes +
  *stubbed rivets* (test token/JWK signer, in-memory state source), with no
  consumer-specific identity service or concrete state backend. Proves the generated model is
  correct, resilient, and at cross-language parity independent of any deployment.
- **Profile B — System/Deployment (future platform todo).** Tests a real platform service
  stack end-to-end under the same chaos: the reusable services and their real identity, state,
  policy, gateway, and eventing paths. It is **not** tacplus's to own, but it should live at the
  platform group level rather than in a consumer repo. See the platform group-level todo at
  `todo/SYSTEM_STRESS_TEST_PLAN.md`.

So the **orchestrator, chaos engine, oracle framework, and report must be built reusable**
(deployment-profile is an input, not hardcoded), so future platform system profiles can point
them at a real service stack without reimplementing the chaos/verification machinery. That
reusable harness is part of the same platform direction as the reusable service move: the
chaos/orchestration engine is a consumer-agnostic platform component, while deployment profiles
supply concrete custom types, vservices, services, and invariants.

The rest of this document specifies **Profile A**. Where a section is profile-specific it says so;
everything in §2 (oracles), §5 (recovery/leak), §6 (orchestrator/cluster), §7 (report) is the
shared harness and applies to both.

## 2. Core principle: random for coverage, deterministic invariants for verification

A pure "sink returns random data" harness can only assert *"it returned and didn't error"* — it
would pass green even with dropped deltas, duplicate deltas, fail-open auth, or a permanently
stale cache. **Randomness drives the schedule; deterministic oracles drive the verdict.**

- **Unary (S2S/C2S):** requests carry a seq/seed; the server response is a pure function of the
  request (echo-with-transform). The client recomputes the expected value and asserts equality —
  catches validation drift, wrong-bytes binding, truncation.
- **State / WATCH (highest value):** the server drives a *known* per-key monotonic revision log.
  Watchers must observe a **gapless, ordered, duplicate-free** sequence with correct
  snapshot→delta framing and correct `OUT_OF_RANGE`/relist on resume. This is the only way to
  catch silent dropped deltas, re-sent ≤R deltas, and stale caches.
- **Auth (negative oracles):** include callers that *must be denied* (wrong namespace, no
  entitlement, expired token / token after a refresh failure). **Fail-open is caught only as an
  expected-deny that succeeded** — you cannot detect fail-open without exercising the deny path.

All randomness is **seeded** (reproducible): a failed run replays deterministically.

## 3. Topology

- **Synthetic node app, one per language (Go, Java, TS, Python, Rust).** Each is *both* a server
  (exposes the test S2S + C2S services) *and* a client (calls peer nodes). Handlers are thin,
  deterministic stubs (the point is the generated model does the work). One container image per
  language; all functionally identical, generated from the same test proto + per-language
  `tacplus.yaml`.
- **Call graph forces cross-language pairs** (e.g. each node calls every other node) so the
  interop matrix is covered for both S2S and C2S. **C2D** is intra-pod (local socket) — tested
  within a pod.
- **Scope: test the tacplus-generated model, NOT a consumer's backing services (corrected 2026-06-07).**
  tacplus does not know about any consumer's concrete identity service or state backing. Those
  live *behind* the model's generated rivets and are the consumer's concern, so they are **out of
  scope**. The harness exercises what tacplus actually generates: the
  ServiceManager lifecycle, the C2S/S2S/C2D clients and server wrappers, the generated auth
  (JWK verification / authorizer / namespace), validation, and the collection/WATCH machinery
  (Hub, replay ring, snapshot→delta, relist). This keeps the harness **consumer-agnostic** — it
  tests the model itself, independent of any one deployment.
- **Stand in the minimal thing each generated rivet requires** — never a concrete consumer
  service. *(A **rivet** is a generated attachment point on the model chassis — identity, state,
  TLS — where a backing service or a handler bolts on. The model defines the rivets; the
  consumer rivets its own backing services and handlers onto them.)*
  - *Identity rivet:* a minimal test token signer + a served JWK set (using tacplus's own
    generated token/JWK primitives), so the generated verify/refresh/identity-manager paths run
    for real. Not a consumer identity service.
  - *State rivet:* the WATCH/collection source is the synthetic node's own in-memory,
    deterministic state machine (the §2 monotonic log) — the generated state service, Hub, ring,
    and watch wrappers are what's under test; the persistence backing is irrelevant. NOT
    Hazelcast.
  - *TLS:* real mTLS/SPIFFE between nodes with test certs/CA (tacplus generates this — in scope).
- **Reconciling "as real as possible":** realism applies to *how the generated model runs* — real
  mTLS, real token issuance/verification/refresh through the generated paths, real K8s scheduling,
  real crash/graceful recovery — **not** to importing a consumer's backing services. The synthetic
  nodes are real generated models (full SM bootstrap, real auth/state usage, real
  readiness/health); only their business logic is a stub.
- The test proto exposes the shapes that stress the runtime: unary S2S + C2S, a WATCH collection,
  a SNAPSHOT/PAGE collection, an auth-required + an auth-denied method, a namespaced method.

## 4. Fault menu (not just SIGKILL)

| Fault | What it exercises |
|---|---|
| **SIGTERM (graceful)** | Bounded graceful shutdown + force-close. Catches unbounded-shutdown / shutdown-hang. |
| **SIGKILL (crash)** | Crash recovery, reschedule, client reconnect. |
| **Network blackhole / latency to state store** | Watch reconnect w/ bounded **jittered** backoff; the per-call-timeout-kills-long-stream bug. |
| **Dependency restart** (identity/state backends) | SM reconnect, cache resync, **auth fails closed** while the issuer is down. |
| **Token expiry / clock skew** | "Open channel isn't enough if refresh failed" send contract; per-message token freshness on streams. |
| **Slow consumer** | WATCH backpressure / flow control; bounded queues. |

## 5. "Recovered" — a definition with teeth, plus leak detection

1. **Fail-fast:** in-flight calls during a kill fail within a bounded deadline — they do **not
   hang** (shutdown/timeout findings).
2. **Resume SLA:** after reschedule, correctness resumes within a bounded time; watch caches
   **re-sync** (no permanent staleness — a terminal-stale cache must be observable, not silent).
3. **No resource creep:** the orchestrator scrapes per-pod goroutines/threads/FDs/memory **as a
   trend across many kill cycles over a soak** and asserts they stay flat. Leaks only show as a
   trend, never a snapshot.

## 6. Orchestrator & cluster

- **Separate cluster lifecycle from test orchestration.** The *outer* CI job creates/destroys the
  cluster and applies the orchestrator; the *in-cluster* orchestrator needs only RBAC to
  deploy/kill pods and scrape telemetry — not cluster-create rights. Safer, cleaner.
- **Cluster:** `kind`/`k3d` for the routine job (cheap, CI-friendly); a real cloud node only for
  periodic large-scale soak (realistic multi-node networking).
- **Orchestrator responsibilities:** deploy the matrix → drive seeded load → inject faults per a
  schedule → consume the model's *own* generated signals (unified readiness
  `Ready = cert ∧ config ∧ first-health`, health, trace/accounting events) **as part of the
  oracle** (so the test also verifies generated observability) → scrape resource trends → assert
  the §2 invariants and §5 recovery → emit a report.
- **Report retrieval then teardown:** report is pulled from the cluster (artifact), then the
  cluster is destroyed.

## 7. Report contents

- Interop matrix result (per language-pair, per RPC shape: pass/fail).
- Recovery-time distribution per fault type (p50/p99); any hangs (bounded-deadline violations).
- Invariant violations: dropped/duplicated/out-of-order deltas, fail-open auth (expected-deny
  succeeded), stale-cache-after-recovery, validation mismatches.
- Resource trends per pod over the soak (leak verdict).
- Injected-fault log vs unexpected-failure log (the report must distinguish *expected* chaos from
  *real* failures).
- Overall verdict + the seed (for deterministic replay).

## 8. Cadence & placement

- **Nightly + on-demand, never per-commit** (too slow/expensive). Per-commit keeps the existing
  compile/contract/soundness gates. A small smoke variant in the PR path is optional (see open
  decisions).
- **Placement (recommended):** a new `cross-test/chaos/` (or `cross-test/stress/`) tree in the
  tacplus repo — it pulls the generated model from the same compiler, so in-repo is natural,
  alongside the other `cross-test/` harnesses. (Alternative: its own repo if the K8s/cloud
  tooling becomes heavy enough to warrant isolation.)

## 9. Phasing (don't boil the ocean)

Maintaining 5 node apps + orchestrator + K8s harness is real ongoing cost. Grow it:

1. **Phase 1 — prove it catches a known bug.** 2 languages (Go + one other), `kind`,
   SIGKILL + SIGTERM, the WATCH monotonic-sequence invariant + one auth-deny oracle.
   **Acceptance bar: re-introduce the COLL-1 dropped-delta bug and confirm the harness goes red.**
   If it can't catch a bug we *know* exists, it isn't yet a test.
2. **Phase 2 — full interop matrix.** All five languages; S2S + C2S + C2D.
3. **Phase 3 — fault menu + leak soak.** Network, dependency-restart, token-expiry, slow-consumer;
   multi-hour resource-trend soak.
4. **Phase 4 — cloud-cluster nightly** at larger scale.

## 10. Open decisions (recommended defaults baked in; confirm or override)

- **Profile-A rivets** — **DECIDED: synthetic/stubbed rivets** (test token/JWK signer,
  in-memory deterministic state source, test mTLS CA; no consumer identity/state/policy services).
  The future platform system profile supplies the real reusable service stack.
  Resolved 2026-06-07.
- **`kind`/`k3d` vs cloud node** for v1 — plan assumes **`kind`** first, cloud for big soak.
- **Location** — plan assumes **`cross-test/chaos/` in-repo**; own repo if it grows heavy.
- **Cadence** — plan assumes **nightly + on-demand**; decide whether a trimmed smoke variant also
  runs per-PR.

## 11. Relationship to existing gates

Complements, does not replace: `current-generation` (compiles), `consumer-contract` (rivet works),
`cmd/soundness` (static parity). This is the **runtime / resilience / interop** layer, and it is
the prerequisite ROADMAP Track B names for promoting the advisory control-plane soundness rows
(auth, watch reconnect/teardown, readiness, task teardown) to **build-failing** — once this
corroborates the generated behavior, those rows can graduate.
docs.NAMING_CONVENTIONS.md:
# Naming and structure conventions

Proposed convention covering the seven consistency entries CON-2 … CON-8. The
maintainer delegated the choice, so this states the rules rather than the options.

Each rule is followed by what it costs to adopt and whether adopting it changes
**generated output**. That distinction is the important one: internal generator
hygiene can be fixed freely, but anything that changes an emitted identifier, file
name, or persisted name is a consumer-visible break and is listed separately at
the end rather than done quietly.

Verified against the current tree. Several CON entries were partly stale — the
specifics below are what is actually there now.

---

## 1. One case converter per transform, in `common/strutil`

**Rule.** Case conversion lives in `pkg/internal/common/strutil`, named for the
transform it performs: `ToSnakeCase`, `ToPascalCase`, `ToCamelCase`,
`ToUpperSnakeCase`. A generator package may define a local converter **only**
when the target language's own toolchain imposes a different rule, and the
function name must say which language it serves.

**Why.** There are currently eleven case helpers outside `strutil`, and two of
them independently implement upper-snake (a third, `toUpperSnake`, went with
`timeseries_group_counts.go` in the 2026-08-25 timedb boneyard):

| function | file |
|---|---|
| `upperSnake` | `pkg/internal/proto/registry_enums.go:173` |
| `pascalToUpperSnake` | `pkg/internal/proto/configholder.go:696` |
| `pascalCaseWord` | `pkg/runner/runner.go:570` |
| `goCamelCase` | `pkg/internal/go/types/helpers.go:511` |
| `toLowerCamel` | `pkg/internal/go/types/extraction_gen.go:386` |
| `upperSnakeCaseToCamelCase` | `pkg/internal/typescript/types/validation.go:1452` |

Three implementations of one transform is three chances to disagree, and NEW-20
is the record of what disagreement costs: a converter change silently altered a
**persisted** table name, orphaning the existing table with nothing failing.

**Legitimately local**, and to be kept — each encodes a foreign toolchain's rule,
not a general transform:

- `pyGeneratedSnakeName` — python codegen's own naming
- `tsGeneratedSnakeName`, `tsPascalIdentifier`, `tsSnakeIdentifier` — TS codegen
- `methodSnakeNameLower` — prost's digit-acronym handling, which deliberately
  diverges from `ToSnakeCase` (see `tonic_names.go`)

**Cost:** small, mechanical. **Generated output:** must be unchanged — the three
upper-snake variants have to be checked for behavioural equivalence before
merging, not assumed equal. Any divergence found is a real bug, and if one of
them feeds a persisted name it needs the NEW-20 treatment.

## 2. Shared template loading, parameterised by language

**Rule.** One `LoadTemplate(subdir, name string)` in
`pkg/internal/common/tmplutil`. No per-language copy.

**Why.** `tmplutil.go` exists four times — python, typescript, rust, java — and
the copies differ only in the package clause, one comment, and the subdirectory
string passed to `fs.Sub`. It is a parameter, duplicated as a file.

**Cost:** trivial. **Generated output:** none. Do this one first; it is the
cheapest demonstration that the convention holds.

## 3. Generator package clause matches its directory

**Rule.** A generator package under `pkg/internal/<lang>/types` declares
`package types`.

**Why.** `pkg/internal/{python,typescript,rust,go}/types` all declare
`package types`. `pkg/internal/java/types` declares `package java`, across all 54
files in it. Same directory depth, same role, different clause — so java alone
cannot be reached by any convention that says "the types package".

**Cost:** a whole-package rename of 54 files. It turned out cheap to apply
because the package has exactly ONE importer, `pkg/builder/builder.go`, and it
already imports under the explicit alias `javatypes` — so no use site referred to
the package by its default name and nothing outside the directory changed.

**Generated output:** none — this is the generator's own package name, not
anything it emits, so `determinism` and `current-generation` prove it byte for
byte.

java is the only real outlier. An earlier draft of this rule also claimed
`package daemon` under python/typescript and `package foo` under java; that was
wrong — those strings are proto/Go fixture content inside `*_test.go` files, not
package clauses. Counting the first `package` line of each file gives 33/37/61/57
`package types` for python, typescript, rust and go, against java's 54
`package java`.

## 4. `_gen.go` means "emits code"

**Rule.** A generator source file is named `<subject>_gen.go` when its job is to
emit generated code, and `<subject>.go` when it is a helper, model, or registry.
The suffix describes the file's role, not its age.

**Why.** The suffix carries no information today. The clearest case:
`java/types/release.go` and `rust/types/release_gen.go` were structurally
parallel — same function names (`writeRelease`,
`generate<Lang>EntitlementBuilder`, `write<Lang>EntitlementFields`), same role —
under two different names. That one is fixed; java now matches rust.

**Cost:** larger than it looks, and larger than the ledger implied. Beyond the
`release` pair, more than fifteen files under `pkg/internal/proto` write output
without the suffix (`state.go`, `record_map.go`, `configholder.go`,
`persisted_store.go`, `entitlement_gen.go`, …). Applying the rule fully is a
15+-file rename touching most of that package.

**Generated output:** none — file names here are generator-internal.

**Status:** the cross-language `release` drift is fixed. The bulk rename is NOT
done. It is mechanical and safe, but it will conflict with anything else in
flight in `internal/proto`, so it wants a quiet moment and its own commit.

## 5. Every emitted file carries the same DO-NOT-EDIT header

**Rule.** Every generated file begins with the copyright line, `Generated by
tacplus`, and `CODE GENERATED - DO NOT EDIT`, in the target language's comment
syntax.

**Why.** The go tree carries 24 pre-rename headers, and swift/csharp templates
carry no DO-NOT-EDIT line at all. A generated file without that marker is a file
someone will eventually hand-edit, and the edit will vanish at the next
generation with no warning.

**Cost:** a header pass across templates. **Generated output:** yes — the header
text of emitted files changes. Harmless to consumers (comments only) but it will
show up as a large diff in every consumer's generated tree, so it should land in
its own commit, announced.

## 6. Package-name transforms are documented and collision-checked

**Rule.** Any transform from a canonical proto package to a target-language
module name is documented in this file, and must be injective. If two distinct
canonical packages can fold to one module name, generation fails rather than
silently merging them.

**Why.** `swiftIdentifier` / `csharpIdentifier` split on every non-alphanumeric
character and PascalCase-join the parts, so all separators are erased:

    foo.bar -> FooBar    foo_bar -> FooBar    foo-bar -> FooBar    foobar -> Foobar

Two names differing only in separators therefore produce one identifier, and the
symbols merge silently — capability loss with no error, the recurring shape.

The ledger recorded this as *module* folding colliding *packages*. That is not
what the code does, and the correction matters for anyone implementing the guard:
`swiftModuleName`/`csharpModuleName` are applied ONCE, to the package base
(`generator.go:91` and `:94`). The transform underneath them, `swiftIdentifier` /
`csharpIdentifier`, is what gets applied per name — to service names, message
names, method names and path segments. **The collision risk is on identifiers,
not on packages**, so a guard placed on module names would sit where two names
can never meet and would never fire.

**Measured, so the next person has a baseline** — no collision exists today:

| population | count | collisions |
|---|---|---|
| proto packages across the platform | 74 | 0 |
| message + service names | 1215 | 0 |

**Cost:** a collision check over emitted identifiers, per scope. **Generated
output:** none today, since nothing currently collides.

**Status:** NOT implemented. The hazard is real but entirely latent, and the
fix must guard identifiers within a scope rather than package names. Recorded
with its measurement rather than implemented in a hurry against a premise that
turned out to be wrong.

## 7. One annotation vocabulary in `spec.proto`

**Rule.** Constraint annotations live in the `assert_*` family. An annotation that
constrains a field is named `assert_<constraint>`. Option numbers are allocated
from a documented range per category, and the ranges live in a comment block at
the top of `spec.proto`.

**Why.** `required_if_false`, `required_if_true` and `required_if_eq`
(`spec.proto:1070,1075,1103`) constrain fields but sit outside the `assert_`
family, so neither a reader nor a tool can enumerate "the constraints" by name.
There is no documented option-number scheme. (The two parallel graph annotation
systems this rule also cited are gone — graph store support was removed
2026-08-25.)

**Cost:** renaming a proto option is a **breaking change** for every consumer
proto that uses it. See the end of this file.

## 8. A registry field name means one thing

**Rule.** A name in `tacplus.proto` has exactly one meaning across the schema.
Where two concepts genuinely differ, they get different names, even if that makes
one of them longer.

**Why.** `graph_type` used to mean two different things in `tacplus.proto`: the
state-graph boundary kind on `BoundaryInfo`, and the graph-store node type name on
`TypeInfo`. The second was removed with graph store support (2026-08-25), so only
the boundary-kind meaning survives — the collision is resolved by deletion, not by
a rename. `EventPublish` and `WatchInfo` are near-twins whose difference is not
recoverable from their names. String-typed enums use mixed casing.

**Cost:** renaming a registry field changes the emitted registry. See below.

## 9. Comments describe the mechanism, not one caller

**Rule.** A comment on a general mechanism names the mechanism. Reach for a
specific service name only when the text is genuinely about that service.

**Why.** A concrete service name appeared in six comments describing generic
behaviour, which tells a reader the mechanism is specific to that service when
it is not.

**Cost:** trivial. **Generated output:** none.

---

## Safe to adopt now

Rules 1, 2, 3, 4 and 9 are generator-internal. They change no emitted byte, and
`determinism` plus `current-generation` prove that: if generated output shifts,
the byte-identical assertions fail. Each should land in its own commit.

Order by cost, cheapest first — rule 2, then 9, then 1, then 4, then 3. Rule 3
is last because it is a 54-file package rename that will conflict with anything
else in flight; do it when nothing else is open in `internal/java`.

**Adopted so far:** rule 2 (shared template loader) and rule 1's upper-snake case
— `upperSnake`, `toUpperSnake` and `pascalToUpperSnake` were three identical
copies of one transform in a single package, now `strutil.ToUpperSnakeCase`. They
were checked for divergence before merging; they agreed.

Rule 9 is adopted, and rule 4's cross-language `release` drift is fixed.

Rule 3 is adopted: `pkg/internal/java/types` now declares `package types` like
its four siblings.

**Not yet adopted:** the rest of rule 1 (the remaining scattered helpers) and
rule 4's bulk `_gen.go` rename. Both are safe; neither is urgent.

Rule 6 is safe **unless** a collision already exists, which is worth finding out
either way.

## Needs an explicit go-ahead — these break consumers

Not done as part of adopting this convention, because each changes something
outside this repository:

- **Rule 5** (headers) — changes the first lines of every generated file. Cosmetic
  but produces a very large diff in every consumer tree.
- **Rule 7** (`required_if_*` → `assert_required_if_*`) — renaming a proto option
  breaks every consumer proto that uses it. Needs a deprecation window: accept
  both names, warn on the old one, remove later.
- **Rule 8** (registry field names) — changes the emitted registry, which
  consumers and the LLM-facing registry read.

The pattern for all three is the same: accept both spellings, warn on the old,
remove after a stated period. That is a maintainer's call on timing, not mine.
docs.NEUTRAL_ANALYSIS.md:
# Neutral Analysis Entry Point

This document is the entry point for neutral tacplus analysis. It is meant to
guide reviewers, agents, and maintainers toward evidence-backed findings while
filtering out personal preference, language preference, and implementation
religion.

For downstream tacplus consumers, the common neutral-analysis contract is
`CONSUMER_NEUTRAL_ANALYSIS.md`. Consumer repositories might not have that file
on disk, so reviewers must read the canonical repository copy:

https://github.com/tacplus-dev/tacplus/blob/main/docs/CONSUMER_NEUTRAL_ANALYSIS.md

When reviewing tacplus itself, read that same downstream-consumer contract and
verify that tacplus actually gives consumers generated surfaces that let them
comply with it. If a consumer is forced to violate the downstream rule because
tacplus has not generated the needed model surface, report the consumer code as
a forced deviation and report the missing generated surface as a tacplus
self-compliance finding.

## Goal

Review tacplus as a generator and as a producer of generated production code.
The analysis should identify concrete engineering risks: bugs, parity gaps,
deadlocks, races, gray failures, fail-open paths, swallowed failures, retry and
timeout gaps, missing crash-on-irrecoverable behavior, and security
vulnerabilities.

The desired output is a list of confirmed or carefully qualified findings with
clear reproduction paths and recommended fixes.

## Ground Rules

- Do not treat any supported language as the reference implementation.
- Do not evaluate whether tacplus should have been written in another language.
- Do not include taste, style, or tool preference unless it creates a concrete
  correctness, security, operability, or maintainability risk.
- Do not assume downstream service names belong in tacplus. tacplus is generic;
  downstream services are consumers.
- Do not drop a finding because it is already known. A known, unfixed issue is
  an open finding: when the local ledger is present, it stays in
  `todo/OPEN_FINDINGS.md` and appears in every analysis report until it is
  actually fixed, with evidence.
- Do not modify files, commit, push, tag, or change downstream repositories as
  part of the analysis unless explicitly asked.
- Keep generated output disposable. Generate into temporary or ignored target
  directories only.
- Separate confirmed findings from hypotheses and discarded leads.

## Contract Inputs

Read these first:

- `README.md`
- `AGENTS.md`
- `roadmap/README.md`
- `docs/API.md`
- `docs/CONSUMER_NEUTRAL_ANALYSIS.md`, or the canonical repository copy at
  https://github.com/tacplus-dev/tacplus/blob/main/docs/CONSUMER_NEUTRAL_ANALYSIS.md
- `docs/DEVELOPMENT.md`
- local `todo/OPEN_FINDINGS.md`, when present — the working ledger of known,
  unfixed findings
- `docs/THEORY.md`
- `docs/USER.md`
- `the archived GENERATED_CODE_ISSUES plan` — the closed historical TCG fix ledger
  (background evidence only; the active ledger is `todo/OPEN_FINDINGS.md`)

Use `docs/API.md` and the annotated proto model as the generated API contract.
Use `docs/DEVELOPMENT.md` for compiler and soundness expectations. Use
`docs/CONSUMER_NEUTRAL_ANALYSIS.md` as the contract tacplus expects downstream
consumers and LLM reviewers to follow. If that file is not present locally, use
the repository URL above. The tacplus analysis must verify that the compiler
and generated code actually make those consumer rules practical, consistent,
and enforceable. Use `roadmap/README.md` for future tracks, historical baseline
references, and plan archives.

## tacplus Assumptions

- `tacplus.yaml` declares only settings that cannot be logically defined in
  proto, such as package naming, language target, output location, and enabled
  generated surfaces.
- Downstream consumers should be able to use the generated model rather than
  hand-roll lifecycle, auth, validation, serialization, state, persistence,
  EventBus, and client wiring. If a downstream consumer must bypass generated
  infrastructure for a common pattern, that is evidence of a possible tacplus
  gap.
- Consumer-local tools should consume `registry.json` or embedded generated
  metadata for tacplus semantics, not parse proto files directly. The registry
  must therefore contain enough information for downstream codegen, policy,
  docs, and LLM analysis tools to avoid ad hoc proto parsing.
- A change to a `spec.vservice` proto should not require manual service
  infrastructure edits. Tacplus should expose enough generated model/registry
  data and generated seams for consumers to handle vservice fallout through
  automated codegen/tooling patterns.
- C2S and W2S are independently enabled generated surfaces, not language
  defaults. TypeScript may use W2S for browser consumers, but TypeScript also
  needs C2S when used on the server and C2S-capable languages need W2S when
  enabled.
- Auth-disabled methods skip authentication and authorization only; validation
  still applies.
- Auth-enabled methods must validate messages, require a valid token, enforce
  authorization, and enforce namespace policy before dispatch.
- Long-lived authenticated streams (client-streaming/bidi) carry exactly one
  token, attached at STREAM OPEN — gRPC metadata cannot change mid-stream, so
  a per-send token preflight is prohibited (it mints a token the server never
  sees and can fail a legitimate send). Servers terminate streams carrying
  expired credentials; generated reconnect paths mint a fresh token per
  attempt. See docs/API.md "Client Send Contract".
- A subject may act only on an object namespace at or below the subject's
  namespace level.
- If tacplus cannot generate a full supported surface for a declared proto
  shape, generation should fail loudly.

## Model Smells

A model smell is any generated surface that is computed from inference,
build-inclusion, or hardcoded literals instead of a scoped first-class
declaration. Per `docs/THEORY.md`, a healthy model has:

- Single source of truth: every constraint, boundary, auth policy, and RPC
  exists in one place — the proto declarations.
- Generation scoped to the owner: a service's surface is a function of what it
  declares and owns, not of which protos its build happens to include.
- First-class declarations, not inference: "who publishes, consumes, or owns X"
  is declared, not recovered from package layout, message names, or a code
  literal.

Recurring variants to sweep for, across `pkg/internal/**`, `pkg/templates/**`,
and `pkg/proto/sys/spec.proto`:

- a build-wide scan that emits per-service output without an ownership filter,
  so an unrelated proto leaks into another service's generated surface;
- two mechanisms encoding one concept, so the generated surface depends on
  which incidental encoding the author chose;
- an owner or role recovered by package, service, or message name inference —
  or a hardcoded literal — where a first-class declaration already exists or
  should exist.

The tell is the cross-entity collapse: adding, removing, or renaming an
unrelated entity silently changes another entity's generated output.

## Generated Output Parity Audit

This section absorbs the retired `deep-parity` harness. When the analysis
needs generated-output evidence (workflow steps 3-5), build a disposable
kitchensink and compare the outputs directly:

1. Create a temporary project directory per generating language, each with a
   minimal `tacplus.yaml` (same `pkg`, explicit client-surface settings) and
   the language's project file (`go.mod` / `package.json` / `pyproject.toml`
   / `pom.xml` / `Cargo.toml`).
2. Run `tacplus build --src <proto-src>` in each. Every supported language
   must build; a generation failure is itself a finding.
3. Compare directory structures across languages for each major generated
   directory (`types/`, `sys/`, `s2sm/`, `c2sm/`, `w2sm/`, `c2dm/`,
   `rest/`): the same services and packages must exist in every language
   that supports the surface, minus documented target-class differences.
4. For each service, compare the generated files — server wrappers, gRPC
   clients, state wrappers, REST clients. Flag any service present in some
   languages and missing in others.
5. Deep-compare two or three representative services: same methods, same
   features (auth, validation, accounting, streaming, TLS), same
   error-code mapping.
6. Compare `sys/` runtime public API surfaces (functions, methods,
   classes) across languages.

Keep the kitchensink in a temporary or ignored directory; never commit the
outputs.

## Consistency And Documentation Pass

Every full analysis run includes this pass over the compiler source and the
documentation: thoroughly look through the code and determine whether there
are any inconsistent patterns, naming, or layout, and make sure the
documentation is correct.

Patterns and layout:

- Layout parity across `pkg/internal/<lang>/` packages: the same concern
  should live in the same-named file in every language generator. Flag
  drift, and flag any gate (for example `cmd/soundness`) forced to hand-map
  per-language file exceptions — a hand-map that goes stale hides defects.
- Emitter mechanism: sibling languages should use the same mechanism
  (template file vs string-building) for the same generated surface; flag
  outliers.
- Duplicated helpers that belong in `common/` — especially copies whose
  behavior has diverged (case conversion, name mapping).
- Package visibility: any `pkg/` package not reachable from `cmd/` belongs
  in `pkg/internal/`.
- Dead code: unused functions, types, constants, and parameters; orphaned
  templates; dangling template references; dead skip lists.
- Committed artifacts that violate stated invariants (for example generated
  output committed under `cross-test/`).

Naming:

- `spec.proto` annotation families: suffix conventions, synonym pairs, enum
  value naming, `reserved` statements for retired field numbers, and the
  option-number range scheme.
- Registry schema (`tacplus.proto`): one name per concept — flag same-name
  different-meaning fields and different-name same-meaning fields.
- Cross-artifact concept drift: a concept should carry the same name in
  `spec.proto`, the registry, `tacplus.yaml`, generated APIs, and the docs.
- Exported identifiers named consistently for what they do.

Documentation correctness — verify every checkable claim against code:

- `README.md`, `AGENTS.md`, and every file in `docs/`: CLI commands and
  flags, `tacplus.yaml` keys, annotation tables, code examples (they must
  compile as written), generated-library tables, architecture and directory
  maps, CI/gate descriptions, and numeric limits.
- Docs must not document surfaces that do not exist, and must not omit
  supported surfaces consumers need.
- Cross-references must resolve; tooling script headers and embedded prompts
  must match current paths and behavior.
- The same standard applies to comments in `spec.proto`/`tacplus.proto` that
  carry examples or annotation references.

Report the results in the standard Finding Format and record them in
`todo/OPEN_FINDINGS.md` like any other finding.

## Analysis Workflow

1. Read the contract documents and the relevant generator code.
2. Re-verify every entry in local `todo/OPEN_FINDINGS.md`, when present,
   against current source.
   Report each entry that is still present as an open finding; move an entry
   out only with fix evidence (commit plus passing regression), and update the
   ledger with new confirmed findings from this run.
3. Generate representative output for each full language when source review is
   not enough to prove behavior (the kitchensink recipe in "Generated Output
   Parity Audit" is the standard fixture).
4. Review generated output as production code, not as an implementation detail.
5. Compare generated surfaces across languages for semantic parity:
   - handler seams;
   - service wrappers;
   - generated clients;
   - C2S and W2S transport behavior;
   - C2D behavior where applicable;
   - collection snapshot and watch behavior;
   - validation, auth, tracing, accounting, retry, timeout, and teardown.
6. **Promise-coverage pass.** For each behavioral guarantee stated in
   `docs/API.md` (and AGENT.md where it makes claims about generated
   behavior), enumerate the code paths where the promise must hold and demand
   mechanical evidence on each path, per full language:
   - a generated/contract test that exercises the path (including the
     NEGATIVE case — the promise observably refusing a violation);
   - or an enforced `cmd/soundness` row;
   - or an explicitly documented, rationale-bearing carve-out in API.md.
   Path enumeration matters more than mechanism existence: a promise like
   "outbound messages are validated" must be checked on EVERY send path
   (unary response, server-stream item, client-stream/bidi outbound, W2S
   REST/SSE/WebSocket writes, C2D responses), not declared satisfied because
   validation code exists somewhere near one of them. A promise with no
   mechanical evidence on some path is AUTOMATICALLY a finding — absence of
   proof is the finding, even with no observed failure and no cross-language
   divergence. (Motivating miss: OF-30 — egress validation existed on some
   paths, was promised in API.md, and had no per-path evidence; two full
   analysis runs passed it because existence checks and divergence checks
   both came back clean.) Two reviewer stances to hold during this pass:
   read each promise from the RECEIVER's perspective (W2S browser apps and
   external consumers are not tacplus-generated — egress guarantees are
   their only protection), and treat a green harness as evidence only for
   behaviors the harness actually exercises.
7. Run a model smell check: sweep the generator and template code for the
   smell variants defined in "Model Smells" above. Report each smell even when
   no runtime failure has been observed yet; the collapse mode is the finding.
8. Run the consistency and documentation pass defined in "Consistency And
   Documentation Pass": inconsistent patterns, naming, layout, and
   documentation correctness.
9. Cross-check tacplus against the downstream-consumer rules in
   `docs/CONSUMER_NEUTRAL_ANALYSIS.md`:
   - generated ServiceManager surfaces must make handwritten lifecycle,
     transport, auth, validation, persistence, EventBus, and helper plumbing
     unnecessary for common service patterns;
   - generated auth and namespace enforcement must be available at the wrapper
     seam so consumers do not need parallel auth systems;
   - generated registry metadata must be sufficient for consumer-local
     generators and LLM tools to avoid parsing proto text for tacplus
     semantics;
   - `spec.vservice` changes should have generated/registry-driven paths for
     service-local wiring fallout;
   - generated identity surfaces (`sys/spiffe`, token wrappers, authorizers,
     service-manager identity) must make the consumer SPIFFE identity rules
     followable: construction, self-describing parsing, comparison, and
     distinct `azp` exposure all come from generated code, so a consumer never
     needs to hand-format or string-compare a SPIFFE ID;
   - generated API and registry metadata should support verb/capability
     analysis and expose enough evidence to detect method overload.
10. Reproduce suspected failures with the smallest useful fixture.
11. Record confirmed findings with severity, evidence, and a recommended fix.
12. Record unconfirmed hypotheses separately, with the missing evidence
    clearly stated.

## Finding Criteria

A finding should be included when it has at least one concrete failure mode:

- generated code fails to compile for a supported declared surface;
- generated code violates `docs/API.md`;
- a behavioral guarantee documented in `docs/API.md` lacks mechanical evidence
  (test, enforced soundness row, or documented carve-out) on one or more code
  paths where it must hold — absence of proof for a documented promise is a
  finding even without an observed failure (promise-coverage pass, workflow
  step 6);
- one language silently differs from another for the same declared surface;
- validation, auth, authorization, or namespace enforcement can be bypassed;
- a failure is swallowed, downgraded, or hidden from the caller;
- an irrecoverable startup or runtime failure does not fail fast;
- retry, timeout, or cancellation behavior can hang or gray-fail;
- a long-lived stream can leak tasks, goroutines, threads, handles, or tokens;
- generated code can deadlock or race under normal use;
- generated code exposes a security weakness;
- a generated surface is computed from inference, build-inclusion, or a
  hardcoded literal rather than a scoped first-class declaration, so a change
  to an unrelated entity silently changes another entity's generated output;
- tacplus contains stale downstream-specific or deprecated concepts that affect
  generated behavior or confuse the contract.
- generated code or templates format `spiffe://` outside `sys/spiffe` and
  tests, project `namespace` as a complete subject identity, expose a SPIFFE
  identity that is read from an untrusted wire claim rather than derived, or
  compare identities by raw string prefix instead of the generated
  `is_at_or_below` / `is_spiffe_at_or_below` relations. The cross-test
  soundness gate (`assert_spiffe_soundness`) should catch raw formatting; a
  shape that slips past the gate is itself a finding.
- tacplus generated code or registry output forces consumers to violate
  `docs/CONSUMER_NEUTRAL_ANALYSIS.md`, such as parsing proto text for tacplus
  semantics, hand-wiring EventBus publishers, bypassing ServiceManager-owned
  lifecycle, or manually patching infrastructure after a `spec.vservice`
  schema change.
- a consumer violation is unavoidable because tacplus has declared a consumer
  rule but does not yet generate the model surface required to follow it.

## Finding Format

Use this shape for each issue:

```text
ID:
Severity:
Confidence:
Status: confirmed | hypothesis | discarded
Surface:
Language(s):
Source:
Generated evidence:
Failure mode:
Reproduction:
Recommended fix:
Notes:
```

Prefer file and line references relative to the repository root. Avoid absolute
paths in written reports.

## Useful Commands

Run these from the repository root as needed:

```sh
rg "BigData|deprecated|reserved|fail open|TODO|panic|unwrap|expect"
rg "spiffe://|spiffe_id|azp" --glob '!**/sys/spiffe/**'
rg '== "(gateway|eventbus|ServiceHealth|Mint)"' pkg/internal pkg/templates
go test ./...
go run ./cmd/soundness -root .
just consumer-build
just consumer-smoke
```

When generating analysis fixtures, keep outputs outside tracked source paths or
inside ignored target directories.

## Expected Output

The final analysis should lead with confirmed findings ordered by severity. It
should then include hypotheses that need more evidence, discarded leads that
looked suspicious but were ruled out, and any open questions that require a
human decision rather than a technical fix.

Do not use the report to relitigate already withdrawn work. If a concept was
parked, withdrawn, or downstream-only (check `roadmap/README.md` for future
tracks and `archive/` for completed/withdrawn plans), treat that status as the
source of truth unless current code contradicts it. Withdrawn status applies
to features and scope decisions only, never to defects: a previously reported
defect that is still present in the code is an open finding every time, and
prior reports, ledgers, and "already known" status are reasons to fix it, not
reasons to leave it out of the report.
docs.PENDING_DESIGN_DECISIONS.md:
# Pending design decisions

Three items that are **not bugs and not oversights**. Each is a modelling or
product choice that needs a maintainer to rule on, and each was deliberately left
alone because picking a direction unilaterally would be the wrong call.

Read this when you want to decide one. Each entry states what exists today, what
is actually undecided, the options with their trade-offs, and a recommendation
you are free to reject.

State verified against the current tree, not carried forward from the ledger —
two of the three turned out to be narrower than previously recorded.

---

## MS-5 — a service's OPA role is inferred from an import

**Where:** `pkg/internal/proto/derive_virtual.go:47-54`

A service is treated as *the OPA server* if its proto imports
`sys/opalib.proto`, and as an *OPA client* otherwise:

```go
// Skip if this service IS the OPA server (imports sys/opalib.proto).
isOpaServer := false
for _, imp := range serviceDesc.Imports {
    if imp == "sys/opalib.proto" { isOpaServer = true; break }
}
```

The core of MS-5 was fixed in `fa4c6d6e` (a hard error replaced a silent path).
What remains is the modelling question, and it is genuinely a question: an import
is a *dependency* statement, and this reads it as a *role* declaration. The two
usually coincide, but nothing enforces that. A service that imports the library
for any other reason silently stops generating an OpaEval client, and the failure
is an absent capability — the shape this codebase produces over and over.

**Options**

1. **Leave it.** Zero churn. The coupling stays implicit and undocumented, and
   the next person to import that proto for an unrelated reason gets a silent
   behaviour change.
2. **Declare the role explicitly** — a `(spec.service).opa_server` bool, with the
   import check kept as a cross-check that hard-errors on disagreement. Costs one
   annotation on one service, and makes a wrong import loud instead of silent.
3. **Derive from the service identity** already in the registry rather than from
   imports at all. Cleanest model, largest change.

**Recommendation:** option 2. It is a few lines, keeps the current behaviour as a
consistency check rather than a guess, and converts the failure mode from "the
client silently disappears" to "generation stops and tells you". Option 3 is
better modelling but not worth the churn for a single service.

---

## NEW-8 — the ANONYMIZE pseudonym key has no provisioning, and no rotation story

**This is the one worth deciding first — the feature does not currently work.**

**Where:** `pkg/proto/sys/grpcconfig.proto:169-175` (`anonymize_hmac_key`,
field 19), consumed by the generated pseudonymize primitives in
`pkg/internal/go/types/sanitize_gen.go:239,255,271,287` and the rust/java
equivalents.

Previously recorded as "a bare parameter with no provisioning seam". That is now
out of date in one direction and understated in another:

- A typed config seam **does** exist. `anonymize_hmac_key` is a per-deployment
  secret carried on grpcconfig, described as the key that makes a value
  pseudonymize to the same surrogate "at any depth, across services and
  restarts".
- **Nothing populates it.** The operator does not set it, and no bootstrap YAML
  sets it. The field is generated, plumbed, and never assigned — the same
  capability-without-a-call-site shape as the credential redactor and the health
  probe defaults.

The practical consequence: the generated primitives fail loud on an empty key
(they panic with "store must supply a per-deployment secret"), so any service
whose records carry ANONYMIZE-capable `(spec.redact)` fields would crash on its
first pseudonymizing egress. It is not a silent data leak — the fail-closed
design holds — but ANONYMIZE cannot be used at all until the key is provisioned.

No service in the platform currently declares an ANONYMIZE-capable
`(spec.redact)` field, which is why nothing is crashing today. The first one to
declare one is the moment this becomes an outage rather than a decision.

What actually needs deciding is not "add a seam" but two policy questions the
seam cannot answer by itself:

1. **Where does the key come from, and how does every service get the SAME one?**
   The cross-service surrogate-stability guarantee is only true if every service
   receives an identical key. That is a distribution problem: operator-generated
   and pushed through config, kernel-minted like other secrets, or supplied by
   the deployer as an opaque input.
2. **Can it rotate?** Rotating changes every surrogate. Previously emitted
   pseudonyms stop linking to newly emitted ones, silently and irreversibly —
   any analysis joining on a surrogate across the rotation boundary is wrong
   without erroring. A key that can never rotate is also a poor answer for a
   long-lived secret.

**Options**

1. **Operator-generated, stored once, never rotated.** Simplest, works, and
   permanently accepts a non-rotatable secret.
2. **Operator-generated with versioned keys** — surrogates carry a key
   generation, consumers can tell "computed under a different key" from "different
   value". Rotation becomes possible and analysis can be honest about the
   boundary. Costs a format change to the surrogate.
3. **Deployer-supplied**, treated like any other external secret, with rotation
   explicitly the deployer's problem and documented as breaking linkage.

**Recommendation:** decide 1 vs 2 now, before anything depends on surrogate
stability, because retrofitting a key generation into an emitted surrogate format
is a data migration. If ANONYMIZE is going to matter, option 2. If it is
speculative, option 1 plus a written statement that rotation is unsupported.

Either way this needs a maintainer: it is a product decision about data linkage,
not a code cleanup.

---

## PAR-9 — Python clients raise bare `RuntimeError` where other languages raise a typed code

**Where:** `pkg/templates/python/types/grpcclient.py.tmpl` (2 sites),
`pkg/templates/python/types/w2sclient.py.tmpl` (7 sites)

Python raises an untyped error for conditions the other languages report with a
structured status:

| condition | python | java | go |
|---|---|---|---|
| token provider missing | `RuntimeError("auth token provider is required")` | `ProtoException(UNAUTHENTICATED, …)` | `status.Error(codes.Unauthenticated, …)` |
| empty token | `RuntimeError("token provider returned an empty token")` | `ProtoException(UNAUTHENTICATED, …)` | — |
| W2S HTTP status | `RuntimeError(f"W2S HTTP status {…}")` | typed | typed |

A Python caller cannot distinguish "not authenticated, get a new token" from any
other failure without matching on message text. Retry and re-auth logic that is
straightforward in go/java is not expressible in Python against these clients.

The reason this was parked rather than fixed: Python clients became a live
surface only after `2a0f82be`, and changing the exception type is a **breaking
change** for any consumer already catching `RuntimeError`.

**Options**

1. **Leave it.** No breakage; Python stays a second-class client surface.
2. **Introduce a typed `ProtoError`** carrying a status code, subclassing
   `RuntimeError` so existing `except RuntimeError` handlers keep working while
   new code can catch precisely. Backward compatible, and the only option that is
   both.
3. **Raise `grpc.RpcError`** with proper codes for full parity with the gRPC
   idiom. Cleanest for consumers who already speak gRPC, hardest for the W2S
   paths, which are HTTP/SSE/WebSocket and not gRPC at all.

**Recommendation:** option 2. Subclassing `RuntimeError` makes it a
non-breaking change, so it can land without coordinating with consumers, and it
covers the W2S transports that option 3 does not fit.

---

## What "decide" means here

None of these is urgent in the sense of a live defect: NEW-8 fails loud, MS-5
affects one service, PAR-9 is an ergonomics gap. But NEW-8's option 1-vs-2 choice
gets harder the longer it waits — once surrogates exist in stored data, changing
their format is a migration rather than a decision.
