# Record / Event / Store / Projection model (annotation contract)

This is the authoritative tacplus contract for the data plane shared by **eventbus**
and **the record store**. Both are generic, app-agnostic services: their hand-written code
names no vservice; everything vservice-specific is generated from the annotations
below. `mv <vservice>.proto .off` makes the vservice disappear everywhere with only
a rebuild.

> **timedb and graphdb went to the boneyard 2026-08-25** (BIG GOAL 3, first move
> #1): out of the fleet build, protos deleted. With them went the `graph_store`,
> `graph_projection` and `timeseries_store` annotations' only hosts, and the
> `TimedbQuery` / `GraphdbQuery` / `TimeseriesQuery` / `TimeseriesGroupCounts`
> query planes. The `graph_store` / `graph_type` / `graph_projection` generator
> code — parser, IR, Go graph helpers (`ToGraph`/`FromGraph`), the graph branch of
> the extraction emitters, and the graph legs of the Go templates — was removed
> from tacplus on the same day (BONEYARD_QUESTIONS Q2), along with the field-level
> `spec.graph`, `graph_index` and `graph_edge` options that only ever applied
> inside a `graph_type` message. All those option numbers are retired in
> `spec.proto`, never reused. `timeseries_projection` has since been retired too
> (option 60067, 2026-08-25, PLAN.md acceptance item 3): it bundled a pure typed
> conversion together with a **retention policy** and with eventbus delivery, and
> those are now three separate declarations. The conversion is
> **`spec.transformation`**; the store lifecycle is **`(spec.record).residency`**
> (below); delivery is the `record`/`event` producer surface and the topic it
> synthesizes. Neither the transformation nor the delivery declaration requires
> the other to generate.
>
> **2026-09-20 (record lifecycle collapse):** the `Residency` enum (HOT/WARM/COLD),
> `RetentionPolicy`/`(spec.record).retention`, `(spec.archive)`, `cold_store`/
> `graph_store` and `(spec.ejectionable)` were all retired in favor of a single
> `(spec.record).residency{idle_seconds, deleted_max_age_seconds}` (two clocks, no
> enum — see `pkg/proto/sys/spec.proto:709` for the full model) plus a new
> field-level `(spec.deleted_flag)` soft-delete marker. `idle_seconds` ages a
> record out of memory on no read/write; `deleted_max_age_seconds` purges a
> flagged-deleted row that many seconds after the flag was set. Both fields reuse
> the old `retention`'s field numbers 1/2, so an old proto still saying
> `retention: {window: ...}` fails to compile rather than silently discarding the
> setting.

## Mental model

- An **event** flows through eventbus: it has a topic and a publish RPC. Producers
  are external clients (C2S, via gateway) and/or internal services (S2S, e.g. the
  `*-proxy` services). The producer surface is **declared, never defaulted** — an
  internal-only event is S2S and is not exposed C2S.
- A **record** *is* an event that is additionally **stored in full** (the record store) and
  is **projectable**. `records ⊂ events`: every record is an event; not every event
  is a record (e.g. a trace event is event-only).
- **The record store** holds the full records. A **projection** is an offshoot derived from a
  record; since the boneyard there is no separate service that hosts one.

```
producer ─[event]→ eventbus ──→ the record store   stores the full record
```

Both producer paths are identical downstream: `client → gateway → eventbus → …`
and `service → eventbus → …`. The store cares only about the type, not the producer.

## Hand-written annotations (the entire surface)

Message-level:

| Annotation | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `event { c2s{…}? , s2s{…}? }` | eventbus **topic + publish RPC**. ≥1 producer surface required. |
| `record { key, owner, c2s{…}? , s2s{…}? , residency{…}? }` | **DELIVERY.** **is-an `event`** + stored in `record_store` + projectable. `key` = id field (default: `event_id`), `owner` = ownership field, `residency` = the store's lifecycle as two clocks — `idle_seconds` (memory eviction on no read/write) and `deleted_max_age_seconds` (purge this long after `(spec.deleted_flag)` was set). Unset residency is a live platform default (`parser.DefaultResidencyIdleSeconds`/`DefaultResidencyDeletedMaxAgeSeconds`), never "never". |
| `transformation {…}` | **TRANSFORMATION.** A pure typed conversion of this message into a derived row type. Requires **no** `record`, **no** topic, **no** subscription — and carries **no** residency (a pure function has no lifetime). |

Field-level (on a `record` message's fields):

| Annotation | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `query_field { op: EQ\|RANGE }` | expose this field as a typed filter criterion in the `query` trait's plane (`<T>Filter`). |
| `redact { mode: DROP\|PSEUDONYMIZE\|MAY_REDACT\|MAY_ANONYMIZE }` | field is **egress-redactable** (data entitlement): stored raw, sanitized at `Get<T>Sample`/`List<T>`/`Watch<T>` per caller. DROP/PSEUDONYMIZE always apply; MAY_* are caller-decided. Generates `Sanitize<T>` + `<T>Entitlement`. |
| `(spec.deleted_flag) = true` | marks this record's **soft-delete state**: exactly one non-repeated `bool` field per record type (`ValidateDeletedFlagAnnotations`). The query plane excludes flagged-deleted rows by default (`include_deleted` opt-in, below); the row is purged `residency.deleted_max_age_seconds` after the flag was set. A record type with no marked field has nothing for the plane to exclude and `include_deleted` is inert on it. |

Service-level (once per service):

| Annotation | Service |
|---|---|
| `record_store {}` | the full-record store |

On a stored event you write only `record` (it implies `event`). You never write the
derived output types or their markers.

**Transformation and delivery are independent declarations.** A `transformation`
on a plain message generates its derived type with no eventbus involvement at all
(fixture: `FixtureProbe` in `cross-test/proto/common2/user.proto`); a `record`
with a producer surface and retention delivers and stores with no transformation
attached (fixture: `FixtureAudit` in
`cross-test/consumer-contract/proto/services/contractfixtures.proto`). Neither
declaration requires the other to generate.

## Generated (never hand-written)

- The **derived output messages** (`SessionRecord`, …) from the
  `transformation` declarations, stamped with the internal marker
  **`timeseries_type`** so downstream codegen finds them.
- The **timeseries table name**, derived from the message name in `snake_case`
  when `(spec.timeseries_type)` sets none explicitly. The conversion is
  acronym-aware: `HTTPMetric` → `http_metric`, `OpenAIUsage` → `open_ai_usage`.

  > **Migration note.** Before CON-3 a naive converter produced
  > `h_t_t_p_metric` for those names. Any deployment created before that change
  > has tables under the old spelling. This name is **persisted** — it is the
  > table the store writes to — and a change to it fails nothing: generation
  > succeeds, the service starts, and it quietly begins writing to a new table
  > while the old one stops receiving rows. To keep an existing table, set
  > `(spec.timeseries_type).name` explicitly; that value always wins over the
  > derived one. The derivation is pinned by
  > `pkg/internal/common/registry/timeseries_tablename_test.go` — changing it
  > requires a migration, not just an updated expectation.

- The eventbus **topic + publish RPC** from `event`/`record`, with exactly the
  declared C2S/S2S surfaces.
- Per-store **subscriptions**: each store auto-subscribes to the events/projections
  it must ingest.
- The **query plane** (below).

## Query plane

- **Asked for by a `(spec.trait)` declaration, not by the generator.** The plane is
  the record store's per-record-type, per-caller **refinable-query API**, generated
  for every `record` — but *which* proto it is emitted into, *who* implements it,
  what the emitted services are called, and *who* may call the peer half all come off
  a trait declaration rather than off generator constants. Today that declaration is
  testapp's `vservices/query.proto`:

  ```protobuf
  package query;

  option (spec.trait) = {
    name: "query"             // entitlement key AND the audience callers authenticate against
    host: "recordstore"           // the physical implementor — it is what declares (spec.record_store)
    s2s_service: "RecordMap"  // the emitted peer-facing service
    c2s_service: "RecordQuery" // the emitted client-facing service
    auth_services: ["argus"]  // peer identities allowed onto the S2S half
  };
  ```

  Delete that file and the plane is not emitted at all — no host to append to, no
  service names, no fallback. That is the paired control the generator constants it
  replaced could not have: the host used to be "whatever declares `record_store`",
  the names were the literals `RecordMap`/`RecordQuery`, and the S2S audience was
  `["argus"]` repeated at eight call sites in platform generator source, where it
  stayed for months after argus left the fleet because nothing in a build could see
  it had gone dead.

  The trait's **proto package is also `query`**, so one word is the trait name, the
  audience (`aud=query`), the proto package and the entitlement prefix (`QUERY_*`).
  The plane still covers **every** `(spec.record)` message in the fleet rather than a
  list kept in the declaration, so a new record type joins the surface by generation.

- **Two services, one plane.** `ValidateServiceSurfaces` refuses a service carrying
  two caller surfaces, so a plane serving both peers and users is emitted twice —
  `RecordMap` (`spec.service_s2s`), reached by a peer and authorized by peer identity
  through the trait's declared `auth_services`; and `RecordQuery` (`spec.service_c2s`
  + `auth_entitled_users`), reached with a user token and authorized by that token's
  entitlements. Both carry `(spec.service_*).label = "recordstore"`: the **host is whom
  the gateway dials, the trait is the audience the caller's token is checked
  against** (`routeIdentityForService`). Pinning the audience to the host would
  re-couple every client to the implementor.

- **Implemented severally, by the record store alone.** `query` has exactly one implementor
  today — not joint or ensemble hosting; timedb and graphdb went to the boneyard
  2026-08-25 and took their query planes with them. A second implementor is
  expressible and would need no client change (the audience is the contract, not the
  concrete service), but none exists, so nothing here has yet been proven to
  generalize beyond the one implementor.

- **Direct clients call it.** The C2S half is reached with a **user token** — through
  the gateway, or straight at the host's gRPC socket — carrying `aud=query` and
  `QUERY_*` grants in `service_entitlements`: the package-wide `QUERY_ANY`, the
  capability wildcards `QUERY_READ_ANY` / `QUERY_WRITE_ANY` / `QUERY_PAGE_ANY` /
  `QUERY_WATCH_ANY`, or an exact grant such as
  `QUERY_RECORD_QUERY_CREATE_TASK_ACTIVITY_QUERY`. testapp's e2e drives exactly that
  path — a logged-in user calling `CreateTaskActivityQuery` and then `ListTaskActivity`
  on `RecordQuery`, which the `query` package makes
  `query.RecordQuery/CreateTaskActivityQuery` on the wire. The S2S half's only
  declared peer is **argus**,
  which left the fleet 2026-08-20, so `RecordMap` has **no live caller today**; it is
  kept because one plane once per audience is the shape, and its audience is now a
  line in a proto that can be read and deleted rather than a literal in generator
  source.

- **The lifecycle.** A caller opens a query over one record type and gets a **handle**
  to a per-caller result set of matching record **references** (keys). The records
  themselves are **immutable** and the set is never a copy of them — the mutable thing
  is the query predicate. Both surfaces spell the ops in the **same governed verbs**
  (the S2S half was `Open`/`Refine`/`Count`/`Sample`/`Pull`/`Close` until the
  2026-08-24 rename and is not any more):

  | RPC | emitted for | meaning |
  |---|---|---|
  | `Create<T>Query(Open<T>QueryRequest) → QueryHandle` | every `T` | open a snapshot or living query; the lifecycle's single entry point |
  | `Update<T>Query(Refine<T>Request) → QueryStats` | filterable `T` | replace the predicate outright; `size` is the new predicate's match count (min_group_size-guarded) |
  | `Get<T>Count(QueryHandle) → RecordCount` | every `T` | size only, never record data (min_group_size-guarded) |
  | `Get<T>Sample(Sample<T>Request) → Sample<T>Response` | every `T` | seeded monte-carlo draw of `n` records — cheap exploration without reading everything |
  | `List<T>(Pull<T>Request) → Pull<T>Response` | every `T` | paged read of all matches (`method_collection` PAGE) |
  | `Watch<T>(QueryHandle) → stream <T>WatchEvent` | filterable `T` | living query: snapshot, then deltas |
  | `Subscribe<T>Count(QueryHandle) → stream RecordCount` | filterable `T` | live size (min_group_size-guarded) |
  | `Delete<T>Query(QueryHandle) → QueryStats` | every `T` | close the handle |

  Only the **RPC names** are verb-governed; the request/response **messages** still
  carry the query vocabulary (`Open…QueryRequest`, `Refine…Request`, `Sample…`,
  `Pull…`). `Open<T>QueryRequest` and `Refine<T>Request` (only the two that install
  or replace a predicate) additionally carry a **`bool include_deleted`**: unset,
  the plane excludes rows with `(spec.deleted_flag)` set; `true` opts back in. It
  has nowhere to go on `Sample`/`Pull`/`Count`/`Watch` — those take only the
  already-opened handle, which is where the flag was recorded. tacplus generates
  only the field; the exclusion itself is enforced by whoever implements the
  handler (the record store, today — see "tacplus knows the typed query and its shape, not
  the query→execution transform" below).

  A query is either a **one-time snapshot** or **long-lived / living** (new
  matching records auto-join). Ops run server-side. `Update<T>Query` replaces the
  predicate outright — nothing compares the new predicate against the old, so a caller
  entitled to create is equally free to widen it; authorization is per-RPC-method, not
  per-filter. **The caller that created a handle owns it** and closes it with
  `Delete<T>Query`; the record store holds the per-caller set, and no intermediary owns handle
  lifecycle or cleanup on the caller's behalf.

  Three ops return record data — **`Get<T>Sample`, `List<T>`, and `Watch<T>`** (each
  stream item is a record) — and **all three apply egress redaction**; the caller's
  entitlements shape the released view at read time, and redaction is **never** baked
  into stored state. `Get<T>Count` and `Subscribe<T>Count` return only a size, never
  record data. tacplus knows the typed query and its shape, not the query→execution
  transform (impl-side).
  - **Egress data entitlement** is generated from field-level `(spec.redact)`: for each
    record type T with redactable fields, tacplus emits `Sanitize<T>(record, <T>Entitlement, hmacKey)`
    — a sanitized **copy** (REDACT → zeroed + indicator set, ANONYMIZE → a keyed
    per-value token). The rule is **FAIL-CLOSED**: `DROP`/`PSEUDONYMIZE` fields are
    hard floors, always applied; a `MAY_*` field defaults to its most-protective
    level (`MAY_REDACT` → REDACT, `MAY_ANONYMIZE` → ANONYMIZE) and egresses raw
    only under an explicit `RAW` level. The **generated WRAPPER** (never the
    handler, never impl code) applies it on **every record-bearing egress path —
    `Get<T>Sample`, `List<T>`, AND each `Watch<T>` snapshot item and delta** (a
    living query must not leak what a `List<T>` would redact), after the handler returns, so a
    handler physically cannot bypass it. The **policy** (which fields a caller may
    see raw) is an identity property of the caller's token: OPA stamps
    `data_grants` into the `service_entitlements` claim at token-exchange time,
    the generated `Build<T>Entitlement` maps those grants onto `<T>Entitlement`
    (a matching grant loosens the field to RAW; never below a hard floor), and
    the wrapper supplies the per-deployment ANONYMIZE secret from config
    (`grpcconfig.Config.anonymize_hmac_key`) — **mechanism in tacplus, policy in
    OPA**. The caller passes no redaction knobs. The seam is per-hop, so a future
    two-stage path (the record store→an intermediary→user) can reuse it unchanged.
  - **Minimum group size** is generated from the message-level
    `(spec.record).min_group_size = N` — a k-anonymity floor on the surfaces that return a
    size and **no rows**. The record-map injector stamps `option (spec.min_group_size) = N`
    onto `Get<T>Count`, `Subscribe<T>Count` (`RecordCount.count`) and `Update<T>Query`
    (`QueryStats.size`, the match count of the newly installed predicate — unguarded, that
    one RPC reproduces the count the guard just refused), on **both** halves of the plane.
    The **generated WRAPPER** (never the handler) refuses a size below `N` with
    **PERMISSION_DENIED**, so a second implementor of `query` cannot ship the plane
    unguarded. The refusal is an error or nothing: no sentinel count, no suppression flag,
    and the message names only the declared threshold, never the actual size. A stream is
    terminated rather than silently filtered — going quiet at exactly `N-1` would disclose
    the crossing by silence. Unset/`0` is no guard, and since `Update<T>Query` /
    `Subscribe<T>Count` are emitted only for a filterable `T`, an unfilterable record is
    guarded on `Get<T>Count` alone.
  - **`total_count` is deliberately outside that guard.** `Pull<T>Response.total_count` —
    the paged read's own size, alongside `items` and `next_page_token` — is **not**
    stamped and **not** refused: it accompanies rows the caller is entitled to and has
    just been handed, so it discloses nothing those rows do not. Neither is
    `Delete<T>Query`'s `QueryStats`, whose `size` is a hardcoded zero. "The count" that
    min_group_size withholds is therefore always a *size-only* count; a future change that
    makes a paged read return counts without rows has crossed that line.
- Combining records of **multiple types** into one working set is done **service-side**
  — the caller opens several single-type queries and aggregates the already-redacted
  results in its own memory; the record store holds no cross-type sets.

## Validations (tacplus errors)

- an `event`/`record` that declares zero producer surfaces;
- a **negative `(spec.record).min_group_size`**, or a threshold declared into a fleet
  where no `(spec.trait)` hosts a record query plane — a guard that can never refuse, and
  a guard with no guarded surface behind it (`ValidateMinGroupSizeAnnotations` in
  `pkg/internal/common/parser/min_group_size_validate.go`). Each service-wrapper generator
  (Go, Java, Rust) additionally fails on a stamped method whose guard it cannot render:
  a client-streaming rpc, or a response with no single integer size field;
- a **store whose source type resolves to no EventBus topic** — the generated
  store would subscribe to nothing and never ingest a row. This is the paired
  control for the transformation/delivery split: a transformation alone is fine
  and a store alone is fine, but a store that claims a source with no delivery
  behind it is a silent dead store, and now fails generation
  (`DeriveStoreSubscriptionsFromRegistry` in
  `pkg/internal/common/boundaries/boundaries.go`).

> A `transformation` on a message that is not a `record` is **explicitly legal**
> since 2026-08-25. It used to be rejected; requiring a record made every
> transformation drag the eventbus-driven store path in with it, which is the
> coupling acceptance item 3 removed.

> **Not implemented, despite having been listed here:** "a `record` or projection
> with no hosting store service". `pkg/internal/proto/validate_virtual.go` records
> that the check was deliberately not enforced — the host store lives in a separate
> service proto and is absent from isolated/partial proto sets, so enforcing it
> per-service-build produced false failures. It was reinstated as neither a
> per-build nor a whole-fleet lint, so **it has never fired**. Listed here as a
> guarantee it does not provide, it was decoration; see
> `BONEYARD_QUESTIONS.md` Q1.

## Implementation neutrality

The contract names no backing store. The record store's distribution/compute (currently
in-memory + a distributed executor; later a unified "fast-store" tier and python3
transformers) is an implementation detail, never present in proto/tacplus. Do not introduce impl names (engine names, vendors, internal
codenames) into annotations or generated output.

# Stability review: generated runtime under small perturbations

Review for #17. Scope: the generated runtime in Go, Rust and Java (chassis templates and generated wrapper templates under `pkg/templates/`). No generator code was changed.

## Method and evidence rules

- Six reviewers worked independently, one per angle in #17 (timeouts and deadlines; retries and backoff; health, readiness and liveness; connection management and keepalive; load and backpressure; startup and restart ordering). They did not see each other's notes.
- A second pass challenged every finding. Findings that did not survive are listed under "Dropped" below. Disagreements that remain are listed under "Disagreements".
- **CONFIRMED** means the amplification mechanism is fully determined by a precise code path that was read in this review (file:line). No fault-injection test was executed in this review. Each confirmed defect has a filed issue (#31–#38) with the reproduction test to write. The reason a test was not run: the fixtures (a multi-process peer restart, a blocked event bus, a fake state store) were not built in this review.
- **SUSPECTED** means the mechanism depends on runtime timing, on external library behaviour, on deployment manifests, or on the size of the fleet. None of these is claimed as proven here.

No fault-injection test was executed in this review. Fleet-scale claims are SUSPECTED.

## Confirmed (worst first)

Each entry is a code-path defect. Its fleet-scale effect is SUSPECTED unless stated.

1. **Accounting emit can park an RPC completion thread for as long as the event bus is down (Java).** [#34](https://github.com/tacplus-dev/tacplus/issues/34)
   - Trigger: the event bus stops draining the accounting queue (restart, slow publisher, one peer blip).
   - Mechanism: the queue is bounded at 1024 (`pkg/templates/java/types/ServiceManager.java.tmpl:1051`). A full queue makes `EventBusSink.emit` loop on `offer(250ms)` until shutdown (`pkg/templates/java/chassis/am/AccountingManager.java.tmpl:446-447`), and the emit runs on the handler's completion path (`pkg/templates/java/types/servicewrapper.java.tmpl:166-170`). Handler threads park, the executor drains, and every service emits accounting, so one bus outage can stall many services.
   - Languages: Java confirmed on the RPC path. Go (`pkg/templates/go/chassis/am/am.go.tmpl:493-505`) and Rust (`pkg/templates/rust/chassis/am/src/am.rs.tmpl:457`) block at the sink too; their caller paths are not confirmed.

2. **Consumer pool closes an endpoint on the first snapshot that omits it.** [#37](https://github.com/tacplus-dev/tacplus/issues/37)
   - Trigger: one missed or partial health snapshot.
   - Mechanism: Rust (`pkg/templates/rust/chassis/servicemanager/src/connection.rs.tmpl:322-336`), Java (`pkg/templates/java/chassis/serviceconnection/ServiceConnection.java.tmpl:334-344`) and Go (`pkg/templates/go/chassis/serviceconnection/serviceconnection.go.tmpl:279-300`) all drop an endpoint absent from one snapshot. The next snapshot forces a redial and a TLS handshake, and readiness drops at once when the last required endpoint goes. The #2 debounce covers readiness only, not pool membership.
   - Languages: all three.

3. **Unary calls reset the caller's deadline per hop (Rust) and retry with no jitter or budget (all three).** [#38](https://github.com/tacplus-dev/tacplus/issues/38)
   - Trigger: a slight latency increase on a snapshot read that pushes calls past 30 s.
   - Mechanism: the Rust client overwrites the inbound `grpc-timeout` with its fixed timeout (`pkg/templates/rust/types/grpcclient.rs.tmpl:66-70`, `:101-105`), so a callee keeps working after its caller gives up. Retries are unjittered with no budget (Go `grpcclient.go.tmpl:121-132`, Java `grpcclient.java.tmpl:112-117`, Rust `grpcclient.rs.tmpl:80-89`). Work per request can grow with chain depth only if downstream calls are not cancelled with the caller, which was not verified. Go derives its per-call timeout from the handler context (`grpcclient.go.tmpl:144-148`) and is safe here.
   - Languages: Rust confirmed; Java unverified (see Not reviewed); Go safe on the deadline, affected on jitter.

4. **Reconnect and resolve backoff has no jitter in Go, Java and Rust.** [#31](https://github.com/tacplus-dev/tacplus/issues/31)
   - Trigger: a shared event (peer restart, kernel roll) drops many clients at once.
   - Mechanism: the schedule doubles to a 30 s cap and is a pure function of the attempt number (`pkg/templates/go/chassis/serviceconnection/backoff.go.tmpl:19-31`, `pkg/templates/rust/chassis/servicemanager/src/backoff.rs.tmpl:17-25`, `pkg/templates/java/chassis/backoff/Backoff.java.tmpl:23-45`). Clients that lose the same peer attempt at the same instants: t+0.5, +1.5, +3.5, +7.5, +15.5, +31.5, +61.5, then every 30 s. Each resolve attempt is a token fetch, a `GetAllInstances` and a TLS dial, which loads the same dependencies that are recovering.
   - The premise of "flat" 0.5 s to 30 s in #17 is wrong: the schedule doubles. It is unjittered and synchronized.
   - Languages: all three. Jitter exists in Go elsewhere (`pkg/templates/go/types/servicemanager_lib.go.tmpl:80-85`).

5. **Java subscriber re-resolves in a tight loop when a stream closes cleanly.** [#32](https://github.com/tacplus-dev/tacplus/issues/32)
   - Trigger: a server ends a subscription with OK status.
   - Mechanism: `subscribeOnce` returns normally (`pkg/templates/java/types/Subscriber.java.tmpl:262-277`), the caller resets its backoff and falls through with no sleep (`:157-158`), and the loop calls `resolveService` again at RPC speed (`pkg/templates/java/types/ServiceManager.java.tmpl:1392-1394`, `:2199-2226`).
   - Languages: Java only. Go (`pkg/templates/go/types/subscriber.go.tmpl:173-183`) and Rust (`pkg/templates/rust/types/subscriber.rs.tmpl:189-193`) sleep on a clean close.

6. **HTTP GET retries 429 and 5xx without reading Retry-After and without a budget; HTTP and gRPC retry policies disagree.** [#36](https://github.com/tacplus-dev/tacplus/issues/36)
   - Trigger: a peer sheds load with 429 or 503.
   - Mechanism: each retryable GET is sent up to 4 times (`pkg/templates/go/chassis/httpclient/client.go.tmpl:34-42`, `:239-300`; `pkg/templates/java/chassis/httpclient/TypedClient.java.tmpl:116-180`; `pkg/templates/rust/chassis/httpclient/src/retry.rs.tmpl:14-37`). `Retry-After` is never read. gRPC never retries INTERNAL or UNKNOWN, but HTTP retries 5xx.
   - Languages: all three.

7. **Java W2S listener and subscribe iterator buffer messages in unbounded queues.** [#33](https://github.com/tacplus-dev/tacplus/issues/33)
   - Trigger: a slow consumer while the server keeps sending.
   - Mechanism: `pkg/templates/java/types/w2sclient.java.tmpl:445` (unbounded), `:452` and `:462` (`request(1)` unconditional, so the socket is read at network speed); `pkg/templates/java/types/statewrapper.java.tmpl:662`, `:668`, `:678` (unbounded queue, no `request(n)` gating). Heap grows with the backlog.
   - Languages: Java. Go is safe because its handler runs synchronously under gRPC flow control.

8. **Java endpoint latency is a `getState` call, not a round trip, so a slow READY endpoint is never shed.** [#35](https://github.com/tacplus-dev/tacplus/issues/35)
   - Trigger: one endpoint becomes slow while staying READY.
   - Mechanism: the ping times `channel.getState(true)` (`pkg/templates/java/chassis/serviceconnection/ServiceConnection.java.tmpl:896-927`), so latency is microseconds for every endpoint. The 0.3 threshold (`:425`) is never met between endpoints, so routing never moves on latency. Go and Rust rank by real Ping RPC latency, so the three languages disagree on the same input.
   - Languages: Java.

## Suspected (not filed)

Each is a plausible amplification whose trigger, timing or size was not shown in the code.

- **Rust bidi reconnect is a fixed 5 s sleep with no backoff, no jitter, and a token re-mint per attempt** (`pkg/templates/rust/types/grpcclient_bidi.rs.tmpl:159-160`, `:59`). Cross-read downgraded this to hygiene: one attempt per 5 s per stream.
- **Ping failure marks an endpoint unhealthy on one sample, and the fleet herds onto the same lowest-latency survivor** (Rust `endpoint.rs.tmpl:160-166`; Go `servicemanager_lib.go.tmpl:146-150`, `:771-816`; Java `ServiceConnection.java.tmpl:908-927`). Go's switch happens on the 30 s rebalance tick, not immediately. Whether all clients rank endpoints the same way on the same tick was not shown.
- **Routing does not fail over on call failure.** `conn()` returns the active channel whatever its health (`pkg/templates/rust/chassis/servicemanager/src/connection.rs.tmpl:244-256`). Failover does happen on the ping-driven tick. The 90 s figure (three attempts of 30 s) applies to snapshot reads only.
- **Token mint lockout: five consecutive 10 s timeouts give a 300 s retry gap** (`pkg/templates/go/chassis/client_im/manager.go.tmpl:395-420`; Rust `manager.rs.tmpl:411-430`; Java `ClientIdentityManager.java.tmpl:426-455`). Attempts are per caller, not on a shared timer, so this is not synchronized; the impact depends on token TTL against the gap.
- **Java dynamic-pool dial waits 5 s for READY and drops the endpoint on failure** (`pkg/templates/java/chassis/serviceconnection/ServiceConnection.java.tmpl:835`, `:360-367`). Rust allows 15 s (`pkg/templates/rust/chassis/servicemanager/src/endpoint.rs.tmpl:126`, `:141`). Re-dial is gated on health reports.
- **Java state fetch retries UNAVAILABLE with no attempt bound** (`pkg/templates/java/chassis/backoff/Backoff.java.tmpl:47-73`). The fetch's own deadline covers validation retries only (`pkg/templates/java/types/statewrapper.java.tmpl:413-416`). Whether request threads block indefinitely depends on the state stub's per-call deadline, which was not confirmed.
- **Java subscriber's outer backoff is effectively dead; the real gap is the inner backoff** (`pkg/templates/java/types/Subscriber.java.tmpl:137`, `:184-185`), which resets only on a clean EOF and not after a long healthy run that ends in error. Rust resets after 60 s healthy (`pkg/templates/rust/types/service_manager.rs.tmpl:2085-2091`).
- **Watch callbacks run synchronously on the watch receive path** (`pkg/templates/go/types/state_wrapper.go.tmpl:622-638`; `pkg/templates/java/types/statewrapper.java.tmpl:1024-1032`; `pkg/templates/rust/types/statewrapper.rs.tmpl:606-612`). A slow callback stalls the stream. The downstream effect (cursor eviction and relist) was inferred, not traced.
- **Redo-log append fsyncs on the caller's thread under a lock; there is no asynchronous persist** (`pkg/templates/go/chassis/diskstore/redolog.go.tmpl:116-128`; `pkg/templates/rust/chassis/diskstore/src/redolog.rs.tmpl:101-107`; `RedoLog.java.tmpl:123-133`). This is a throughput design choice, not an amplifier by itself. The premise in #17 that it is asynchronous is wrong for all three.
- **Identity managers exit the process after 5 minutes of token failure** (Java `pkg/templates/java/chassis/service_im/IdentityManager.java.tmpl:65-66`, `:286-309`; Rust `pkg/templates/rust/chassis/service_im/src/manager.rs.tmpl:30-31`, `:225-265`). The timers start at outage onset, so pods exit together under a sustained authority outage. This is designed exit-for-restart and matters only for long outages.
- **First health publish treats UNAUTHENTICATED, PERMISSION_DENIED, FAILED_PRECONDITION and INVALID_ARGUMENT as permanent, so boot exits with no retry** (`pkg/templates/go/chassis/healthreporter/healthreporter.go.tmpl:356-363` and `pkg/templates/go/types/service_manager.go.tmpl:1501-1503`; Rust `pkg/templates/rust/chassis/healthreporter/src/lib.rs.tmpl:365-377`; Java `pkg/templates/java/chassis/healthreporter/HealthReporter.java.tmpl:331-337`). Unauthenticated is the stale-token symptom during an authority restart, so this can crash-loop. Whether a kernel returns these codes during a roll is not in this repo.
- **Rust and Java gate startup on the first TLS certificate; Go serves on the bootstrap certificate** (Rust `pkg/templates/rust/types/service_manager.rs.tmpl:886-900`; Java `pkg/templates/java/types/ServiceManager.java.tmpl:385-392`; Go `pkg/templates/go/types/service_manager.go.tmpl:1340-1363`). The Go comment says this is deliberate, so this is an inconsistency, not a proven amplifier.
- **Rust clients do not back off on connect failure and do not adjust keepalive on GOAWAY `too_many_pings`** (`pkg/templates/rust/types/service_manager.rs.tmpl:1079-1080`; `pkg/templates/rust/chassis/servicemanager/src/endpoint.rs.tmpl:123-124`). Go clients self-heal because grpc-go doubles the client ping interval. The tonic reconnect behaviour was read from cache, not verified against the pinned version.
- **Go server keepalive `MinTime` defaults to 30 s, equal to the client ping, so idle subscribers can be given GOAWAY `too_many_pings`.** This is evidence for #28 (see its comment), not a new issue. Borderline, since the repo pins grpc v1.81.1 and the strike logic was read from another version.
- **Go readiness does not count ping failures; Java counts them after about 90 s; Rust after 3 failures or 30 s** (`pkg/templates/go/chassis/serviceconnection/serviceconnection.go.tmpl:110-116`; Java `ServiceConnection.java.tmpl:81`, `:83`, `:947`; Rust `endpoint.rs.tmpl:21-26`). The cadences differ across languages. This is a divergence, and it makes Go absorb a silent peer rather than amplify.
- **Java's stub latency and Go's `ping_interval_ms` are unused.** `pkg/proto/sys/grpcconfig.proto:71-73` declares an interval that no template reads; Go's loop hardcodes 30 s (`pkg/templates/go/types/servicemanager_lib.go.tmpl:57`, `:431`).
- **Dynamic-pool endpoint lists and per-caller state grow without bound** (not reviewed in depth; see Not reviewed).

## #2 / #30 (fleet-plane flaps): producer-side status

The panel did not find the single root cause of the 1–2 minute cadence. What it found is recorded as evidence on #30 (see that issue's comment):

- The arithmetic alone does not produce a 1–2 minute cadence: the reporter publishes every 10 s, and a steady peer keeps its HEALTHY stamp fresh, so a single non-HEALTHY snapshot cannot reach the 30 s staleness threshold.
- Credential-rejection counting is a candidate producer-side cause, and it is wrong in both Go and Rust. Go counts every rejection (`pkg/templates/go/chassis/service_im/service_im.go.tmpl:1701`). Rust's comment says it counts generations, but `note_credential_rejection` bumps `GENERATION` on every call (`pkg/templates/rust/chassis/service_im/src/auth_recovery.rs.tmpl:118`), so it counts every rejection too. Java coalescing was not verified. This can keep a service UNHEALTHY on an idle fleet, but it is not yet shown to be the cause of the cadence.
- The consumer side is debounced in all three languages (#2). The fleet view can still show a non-HEALTHY status for a live peer, which is the open question in #30.

## Disagreements kept in the review

- **Rust credential counting (#30).** The first reviewer said Rust coalesces by generation. The cross-read showed `GENERATION` is bumped on every call, so Rust counts every rejection and its comment is wrong. Verified by reading `auth_recovery.rs.tmpl:100-125`.
- **Go unary retry multiplication.** One reviewer put the cost at 9 attempts at the leaf for a three-hop chain. The cross-read showed Go derives per-call deadlines from the caller's context, so the multiplication holds for Rust and (unverified) Java, not Go.
- **Java deadline propagation.** Whether grpc-java takes the minimum of a stub deadline and an inherited Context deadline was not verified. Java is therefore not stated as affected in #38.
- **Readiness chaining across hops (H-4).** One reviewer described B's published health going NOT_SERVING when C is down. The cross-read found B's fleet status comes only from its own `SetStatus` (`pkg/templates/go/types/service_manager.go.tmpl:1479`, `:1484`), so the chain as described does not exist.

## Dropped after the cross-read

- Go subscription backoff reset per successful resolve (R-2): the Go subscriber caps consecutive failures at 10 and returns to its caller, so the reset happens once per cycle, not every 500 ms.
- Readiness chaining across hops (H-4): see above.
- Liveness restarts from a dependency outage (H-5): the chassis comments describe the gRPC health service as readiness; the restart premise depends on deployment manifests, which are not in this repo.
- Go `Conn()` returning nil (C-5): internal callers check for nil (`pkg/templates/go/types/servicemanager_lib.go.tmpl:603-606`, `:894-897`). Only the public `Conn()` is a footgun, which is low severity.
- The Rust server keepalive gap (#29): no amplifying failure found in source reading (see its comment). Residual missing policy only.
- The Go credential-rejection counting as the cause of the 1–2 minute cadence: a candidate, not a finding of this review (see #30).

## #17 questions answered directly

- **"40 clients lose the same peer, reconnect backoff 0.5 s to 30 s flat."** The premise is wrong: it doubles. It is unjittered, so the clients move in lockstep through a fixed schedule (#31).
- **"Do all generated servers apply `PermitMinTimeSecs`?"** Go's server overrides it from config with a default of 30 s, so it does not apply the 10 s constant when config is set (#28 evidence). Java applies the constant (`pkg/templates/java/chassis/grpcserver/GrpcServer.java.tmpl:294`, `serverBuilder.permitKeepAliveTime({{.KeepalivePermitMinTimeSecs}}, ...)`). Rust applies no enforcement policy; no amplifying failure was found from source (#29).
- **"Is there an ungated liveness signal?"** The chassis exposes only the readiness-gated gRPC health status in all three languages. Whether deployment manifests point liveness at it is not in this repo (see Not reviewed).
- **"What happens when the redo-log disk is slow?"** Append blocks the caller under a lock in all three languages; there is no asynchronous persist (see Suspected).

## Not reviewed

- Fleet runs and fault-injection tests: none were executed. Every confirmed defect's reproduction is written as a test to add (see the filed issues).
- Deployment manifests: whether any liveness probe targets the gRPC health service.
- Java `grpc-java` deadline semantics (min of stub and Context deadlines) and the Java credential-rejection coalescing.
- The Rust server's actual resolved `h2` version (no lockfile in the repo); the Go `grpc` version was read from `go.mod` (v1.81.1), and strike logic was read from a different cached version.
- Python, TypeScript, C# and Swift chassis: out of scope for #17's three languages.
- Diskstore beyond the append path, and the snapshot and roll behaviour (#15, #25).
- The Go endpoint-list growth, the Go and Rust healthreporter in depth, and the grpcserver shutdown fan-out.
- The Rust and Java bidi streams beyond the fixed-sleep and clean-close findings above.

# Everything Everywhere Is Typed All At Once

*In tacplus, every field constraint, state boundary, auth policy, and RPC exists in one place — the proto definitions — and every supported generated surface comes from that single source of truth.*

---

## The Problem

Building microservices is repetitive. Every service needs the same infrastructure: typed messages, validated inputs, serialization, authentication, authorization, state management, health reporting. In a multi-language platform, each service needs all of this in its own language, following the same contracts as every other service.

The usual approach is a combination of hand-rolled validation, shared libraries, documented conventions, and discipline. It works — until it doesn't. A validation rule changes in one language and not another. A service starts writing state it doesn't own. An auth check gets added here but not there. Contracts drift. Bugs happen. And somewhere in the system, an important invariant exists only in a developer's head.

The deeper issue is that the *contract* — what values are valid, what services can call what, who owns which state — is scattered across code in multiple languages. There is no single place that says what the system actually is.

---

## The Insight

Proto files already describe the shape of your data. Every message, every field, every type is declared once, in a language the whole system agrees on. What if they described *everything* — not just the shape, but the constraints, the ownership, the auth policy?

Then a compiler could read those richer definitions and generate everything that flows from them. Not just serialization stubs — the complete service infrastructure for the server languages, plus compatible client packages for client-only targets, from a single source of truth.

---

## What tacplus Is

tacplus is that compiler. It reads `.proto` files annotated with custom `spec` options and produces complete, runnable service infrastructure. Not just types — entire services.

**Input:** Annotated proto files + a `tacplus.yaml` declaring project-local generation facts that do not logically belong in proto, such as target language, package name, output directory, and proto source.

**Output:** A `tacplus/` directory with everything a microservice needs to run:

```
tacplus/
  types/        -- Protobuf bindings, validation, serialization
  sys/         -- Generated runtime libraries
  s2sm/         -- Service lifecycle, state accessors, gRPC clients
  proto/        -- Processed proto files
  registry.json -- Semantic IR (types, boundaries, auth, norms)
  AGENT.md      -- Architectural norms for agentic analysis
```

The rule is simple for full-service targets: if tacplus generates service runtime behavior, it does so for Go, Java, and Rust with parity. Swift, C#, Python, and TypeScript are client-only targets and must reject service-side/runtime generation instead of emitting partial servers. They come in two tiers: Swift and C# are "lite" client targets (C2D, C2S, and W2S clients; Swift's W2S is unary + server-streaming over SSE, C#'s is unary-only, and the streaming methods neither can carry are emitted as unavailable stubs), while Python and TypeScript are full-client targets that generate every client surface (C2D, C2S, W2S, REST).

---

## The Type System

Every field carries its constraints. A `string listen_addr` annotated with `(spec.assert_listen_addr)` doesn't just say "this is a string" — it says "this must be a valid `host:port`." A repeated field annotated with `(spec.assert_max_size)` has a hard upper bound. An enum field annotated with `(spec.assert_enum_defined)` cannot be the zero value.

```protobuf
message Config {
  string listen_addr = 1 [
    (spec.assert_required) = true,
    (spec.assert_listen_addr) = true
  ];
  int32 max_connections = 2 [
    (spec.assert_gt) = 0,
    (spec.assert_le) = 10000
  ];
  string cert_pem = 3 [(spec.assert_enc_type) = ENC_TYPE_X509_CERT_ANY];
}
```

tacplus generates native types with protobuf bindings, validation functions for all constraints, and serialization helpers for JSON, YAML, TOML, and binary — per supported target surface, with identical semantics where that surface exists. Full-service targets run generated validation at every service boundary. Client-only targets validate before sending.

The system is intentionally liberal in what it accepts and conservative in what it emits. Input-side annotations allow field aliases and format variations for compatibility. Output-side serializers are typed and normalized.

---

## The State System

Services own their state. A message annotated with `(spec.service_state)` becomes a named partition of distributed state, backed by a state store that tacplus defines as an interface and a downstream runtime implements. tacplus generates the gRPC state service, typed client accessors, Watch streams, and cross-service access control against that interface, independent of any particular backing store. Every message-typed field is a boundary — stored independently and convergent (lockless, last-writer-wins / append-only).

```protobuf
message ServiceState {
  option (spec.service_state) = {label: ["myservice"], export: true};

  Config config = 1;
  Session current_session = 2;
  repeated Session sessions = 3 [
    (spec.indexed) = true
  ];
}
```

A service has read-write access to its own state. Other services declare
read-only imports on the fields that project exported state:

```protobuf
message ConsumerState {
  option (spec.service_state) = {label: ["consumer"]};

  myservice.Session current_session = 1 [
    (spec.state_import) = "myservice.ServiceState.current_session"
  ];
}
```

The import is read-only by design, currently supports singular message
projections, and the access is enforced server-side. The backing store validates
every gRPC call against the proto-declared permissions. There is no way to
bypass this with a custom client — the caller's identity is in the token, and
the server checks it against the declared imports.

This enforces a single-writer model. Services communicate state changes through formal contracts, not direct mutation. Distributed state stays disciplined.

---

## Services, Vservices, And Traits

A **service** is a long-lived deployable unit such as the record store, eventbus, or kernel.
It is a process: something that is built, deployed, and dialed.

A **vservice** and a **trait** are both tacplus-declared, service-implemented
contracts. Neither is a process. Both carry the same identity shape — a canonical
name that is the entitlement key, plus an optional stable `TokenEntitlements` field
id — and both are hosted by a physical service while callers are entitled against the
contract's name, never the host's. They differ in what they declare:

| | declares | hosted by |
|---|---|---|
| `(spec.vservice)` | a **data** contract: event type, projection set, subscribe surface, entitlement model | the service whose `(spec.service_s2s).label` claims it |
| `(spec.trait)` | an **RPC** contract: a named surface with a host, its emitted service names, and its peer audience | the service named in `(spec.trait).host` |

The useful mental model is a database with tables:

| Database concept | tacplus concept |
|---|---|
| database | service |
| table | vservice |
| create a table | add a vservice proto, regenerate tacplus, rebuild the service |
| schema migration | revise the proto for that vservice |

A trait is the other axis. Where a vservice asks "who owns this data", a trait asks
"who implements this surface" — and answers it in the proto rather than in generator
source. The declaration names the host, so the plane exists because of the
declaration, not because of a constant somewhere: delete the trait proto and the
surface is not generated at all. The **audience is the contract, not the
implementor** — the host label is only whom the gateway dials, while the caller's
token is checked against the trait name — so a second implementor of the same trait
needs no client change.

The `query` trait is the worked example: `name: "query"`, `host: "recordstore"`, and the
record query plane emitted onto both caller surfaces from it. Note the honest limit —
`query` has exactly one implementor today, so the second-implementor property is
expressible but unproven. See
[`RECORD_EVENT_MODEL.md`](RECORD_EVENT_MODEL.md) for the plane it generates.

Vservices and traits are flexible and service implementations are stable. Adding or
changing one contract should not destabilize unrelated contracts hosted by the same
service. Service-local generators should consume `registry.json`, not parse proto
files directly, so the service and everything it hosts use the same semantic IR that
tacplus used to generate code.

---

## The Auth Model

Auth policy is declared in proto, not hand-coded. A service annotated with `(spec.service_s2s)` accepts only authenticated service-to-service calls. A service annotated with `(spec.service_c2s)` is client-facing — the generated auth interceptor verifies the token and checks entitlements before dispatching.

```protobuf
service InternalAPI {
  option (spec.service_s2s) = {auth_services: ["caller-a", "caller-b"]};
}

service PublicAPI {
  option (spec.service_c2s) = {auth_entitled_users: true};
}
```

The generated auth layer handles JWT verification, entitlement checking, and token propagation. Services declare their auth policy in proto and implement their logic in handlers. Auth is not a cross-cutting concern — it is a generated structural property of the service.

---

## The Identity Model

Identity is typed, derived, and separated from attestation.

**Typed**: a SPIFFE ID's kind (service, workload, user, client, credential, resource) is recoverable from fixed path tags in the URI itself — no out-of-band context needed to know what a principal is. Reserved tags make the parse unambiguous at every depth.

**Derived**: the SPIFFE ID is a computation over token claims (`namespace`, `sub`, `sub_type`) plus deployment config (trust domain, location), never a claim itself. Claims stay small and stable; the full identity is reconstructed wherever needed through one generated helper library with shared cross-language test vectors. Durable keys (X509 URI SANs, workload revocation, health identity, event owners) store the normalized derived form.

**Separated from attestation**: *who* a principal is and *how* it proved itself are different axes. A user is a tenant-scoped role — the same human logging in via OAuth or a credential pair is the same subject; the login path lives in `azp` (authorized party), set only by the minter from trusted context. This prevents the classic smell of identity forking per auth method. Credentials (cred-pairs) are durable resources that *attest* a principal, never principals themselves.

Two further rules keep identity sound: segments are validated against a strict allowlist and **rejected, never sanitized** (a sanitizer maps two different external values onto one identity; a rejector fails closed); and external identifiers enter the tree only through a deterministic opaque-segment hash, domain-separated by kind, byte-identical in every language.

---

## Cross-Language Parity

The same proto definitions generate equivalent full-service infrastructure in Go, Java, and Rust. The same validation rules apply. The same state semantics are honored. When a field is annotated `(spec.assert_required)`, each supported target surface gets the same required check. When a message is annotated `(spec.service_state)`, each full-service target gets the same accessor interface.

Parity is a build-time invariant, not an aspiration. A deep analysis pass can run against the full-service outputs and client-only surfaces and report divergence. The same analysis is used to generate equivalent services in the full-service languages as a pressure test against most-favored-language bias. The generated outputs can be discarded; the purpose is to verify the abstractions are genuinely language-neutral.

No language is treated as universally superior. Each is chosen for its tradeoffs at a particular layer. The non-negotiable bias is toward machine-checkable contracts.

---

## The Semantic IR

tacplus compiles proto annotations into `registry.json`: a normalized, language-neutral semantic model of the service. It includes types, services, state roots, views, auth metadata, generation intent, and architectural norms.

Every language generator emits the same `registry.json` from that model. This centralizes interpretation and prevents per-language semantic drift. `registry.json` is an output — downstream tooling and runtimes consume it, the generators do not. At runtime, a service that serves `registry.json` from a well-known endpoint is self-describing — tooling, agents, and introspection APIs read the same model that generated the code.

This is the same file at build time (for generation, linting, testing, docs, and analysis) and runtime (for discovery, agents, and introspection). One source of truth, two consumers.

---

## Architectural Norms and Agentic Analysis

Some rules are hard guarantees enforced in every build: type correctness, constraint validation, code generation consistency.

Other rules are architectural norms: patterns that should generally hold but are higher-order than type correctness. tacplus carries them in the `AGENT.md` it generates for each build and embeds into `registry.json` alongside the rest of its own documentation set. (tacplus does not read consumer-authored `agent.md` files — there is no ingestion path for them.) The agentic analysis pass checks for cross-language parity drift, suspicious service shapes, and anti-patterns — and can be run on demand without affecting the build.

This is governance carried in machine-readable form. The norms travel with the code.

---

## What "Plus" Means

tacplus generates beyond types — that is what "Plus" means:

- **Validation** — constraint enforcement at every boundary, generated from annotations, not hand-written
- **State** — distributed ownership, Watch streams, cross-service access control
- **Auth** — S2S and client-facing auth, token verification, entitlement checking
- **Discovery** — a canonical semantic IR at build time and runtime
- **Lifecycle** — cluster connection, config subscription, health reporting, graceful shutdown
- **Parity** — the same contracts, enforced the same way, for every supported target surface

The result: services are defined by their proto files. The implementation is a thin handler layer. Everything else is generated, typed, validated, and enforced.

For usage details, CLI reference, and annotation tables, see [USER.md](USER.md).
For generated API contracts, see [API.md](API.md). For compiler development
guidelines, see [DEVELOPMENT.md](DEVELOPMENT.md).

## Patterns for Service Implementers

See [API.md](API.md) for generated API contracts and [DEVELOPMENT.md](DEVELOPMENT.md#compiler-development-patterns) for compiler-side pattern rules. Code examples for each pattern are below.

### Use the Generated Service Manager

```go
// Correct: create the generated manager, then run your handler
func main() {
    sm, err := s2sm.New()
    if err != nil {
        log.Fatal(err)
    }
    if err := sm.Run(internal.NewHandler()); err != nil {
        log.Fatal(err)
    }
}

// Wrong: manually wiring gRPC servers, TLS, auth interceptors
lis, _ := net.Listen("tcp", addr)
grpc.NewServer(grpc.Creds(...), grpc.UnaryInterceptor(...))
```

### Use Generated gRPC Wrappers

```go
// Correct: implement the generated Handler interface and run the manager —
// the generated wrappers dispatch transport/auth/validation to your handler.
sm.Run(&myServiceImpl{sm: sm}) // myServiceImpl implements the generated Handler

// Wrong: manually implementing grpc.ServiceDesc, calling grpc.Dial directly
```

### Use Generated Clients and State Accessors

```go
// Correct: reach downstream service clients and state through the manager.
api := sm.Grpc().Clients().Other().OtherApiClient() // typed downstream client
sc := sm.StateClients()                             // typed access to state boundaries

// Wrong: dialing the service/state gRPC address and calling raw RPCs
```

### Use Generated Serializers and Deserializers

```go
// Correct: use the generated helper
config, err := mypkg.ConfigFromBytes(data)
bytes, err := mypkg.ConfigToJSON(config)

// Wrong: json.Unmarshal(&config, data) — bypasses aliases, defaults, error typing
```

### Use Generated Validation

```go
// Correct: validation helpers are package-level functions, not methods
if err := mypkg.ValidateFooRequest(req); err != nil {
    return nil, err
}

// Wrong: manual string length checks, regex matching, etc. for annotated fields
```

### Hand-Written Code Is Allowed Exactly Here

```go
// internal/handler.go — the ONLY hand-written file: implement the generated
// Handler interface, then run the manager.
func NewHandler(ctx context.Context, sm *s2sm.ServiceManager) error {
    return sm.Run(&myServiceImpl{sm: sm})
}
```

Service implementations (`myServiceImpl`) contain business logic. Everything else — transport, auth, state, serialization, health — is generated.

## tacplus.yaml Reference

`tacplus.yaml` is the project-local generation config. It should declare only facts that cannot logically be defined in proto: the target language, generated package/module name, output location, proto source, config composition, and which client transport surfaces this package emits. Service shape belongs in proto annotations: service categories, auth policy, state imports/exports, gRPC client dependencies, REST routes, and store/state behavior are all derived from annotated proto definitions.

Only `language` and `output-dir` are required. `pkg` is commonly set explicitly, but may be derived from the host project when omitted.

### Top-Level Fields

| Field | Type | Required | Description |
|-------|------|----------|-------------|
| `language` | string | Yes | Full-service targets: `go`, `rust`, `java`. Full-client targets: `python`, `typescript`. Lite client targets: `swift`, `csharp`. |
| `output-dir` | string | Yes | Output subdirectory relative to project dir |
| `pkg` | string | No | Canonical package name (Java-style reverse DNS, e.g. `com.example.myservice`). Each segment must be a valid identifier (letters, digits, underscores — no hyphens). Converted to native format per language (see table below). |
| `kind` | string | No | What this project is: `service` (hosts a surface, has a registry identity; a fleet runs it), `client` (calls services, hosts nothing: a CLI, daemon or app), `library` (contracts only: protos other projects build against). A statement of intent the generator and the fleet build can check against the protos. Unset means not stated. |
| `depends` | list | No | Services this one calls, by registry name: `llmproxy` or `weather@1.2` (MAJOR.MINOR, the latest patch; never a patch pin). Each is resolved through the global registry named by `global:` in `proto/registry.yaml` to the repo that declares it, fetched at that version, and merged into this generation, so the `(spec.grpc_s2s_client)` declared in proto has a proto to generate from. Direct dependencies only; the fleet build follows them transitively. |
| `tacplus` | string | No | Minimum tacplus `MAJOR.MINOR` this project needs, e.g. `"2.2"`. A floor, not a pin: MAJOR must match and the running MINOR must be at least this. A patch component is rejected (consumers always run the latest patch of a MAJOR.MINOR). Unset means no floor. An unstamped local build (`0.0.0`) cannot satisfy a floor. |

#### Package Name Conversion

Given a canonical `pkg` (e.g. `com.example.myservice`) and `output-dir` name
(default `model`), the native package/module/crate name is derived per language:

| Language | Rule | Example (`com.example.myservice`, output `model`) |
|----------|------|---------------------------------------------------|
| java | `pkg.output` | `com.example.myservice.model` |
| go | reverse TLD to host, `/`-join rest, append output | `example.com/myservice/model` |
| rust | last segment + `-` + output | `myservice-model` |
| typescript | last segment + `-` + output | `myservice-model` |
| python | last segment + `_` + output | `myservice_model` |
| swift | PascalCase(last segment) + PascalCase(output) | `MyserviceModel` |
| csharp | PascalCase(last segment) + PascalCase(output) | `MyserviceModel` |

Swift and C# use the same PascalCase folding: segments split on `-`, `_`, and
`.` are title-cased and concatenated. This means distinct canonical packages
that differ only in segments before the last (e.g. `com.a.identity` vs
`com.b.identity`) produce **the same** native name for rust/ts/python/swift/csharp.
Proto package names must be globally unique; choose last segments that are
unique across the system to avoid collisions in these languages.
| `src` | string | No | Primary proto source — local path or git URL. No default — must be supplied via `--src` or `tacplus.yaml`. In a GitLab CI job an `https://` URL on `CI_SERVER_HOST` is fetched with `CI_JOB_TOKEN`; no other host receives a credential. |
| `layer` | string | No | Layer name of `src` (e.g. `app`). Carried as `source` on every `registry.json` service and entitlement grant whose package comes from that tree. Not derived from the path, so a local checkout and a git URL label the same tree the same way. |
| `sources` | list | No | Additional proto sources merged with `src` into one generation (e.g. a shared base plus a reusable service's protos). Each entry is a path/URL string, or a `{src: <path/URL>, layer: <name>}` mapping to name its layer. All sources form one proto tree; a file at the same path in two sources must be byte-identical (deduplicated; the first source listed keeps the file's layer) or it is a hard error, and `dependencies.yaml` is merged across sources (conflicting pins error). Repeatable `--src` on the CLI overrides `src`+`sources` and its sources carry no layer. |
| `import` | string | No | Path to base config to import (resolved relative to this file) |

### Client Transport Surfaces

Client transport surfaces are a function of the proto graph, not YAML config.
Tacplus generates the surface for a declared client dependency; there is **no**
`clients.*.enabled` switch (it is obsolete and rejected — see the note below).

Proto declares the dependency:

- `option (spec.grpc_c2s_client) = {service: "pkg.Service"};` → a C2S
  (native gRPC) client manager (`c2sm`).
- `option (spec.grpc_w2s_client) = {service: "pkg.Service"};` → a W2S
  (gRPC-over-REST / web) client manager (`w2sm`).
- a `service X { option (spec.service_c2d) = {...} }` in the package → a C2D
  (client-to-local-daemon) client manager (`c2dm`).

If a dependency is not declared, no manager for that surface is emitted. C2S and
W2S are distinct surfaces from distinct declarations (they are not merged); W2S
is the runtime web-transport alternative to C2S, and the application chooses
which client to use at runtime.

Language targets do not all support the same surface set:

- Full-service targets (`go`, `rust`, `java`) generate service runtimes and any
  declared C2S/W2S/C2D client surfaces.
- Full-client targets (`python`, `typescript`) generate C2S, W2S, C2D, and REST
  *client* surfaces. Service-side output — S2S clients, server wrappers,
  ServiceManager runtime, EventBus subscriber/publisher runtime, health runtime,
  SMB runtime, service state, or service stores — is rejected loudly.
- Lite client targets (`swift`, `csharp`) generate C2D, C2S, and W2S client
  surfaces. Swift's W2S carries unary methods over HTTP/JSON and
  server-streaming methods over SSE (as an `AsyncThrowingStream`, with no
  deadline — cancel the enclosing `Task` to end it). C#'s W2S is unary-only.
  A streaming method the target cannot carry — client-streaming and bidi for
  Swift, which the gateway serves over WebSocket, and every streaming method
  for C# — is emitted as a **compile-time-unavailable stub**, not omitted, so a
  mixed unary+streaming service still produces a compilable client and no
  declared method silently disappears. Use the Go/Java/Rust W2S client for
  those. Unlike the full-client tier they currently emit no client-side request
  validation and no default request deadline. Any service-side surface is
  rejected loudly.

Full-service targets generate a `c2dm` manager for services marked with
`(spec.service_c2d)`, with typed gRPC clients over local daemon IPC. Go and Rust
dial a Unix-domain socket. Java accepts a caller-supplied local-daemon
`ManagedChannel` so the embedding app chooses the local IPC adapter.

Swift and C# emit lite client packages that include a C2D surface: Swift emits a
SwiftPM package with a Unix-domain socket `C2DClient` helper, while C# emits a
.NET package that defaults to named pipes on Windows and Unix-domain sockets
elsewhere. They also emit C2S and W2S client surfaces (Swift's W2S adds server-streaming
over SSE; C#'s is unary-only). Python
and TypeScript emit a C2D client-side surface for `(spec.service_c2d)` services,
alongside their C2S/W2S/REST client surfaces.

W2S is a full client surface, not a REST-only subset. Unary RPCs use HTTP/REST,
server-streaming RPCs use SSE, and client-streaming or bidirectional RPCs use
WebSockets. Tacplus surfaces blocked or timed-out transports as errors; polling
fallback is application behavior.

The obsolete `clients.c2s/w2s/c2d.enabled` YAML block is **rejected** with a
config error. Two builds of the same proto graph, service identity, language, and
package name produce the same surfaces regardless of local build settings —
declare client dependencies in proto, not in `tacplus.yaml`.

### How `pkg` Becomes A Native Package Name

`pkg` is a canonical reverse-DNS name (`com.example.identity`). Each target
language renders it differently, with the `output-dir` name appended as the
generated-model segment (`model` below):

| Language | Transform | `com.example.identity` → |
|---|---|---|
| java | canonical + `.` + output name | `com.example.identity.model` |
| go | TLD and host swapped, rest joined with `/` | `example.com/identity/model` |
| rust, typescript | **last segment** + `-` + output name | `identity-model` |
| python | **last segment** + `_` + output name | `identity_model` |
| swift, csharp | **last segment**, PascalCased, + PascalCased output name | `IdentityModel` |

Only java and go carry the whole canonical name. The other five keep the last
segment alone, and swift/csharp additionally fold `-`, `_` and `.` away, so
`com.example.identity`, `com.other.identity` and `com.other.ident_ity` all render
as the same swift module. tacplus cannot detect that: one build sees one `pkg`.
Distinct services must therefore differ in the LAST segment of `pkg`, not only in
its prefix — the D-5 convention that proto package names are globally unique
applies to that segment.

### Config Composition

Configs can import a base file and override specific fields:

```yaml
# tacplus-base.yaml
language: go
src: https://gitlab.com/org/proto.git
pkg: com.example.myservice
output-dir: tacplus

# tacplus.yaml
import: tacplus-base.yaml
pkg: com.example.myservice.ci
```

Multiple config files via CLI:

```bash
tacplus build -c tacplus-base.yaml -c tacplus-overrides.yaml
```

Merge rules:

- **Strings**: overlay wins if non-empty
- **Lists**: overlay replaces entirely if non-empty

### CLI Flag Equivalents

| YAML Key | CLI Flag |
|----------|----------|
| `src` | `--src` |

CLI flags override YAML values when both are specified.

## Service Registry

Service and vservice ids are field numbers in the generated `TokenEntitlements`
message and values of the `ServiceName` enum, so they must be unique across every
proto repo that may be composed into one kernel. `registry.yaml` at a proto root
records them. Three shapes exist:

- **An authority** declares `scope: global` or `scope: private` and allocates ids.
  The global registry (`github.com/tacplus-dev/registry`) is the one place ids that
  must be globally unique come from; it allocates 101-1023. A private registry is
  one a fleet owner keeps for services that will only ever live in fleets they
  control; it allocates 1024-2047. Both are append-only: ids are never reused or
  renumbered. Each entry names the service's **contract**, the repo that holds its
  proto. That repo may be public, shared with a partner, or private: the registry
  decides ids, not who may read what. Register from a checkout of the authority:

  ```bash
  tacplus registry register NAME --kind service --contract <proto repo URL> --visibility public --proto-dir .
  ```

- **A lock** is a per-proto-repo `registry.yaml` that names its authorities in order:

  ```yaml
  registries:
      - https://github.com/tacplus-dev/registry.git
      - https://gitlab.com/acme/registry.git
  services:
      - name: doppelganger
        id: 101
  ```

  `tacplus registry --proto-dir .` unions the authorities (a name or an id in two of
  them is an error, never a precedence call), syncs the lock for every service
  declared in the tree, and refuses to allocate or renumber. A declared service in
  no authority is an error naming the registration step. Builds read only the lock,
  so generation is reproducible offline.

- **A legacy per-repo registry** has neither `scope:` nor `registries:` and keeps the
  original allocation (1-99 with an optional `id_min` floor), unchanged.

Ids 1-99 are frozen wherever their service sits; 100 is reserved. The registry
never pins versions: a fleet's manifest pins what that fleet runs, and a service's
`depends` names the oldest MAJOR.MINOR of a dependency it was built against. Which
implementation of a service a fleet runs is the fleet manifest's choice; the
registry's contract field only says where the proto lives, so a fleet may run its
own implementation of, say, kernel under the same name and id.

| Command | Purpose |
|---------|---------|
| `tacplus build` | Generate proto types and services for a single language |
| `tacplus validate` | Validate proto files |
| `tacplus verify` | Run formal verification on Rust or Java code |
| `tacplus registry` | Update the service / vservice / trait registry from proto definitions |
| `tacplus fleet build` | Build a fleet from a deployment repo's `fleet.yaml`: resolve every service's implementation, check ids and dependencies against the registries, merge the protos, run the whole-fleet checks, write `fleet.lock` (see [Fleet Build](#fleet-build)) |
| `tacplus upgrade` | Upgrade tacplus to the latest patch release |
| `tacplus version` | Print the version and build information |

```bash

# Layer multiple configs (later files override earlier)
tacplus build -c tacplus-base.yaml -c tacplus-overrides.yaml

go generate ./...
```

## Annotation Reference

RPC naming is governed: every RPC is `Verb<Noun>` against a closed verb
registry with fold rules (Search/Query→List, New/Add→Create,
…). The authored compiler dictionary lives at
`pkg/internal/common/verbs/registry.json`; the registry, pattern taxonomy, and
fold test are documented in [API.md → RPC Patterns And Verbs](API.md). Name new
RPCs canonically; the classifier rejects non-canonical names during descriptor
parsing.

### Field Constraint Annotations

| Annotation | What It Validates |
|------------|-------------------|
| `assert_required` | Non-zero value (scalars), non-empty (strings/repeated) |
| `assert_ipaddr_type` | IPv4, IPv6, subnet mask, CIDR network |
| `assert_net_port` | Valid TCP/UDP port (1-65535) |
| `assert_url` | HTTP, HTTPS, or either |
| `assert_email` | Email address format |
| `assert_fqdn` | Fully qualified domain name |
| `assert_host` | IP address OR FQDN |
| `assert_listen_addr` | host:port format |
| `assert_base64` | Valid base64 encoding |
| `assert_enc_type` | RSA/EC/Ed25519 key or X.509 cert in PEM |
| `assert_semver` | Semantic version (e.g., "1.2.3") |
| `assert_duration` | Positive or non-negative duration |
| `assert_file_path` | Absolute, relative, or either |
| `assert_enum_defined` | Enum is not the zero/unspecified value |
| `assert_max_size` | Maximum byte size for string/bytes (default 32KB) or element count for repeated/map (runtime default 1024; user protos should set explicit bounds) |
| `assert_gt` / `assert_ge` / `assert_lt` / `assert_le` | Numeric comparisons |
| `assert_numeric` | Complex numeric constraints (in, not_in, multiple_of) |
| `assert_float` | Float constraints with epsilon tolerance |
| `assert_sql` | Valid SQL statement of permitted type (SELECT, etc.), rejects injection patterns |
| `assert_invariant` | Formal invariant (constrains a `#[kani::proof]` harness via `kani::assume()` in Rust, a JBMC harness via `CProver.assume()` in Java) |
| `assert_min_size` | Minimum byte length (string/bytes) or element count (repeated/map) |

### gRPC Client Dependency Annotations

These are **file-level** options declared once per proto file. Proto package names are globally unique (a gRPC requirement), so no file path is needed — tacplus resolves the package name to its proto file at build time.

```protobuf
// S2S: this service calls identity.Mint (service-to-service, uses service credentials)
option (spec.grpc_s2s_client) = {service: "identity.Mint"};

// Client-facing service dependency. tacplus.yaml selects C2S, W2S, or both.
option (spec.grpc_c2s_client) = {service: "gateway.TokenMint"};

// Older transport-named spelling, also treated as a client-facing dependency.
option (spec.grpc_w2s_client) = {service: "dashboard.Dashboard"};
```

Multiple clients of the same type can be declared with repeated options:

```protobuf
option (spec.grpc_s2s_client) = {service: "identity.Mint"};
option (spec.grpc_s2s_client) = {service: "eventbus.Admin"};
```

tacplus generates typed client wrappers for each declared dependency and makes them available via the service manager (`sm.Grpc().Clients().<Host>().<Service>Client()` in Go; in Rust use `sm.s2s().<host>().<service>_client()` from an S2S service, or `sm.grpc().<host>().<service>_client()` from a c2s/w2s/c2d client).

### Local Daemon Services

Services marked with `(spec.service_c2d) = {socket_path: "/run/mydaemon.sock"};` are local daemon RPC surfaces. `socket_path` is required — there is no default (a shared default would collide between daemons on the same host).
When a package's proto graph declares in-scope `(spec.service_c2d)` services,
full-service targets emit a `c2dm` manager and client-only targets emit their
language-specific C2D helpers for those services (no YAML flag is involved). C2D
clients do not attach generated bearer tokens; the local IPC boundary is the
operating-system transport and its permissions.

### Serialization Annotations

| Annotation | Effect |
|------------|--------|
| `json_key` | Override JSON output key (when proto field was renamed) |
| `json_aliases` | Additional keys accepted during JSON deserialization |
| `default_string` / `default_int` / etc. | Default values generated per language |
| `string_const` / `int_const` / etc. | Constants generated at file level |

### Enum Annotations

| Annotation | Effect |
|------------|--------|
| `json_return_value` | Override JSON representation of an enum value |

## Conditional Requirements

Fields can be conditionally required based on sibling field values:

```protobuf
// Required when disable_tls == false
string cert_path = 5 [(spec.required_if_false) = "disable_tls"];

// Required when action == "ACTION_REDIRECT"
string redirect_url = 3 [(spec.required_if_eq) = {field: "action", value: "ACTION_REDIRECT"}];
```

---

## Formal Verification Annotations

A field can carry a formal invariant via `(spec.assert_invariant)`, which is
emitted into a generated proof harness:

```protobuf
string token = 1 [(spec.assert_invariant) = "self.ttl > 0 && self.ttl <= 86400"];
```

In Rust the harness is a `#[kani::proof]` that constrains the field with
`kani::assume(...)`; in Java it is a JBMC harness that constrains it with
`CProver.assume(...)`. The `tacplus verify` command runs these proofs (Rust or
Java only).

> `(spec.proof_requires)` / `(spec.proof_ensures)` exist and are parsed, but no
> generator consumes them yet — they emit nothing today.

---

## REST Method Control

RPC methods can declare additional HTTP methods beyond the implicit POST:

```protobuf
rpc GetConfig(GetConfigRequest) returns (Config) {
  option (spec.rest_method) = {methods: [REST_METHOD_GET]};
  option (spec.rest_path) = ".well-known/openid-configuration";
}
```

`rest_path` creates an alias REST route in addition to the convention path. Available methods: `GET`, `PATCH`, `PUT`, `DELETE`.

A c2s RPC whose REST route is a browser form target, such as an identity
provider's `form_post` callback, declares `rest_browser`:

```protobuf
rpc BrokerFormPostCallback(FormPostCallbackRequest) returns (FormPostCallbackResponse) {
  option (spec.rest_browser) = {form_body: true, redirect_field: "redirect_url"};
}
```

- `form_body` makes the route accept an `application/x-www-form-urlencoded`
  body as well as JSON. Each pair becomes a string value keyed by proto field
  name. A key sent twice gets a 400.
- `redirect_field` names a singular string field of the response. The route
  answers `303 See Other` with `Location` set to that field and
  `Cache-Control: no-store`, instead of JSON.

Both are emitted into the generated route table (Rust
`rest_dispatch::RouteInfo` `form_body` / `redirect_field`, Go
`restdispatch.RouteInfo` `FormBody` / `RedirectField`, Java
`RestDispatch.RouteInfo` `formBody` / `redirectField`; the redirect field is
spelled as its proto3 JSON name in all three) and carried out by its
`form_body_to_json` and `redirect_response` (Rust), `FormBodyToJSON` and
`RedirectResponse` (Go) or `formBodyToJson` and `redirectResponse` (Java),
which a REST host calls. Generation refuses the option on a streaming RPC, on
an RPC with no c2s REST route, and when `redirect_field` is missing from the
response or is not a singular string.
